div.p: KEATING'S COUGH LOZENGES "94. Commercial Road, Peckham, July 12. 1889. " Dear Sir,—l am a poor hand at expressing my feelings, but! should like to thank you. Your lozenges have done wonders in relieving my terrible cough. Since I had the operation of ' Tracheotomy ' (the same as the late Emperor of Germany, and unlike him, thank God, I am still alive) per- formed at St. Bartholomew's Hospital, no one could possP.ly have had a more violent cough ; it was so bad at times that it quite exhausted me. The mucus, which was very copious and hard, has been softened, and I have been able to get rid of it without difficulty.—l am. sir, yours truly, J. HILL. - MEDICAL NOTE. The above speaks for itself. From strict inquiry it appears the benefit from using Keating's Cough Lozenges is under- stated. The operation was a specially severe one, and was performed by the specialist, Dr. H. T. Butlin, of St. Bartho- lomew's Hospital. Since the operation the only means of relief is the use of these Lozenges. So successful are they that one affords immediate benefit, although from the nature of the case the throat irritation is intense. UNRIVALLED TESTIMONY. Under date Sept. 8, 1891, Mr. Hill writes: " I should long since have been dead, but for your Lozenges—They are iv,rt;. their weight in gold. I will gladly see and tell anyone what a splendid cough remedy they are:" Keating's Lozenges are sold in tins, is. 11d. each. The un- fivalled semedy for COUGHS,HOAUSENESS, and THROAT TROUBLES.

Mr. Gladstone will open a reading and recreation room at Bebington, Chester, on the 21st inst. The builaing has been provided by Messrs. Lever Brothers for their employ6s. Mr. Gladstone will be the guest of Mr. Edward Evans, Spital Old Hall, Cheshire, President of the Wirral Division of Cheshire Liberal Association.

According to the " Lancet," the use of Koch's patent tuberculin has been to a great extent given up. There are, however, a few doctors who still continue to administer it from a desite "to give it a fair trial" and to know more of its operations. Nice doctors these! For the safety of the public, it would be better if their names were, published, perhaps with a table appended showing the rate of mortality among their patients.

Mr. Goschen's finance is having a warm time of it. Sir William Harcourt gives it a .column and a half in the morning papers., Mr. Labouchere gives it three columns in "Truth," and Mr. Seale-Hayne has a turn at it in a lengthy-letter to Mr. Goschen him- self. It is just as well that prominent Liberals are speaking out plainly on this squestion,for if there is one thing that the .discussion has made clear it is this,that Mr. Gosch en's surpluses and otlerdluancial achievements have been chiefly accomplished by drawing bills on futurity which the next Chancellor of the Exchequer will have to meet.

The laussiati • Government seems to be dealing with the famine in the most peddling fashion. The last idea is to dock the diet of the prisoners in the goals, in order to increase the available food. In other words, Peter is to be starved to feed Paul. We shall hear next that a Special famine tax is to be levied on the exiles in Siberia. Where are the pro- ceeds of the last Russian loan, the success of which has been trumpeted so loudly'? Why, doesn't the Czar's Government reduce its military expenditure, , and spend a few millions on importing grain from America, where there is enough, and .to spare?

Mr. Chamberlain ha a promised to visit Salisbury. This visit is to be made at the invitation of the local Tories. Its acceptance was .conveyed by the Earl of Pembroke; and made known at a Tory meet- ing by Earl Nelson. Singularly enough these, two noblemen were locally the most vigorous in their 'denunciation of the notable speech which Mr. Chamberlain delivered at Ironbridge, in, Wiltshire, in October, 1885, in which he had laid it down that the local authorities should have ,power to take land by compulsion at a fair pride for every public pur- pose. It was in this speech also that 'Mr. Goschen was described .as the skeleton of the feast, and Mr. Chamberlain's host on that occasion was Mr: aosclien's present critic, Mr. Fuller, MX.

The Hon Jahn Ballance,.Premier of. New Zealand, who according to the cable has declared himself In favor of giving a . "full and fair trial" to General Booth's emigration project, Is, a native of the county Antrita, Ireland, and is now in his•s2nd year. Soon .after obtaining his majority he crossed", over to England and acted for several years aS commercial traveller for a Birmingham house. On einigrEtting to New Zealand, he started a nevvspapet and developed into a successful journalist. Be has been in the New. Zealand Parliament since'lB7s. He first took Wilco in 1878 aS Treasurer in the Ministry of Sir George Grey, the Radical leader,who recently carried "one man one vote" through the New 'Zealand Parliament. The sympathetic adh,,sion of Mr. Ballance is the greatest conquest that •General Booth has made during his colonial tour up to date.

The :municipal elections are splendid. The, Liberal gains total up to 59. More than half these gains have taken place intoroughsmow-represented in Parliament by Unionists. No one,can fail to see. the handwriting on the wall here. It means that at the corning general election the Tories will be, ousted from these boroughs. We can make this prophecy all the more confidently when we take, into account the results of the municipal elections during the last five years. This year has not . been, exceptional. Liberals'have not snatched victories by side issues. They have been steadily gaining. in 1887 the'Liberal gain was .18 seats; in 1688 it was 35 seats:; next year the Liberals captured :84 seats, in 1890 their gain was 45, which, added te this year's results, makes a total Liberal gain in five years of 241 seats. -This is an element of political meteoro- logy which 'politicians cannot neglect.

Wales will .figure in this year's Lord Mayor's. Show in a way it has probably never done before. Alderman Evans • has determined to emphasise his nationality by making the procession on the 9th as Welsh in its character as possible. Three of the five triumphal cdrs will be illustrative of the his- tory of Wales and of Welsh industries. ,One car. will give a representation of Edward I. bestowing Wales as a ." principality " upon his son. In a second .car an attempt will be made .to set forth the costumes of the Welsh bards in the .minstrel days,. and the peculiar apparel yet to be seen in some of the rural parts of Wales. The third car is to be emblematical of the industries of Wales. A num- ber of miners from South Wales, armed witt the 'appliances of their craft, are to be engaged for the occasion. The only thing .wanting to crown the. proceediwYs is that the Lord AI ayor shall arrange to have a Wail speech delivered at the .Guildlaall ban- quet.

Another unqualified medical practitioner has made his appearance in the Court of the Birming- ham Coroner. The inquiry related to the cause of death of a lad whom he had attended. His treat- ment appears to have been decidedly peculiar. The lad was suffering from bronchitis, pleurisy,. and congestion of the liver, and the diet prescribed for him included twenty ounces of nuts and three ounces of 'fig,s and Brazil nut kernels to only six ounces of bread. This mixture was described by a medical witness as" very good for a monkey." The, mother of the deceased declared that she was 'under the belief that her doctor was "a physician," but when asked" Why ? " she could only answer, ". because the lady who lives next door to me re- commended him, and said that if any one could cure my son he could." On examining the remark- able dietary already quoted, it was found that be appended to his signature the letters" M.D. Cont." As he explained that his diploma had been granted at Bonn," Cont." may be assumed to mean Contin- ental. It is fair to add that the inquiry terminated in a verdict of " death from natural causes."

Several readers of " Truth " have asked my opinion about the following advertiwiment, which has appeared lately in the "Times," "Daily Tele- graph," "Black and White," and other papers— A woman of title, moving in the best society, will receive a young lady into her house as a friend. Terms, £2,000 per annum. Any introduction of such will be handsomely acknowledged. Patrician, 13,720, &c. This advertisement, I understand, emanates in- directly from the widow of a baronet, who is, I am assured, in a position to offer the social advantages which the advertisement implies. I should not; therefore, feel justified in warning any would-be debutante, or her parents, against dealing with this latter-day "Pat.rieian," if they think any amount of "the first society" worth board and lodging at .£2,000 a year. But I feel fully justified in warning the Patrician herself that this is a very risky game, that her proceedings are not unknown, and that if she should come to terms with any young lady "friend," as the result of this advertisement, she will not be much longer "moving in the first society.'

div.head: EXAMINER, SAT URDA Y, NOVEMBER 7, 1891
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAT URDA Y, NOVEMBER 7, 1891
STORIEB OF SMUGGLING.

The town of Poole,in Dorset shire, was a favourite resort of smugglers. One day an officer of the In- land Revenue was riding down a quiet country lane in the vicinity-of the town, when he espied a man carrying a keg,of spirits on his shoulder. Ile called out to the man to halt, and inquired what- he was doing. Tini inin hung his head for anion-lent, but quickly looked up into the officer's faqq, and asked if he was the lieutenant.. Being answered in the affirmative, the man said he was told by one of the Custom House men to carry the keg of spiritate him, and-that, as the day was so warm, he would hand it over to him. Putting a shilling into the man's hand, the officer told him to take the keg to his house, as, being on horseback, be could pot man- age it himself. The official then rode off. On re- turning home he was startled to find that he had-let the smuggler escape, and also given hiina shil- ling to carry the keg of spirits to his ,own den. It is said that at one time a large quantity of contra- band goods used to reach a certain town,but by what -means could not be ascertained by the authorities. On one occasion an officer of the Customs was in an out-of-the-way-place on the outskirts of the town, when he saw a boy hugging along a small barrel of spirits. He quickly followed, net .only expecting to catch the culprit, but also to obtain a clue to the rest of the gang. By this time the .boy had turned round the end of a barn, standing on a high band out of sight of the officer. • The latter, however,soon came up, and was astonished to had what appeared to him to be a different boy altogether to the one -he had first seen. Ile inquired of theboy if he had , seen another boy pass that way. The lad said he had not. The bfficer was puzzled, and being sus- picuous of the boy, locked him in the barn, while he instituted a search around. Huscon found out what had become of the spirits. The key had been sent rclling down the bank, its trazdr being very plainly visible. He then returned to the boy with the keg of spirits,•and on making a careful inspection perceived that the lad's coat and hat had two faces, that when the boy got round the corner of the barn, he had simply turned his coat and hat inside out, , thus deceiving him.. The boy seeing that he was found out, began to sob bitterly, and promised never so do such a thing again. Thinking that he might be able to 'find out the gang of smugglers, the official gave the boy the keys of his cellar, and told him to take the keg to his house and give it to is housekeeper, at the same time giving minute details as to where it had to be placed. The boy marched off with his load, while the revenue (pincer. continued his search. This proving unsuccessful, he went home. On arriving at his domicile he asked his housekeeper for the keg of spirits which he had sent. She answered that she had received none, but that a boy had come with the keys •of the cellar, and said that he was sent for a barrel of spirits; describing exactly where it was to be found, and that she had given it to him. Urns the official of the Inland Revenue , not only lost the keg of spirits that he had taken 'rom the boy, but also another from his own cellar.

CILARGE OF ALLOWING GAMING ON - LICENSED PREMISES. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Fran- comb), Alderman Wright, Mr. E. M. Crosfield, and John Allen- of the Pelican Inn, Butter- market-.st., was charged with allowing gaming to be carried on on his premises on the 28th 411 t. P.S. Cox, said about five minutes past threein the morn- ing of the.datementioned, P.C. Meacock informed him that there was some card playing going on at the defendant's house. Witness and P.C. Sheehy stood outside the window, and saw twelve games .played between a quarter past three and ten min- utes to four, and heard money thrown on the table time after time. The defendant at ten minutes to. four let a man and his wife out of the house, and witness called his attention to the time, and asked him why he was allowing card playing for money at that time. He said some friends had just been having a bit of supper with him. .0n the table there were bread and cheese and some glasses, one containing beer, the others nothing.—Mr. Browne, who appeared for the defence, admitted that all that Inspector . Cox said was true and tech- nically an offence had been .committed, bunt morally was it an offence ? That was the question. Mr. Allen invited several friends of his, licensed , victuallers, including Mr. Brimelow' secretaiy of the local Licensed Victuallers' Association, to have-a rne supper with him, as he wished to confer with them as to what course they should take at the quarterly meeting of the association, and after Supper they had some games of" nap". Mr, Thomas Critchley, of the Higher Angel Inn, one of those who went, told the constablg on the beat where he was going. No one was there' except licensed" victuallers and their wives, and was, (Mr. Browne) did not think one of the company knew that it was an offence toplay-" nap" for money in a Public-house after closing hours, And he had advised his client it was not, being 'under.that impres- sion, but he had found a case-exactly on all fours with the present, in which,, in 1878, it had been decided that this was an offence. However, it ;did seem hard that a ' licensed victualler, who was a householder, shquld not. have the right of a private citiien in his • own house and ask a few friends to have a friendly game at cards. What harm Could there be in that The Act was never intended to apply to such 'things. In Liverpool there Was t license for dancing—as he hoped wpuld soon be the case in Warrington, and . the landlady of a.public- house in Liverpool was S-unmioned,before the stipendiary magistrate there for permitting two little girls, her own children, to dance in the 'house. The magistrate held that the case was an offence.legally, not morally at all, and dismissed the case. Had Mr. Allen been .playing cards for money with his own wife only, he would have been liable to be convicted.. Mr. Browne remarked that had Mr. Allen informed the Chief Constable that he was going to have a few friends at his house on'the night in question, nothing probably would have been heard of ,this case; and promised that if the Bench would, dismiss it, his clients would pay costs and not repeat the offence. ,He observed, amidst sunelaughter; that.he had himself played-in licensed.prernis4 in Warrington a 'few years ago, not knowing there was any offence, and,he believed the Deputy Magistrates' Clerk .was with him.—The Deputy Magistrates' Clerk denied thatthis was so.—The Bench dismissed the case on payment of costs.
YES, BUT HIS PIPE WAS A SOLACE
ONLY.

"Dr. Parr smoked in season and out of season, and .his pipe was as long as his wig was„curly.; and, finally, Milton on the maturity of his age rarely retired to rest 'without a pipe of tobacco and a glass of water. The nicotian weed may have cantled the author of Para., disc Lost' for his blindness even it'solaced 'Carlyle iti his dyspepsia."

So says the London Daitii Telcyreph, editorially, in its 'issue of August 17th, 1891. Probably there is no country on earth in which an apology for the use of tobacco is so little called for as in England, where the pipe stern is stuck in the mouth of every Other man you meet, and when what the early •Spaniards c3ll herpg, seuictq is almost as•meat and drink to millions. And the T'etegraph does not apologise ,for it. It simply comments on the styles of .pipes.ltra-learned and entertaining way. '

But we remember that while tobaeco may have splaced Carlyle in his dyspepsia it was not mighty to save the Scotch philosopher from the malady that aggravated his peppery, temper by day, ,and gave him the nightmare to ride hi 'hours of darkness. And there are hosts of other men in the same predicament, althOuih not sufficiently well known to attract public sympathy. Yet they suffer just as much as did the man who wrote Sartor Resart us.

Here is one—" One of us "—as the French said of Rossini when they buried him. Ten years ago, .Mr. Richard 'Wickham Meredith, of Tomarton, Gloucestershire, heoan to -realize that good health is as unstable as all our other blessings. With- out any reason that he could apprehend his appetite fell away and his bounteous farmer's table lost its attractions for him. As a natural result his spirits and energy de- clined with the lack of bodily nourishment. This is the law for all animal life. He wiz° can't eat can't work or enjoy himself. We have all had mare or less experience of that some time or other.

In speaking on the subject in April, .891, Mr. Meredith said, "What little I did eat pained me. The food lay on. my stomach without warmth or motion,and the pain. in my back and chest appeared to pass to and fro through my body. I had a foul taste in the mouth, and an.offen- ve slime" covered my mouth and adhered to l!my teeth. With this there was a senqe of tightness or constriction across the chest,as if I was under some invisible pressure from about me. I was greatly troubled with flatulency and felt so dull, tired and stupid, that Iwould sit all day long, and as unfit for work of any kind."

. . This statb of things, we should explain, was caused by the fermentation of the food in the stomach. Diges- tion having almOst wholly ceased, the food turned sour and emitted a poisonous gas, as it would if stood in a, ,tub under the rays Of the summer sun, .and this soon pervaded all parts of the body to which it was possible for it .to gain access, thus causing headache, wake- fulness, and various - forms of nervous weakness and

prostration. ' But to return to Mr. Meredith, who further says : " In time I got so bad I felt as though. I should be as well dead as alive. Then'followed two years of this ; a time a man passes through in pain and looks back upon with sadness and disgust. :During these two years I had a physician attending me. His treatment, however,had rno effect. In 1883. a gentleman of the neighbourhood spoke so favourably and hopefully of Mother Seigel's Syrup that I decided to test its virtues (if it had any) as a last resort. One bottle brought about a welcome relief and four more a cure. Years have passed ; the cure seems permanent. Since then I have been as strong as ever I was in my life; able to go about my farm and do any kind of work with ease. I sincerely believe that had I not used Mother Seigle's Syrup when I did I should have ended my days Oefore this." Very likely:; very likely indeed ; for so multitudes are constantly doing. If, the epitaphs told „ the truth at least half of them would contain this sepulchral line : "Died of Indigestion and Dyspepsia." As it is, they are either silent on the point or give the cause of death the name of one of dysptpsia's many symptoms.
Thus we perceive that even if Carlyle's pipe was a salace to him in his lyspepsia Seigel's Syrup would have served him in better stead—it would have cztred him.
THE CONTEST AT CORK.

The nominationof candidates for the seats now vacant at Cork took place on Tuesday. Mr. John Redmond (Parnellite), Mr_ Martin Flavin (Anti-Parnellite), and Captain Sarsfield ',Unionist), were nominated. In giving on Tiiesday what he described as an exact narrative of the iloulogne negotiations, Mr. W. O'Brien, M. P. ,inti mated tat very great difficulty was experienced in coming to terois with Mr. Parnell, but that ultimately the heads of an agreement were accepted which provided that in the event of Mr. Gladstone giving certain assur- ances to Mr. M'Carthy on the Irish land and police qu2s- dons Mr. Parnel: would retire from the leadership. The retirement, as could be-proved by letters of Mr. Parnell's colleagues, wasintended to be a real retirement. Under the agreement Mr. Dillon was to be appointed leader. He, however, iaised objections, which caused the settle- ment of the matter to be deferred, and in the meantime Mr. Parnell wrote backing out of the arrangement, the reason he gaNe for taking this course being that he heard certain rutneors as to Liberal policy and as to the re- tention of he Irish members at Westminster. Mr. O'Brien addA that he did not enter Galway Goal until every effoic at conciliation had failed, and the view taken by tie men who were now attacking him and his friends wa3 sufficiently proved by the fact that even in February ast they were longing for the terms offered by , the Anti-larnellites to be accepted. Several men have been treated in the infirmary for injuries received on Wedoesday night in a conflict betweenthe Parnellities and anti-Parnellities, the pro- cession 3f the former attacking the latter. Messrs, William O'Brien, Condon, and Gilhooly, members of Parliaoent, were struck by stones, but not hurt. The drivel of their car was injured badly.

div.head: CHEMICAL WOILKERS AND THE EIGHT
div.p: CHEMICAL WOILKERS AND THE EIGHT
HOURS DAY.

The chemical workers of St. Helens and district held a demonstration in favour' of the eight hours day on Sunday afternoon. The proceedings com- menced with a procession round the town, headed by.the idnes ,St. Mary's •brass band. k public meeting was afterwards'held in the Town Hall. and there was a crowded attendance. Mr. P. J. King, president of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union, occupied the chair, and:was supported by Mr. Chisholm .Robertson, .of Glasgow, Labour can- didate 'for Stirlinf.Y.,slare.;- -Mr. E. M‘Hugh, of the Dockers' 'Union, Liverpool; Councillor R. Hunter, Mr. '6lover, and other local labour lenders. The Chairman said they were met not for political or party purposes, but as chemical and copper workers to give one solid expression of opinion in favour of tbe eight hours day. He declared thatif they could not have that eight hours day by legislative enactment they would take it•thernselves: '<Cheers.) He advocated amalgama- tion with the Dockers' Union, so. that they might be better able to strike a strong and successful blow for the benefit of the working-classes. Mr. Chisholm Robertson, in the course of a vigorous 'address, referred to the degradwion and poverty 'existing amongst the working classes of the country, and said he regarded the two politizal.,parties as frauds on the intel- ligence of working-men. They could not depend on getting justice from either of the political parties, and if they would be free they must work for themselves, they must join their organisations, must stand behind their leaders and indicate to each and every party that as working-men they had a ,price and that price was the eight hours day. (Applause.) He urged that the work- ing classes of the country should -found a strong labour- -party apart from politics, and they should die, if neces- sary, in the attempt to secure the great reform they needed, (Cheers.) ' Mr. E. M‘Hugh, of Liverpool, who was well received, said he only knew and recognised two. parties—the men 'who produced the wealth of the nation, and those who did nothing at all but consume the wealth. He strongly denounced the wealth consumers, and said that if a poor starving man stole a threepenny bit. or a loaf of bread he was sent to prison, but if a man was only" fly" enough to steal half a million he was sent to Parliament to make laws for the country. He contended that the timehad now come when workingmen • had as much right to say how much work they would do as the employers' had to say how much wages they Ought to get. (Applause.) Mr. Healy (a chemical worker) pro- posed "That this great meeting of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union, and iother.wealth producers of St. Helens. proclaims its solemn determination to redouble their efforts, and to consolidate our trade and labour unions, so that we may speedily secure the'enact- ment by Parliament of an eight hours day, and that if unable to obtain it by legislative enactment we are determined to go in and win this act of •justice for our- selves." Mr. P. Callaghan seconded the resolution, which after a few remarks from Mr. King, was then put and carried mien imously. 'Votes of •thanks closed the proceedings.
GLADRONE'S ADVICE TO TILE
BRITISH FARMER.

Mr. Gladstone, writing to a Liverpool correspondent. on agricultural ,questions, says :—I hope the Liberal party will always view with sympathy the necessary and invaluable but very arduous .operations of our farmers, even as they showed their sympathy by pass- ing the Agricultural Holdings Act to give them a title to compensation for unexhausted improvements, and the Ground Game Act to save their crops from being. ravaged. As for being told that it was•the malt tax: which bore them down, they in 1880 removed that tax' from the statute book. I trust, he continues, it may please Providence to send a series of better-seasons, and if any rent still requires adjustment, the farmer is, I hope, in a condition to obtain it. But we must never forget that his trade is one requiring much ;more know- ledge, skill, and perseverance than many forms of busi- ness which yield larger returns, that the economical management of his business is an absolute necessity and thrifty living an enormous advantage. I trust he will obtain some degree of benefit from the extension of the small culture, both animal and vegetable. I rejoice to witness the perceptible extension of that cultaire, and you may depend upon it that as the scale of it is ex- tended and the pursuit congolidated the ratet of earn- age will be progressively lowered.

div.head: ON THE STUDY OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY.
div.p: ON THE STUDY OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY.

The situation of man on the globe he inhabits, and. over which he has obtained the control, is in many respects exceedingly remarkable. Compared with its other denizens, he seems, if we regard only his -physical tonstitution; in almost every respect their inferior, and equally unprovided for the supply of his nateral wants, and his defence against the innumerable enemies which surround him. No. other animal passes so large a portion of its exist- ence in a state of absolute helplessness, or falls in old age into such protracted and lamentable imbecility. To no other warm-blooded animal has nature denied that indispensable covering, without _which- the Vicissitudes of a temperate, and the rigours of a cold climate, are equally insupportable ; and to scarcely any has she been so sparing in external weapons, whether for attack or defence. Destitute alike of speed to avoid, and of arms to repel the aggressions of his voracious foes; tenderly 'susceptible of atmospheric influences, and unfitted for the coarse aliments which the earth affords spontaneously, during at least two-thirds of the year, eveu in temperate climates—man, if aban- doned to mere instinct, would be of all creatures the most. destitute and miserable. Distracted,' by terror, and goaded by famine; driven to the most I abject expedients for concealment from his enemies, .and to the .most 'cowardly devices for the seizure and destruction.- of, his nobler,. prey, his existence would he one continued subterfuge or. stratagem; his dwelling would he in the dens of the earth, in . clefts of rocks, or in the hollow of trees; his food worms and the lower reptiles, or such few and crude productions of the sodas his organs could. be brought to assimilate, varied with occasional relics, mangled by more powerful beasts of prey, or con- ',tenined. by their more pampered choice. Remark- able ' only for the absence of those powers and -qualities which obtain for other animals.a. degree of security and respect, he would he disregarded by some; and hunted doww"by others, till after a few . generations his species wOuld become altogether extinet, or, at best, would, be restricted to ,a few -islands in tropical regions, where the warinth of the climate, the paucity of enemies, and the • abundance of -vegetable food, might permit it to

, Yet man is the undisputed lord of the creation. - The strongest and fiercest of his fellow-creatures— the whale, the elephant, the. esgleaand the tiger— are slaughtered by him to supply his most capri- .cions wants, or tamed to do him service, or im- prisoned to .make him sport. The spoils of all nature are in daily requisition for his most common uses, yielded with more or less readiness, or wrested with reluctance from the mine, the forest, the ocean, and the ,air. Such are the first fruits of reason. Were they the only or the principal ones, were the mere acquisition of power over the materials, and the less gifted animals which sur- round us, and the consequent increase of our ex- , ternal comforts, and our means of preservation and sensual enjoyment, the sum of the privileges which the possession of this faculty conferred, we should, after all, have little to plume ourselves upon. But this is so far from being the case that every one who passes. his life intolerable ease and comfert, or rather, whose whole time is not anxiously consumed in providing the absolute necessaries of existence, is conscious. of wants and cravings in which the senses have no part, of a series of pains and pleasures totally distinct in kind from any which the infliction of bodily misery, or the gratification of bodily appetites, has ever afforded him; and if he has experienced these pleasures and these pains in any degree of intensity, he will readily admit them to hold a much higher rank, and to deserve much more attention, than the former class. Inde- pendent of the pleasures of fancy and ithagination, and social converse, man is constituted a speculative being; he contemplates the world, and the objects around him, not with.a passive indifferent gaze, as a set of phenomena in Vihich he has no farther interest than as they affect his immediate situation, and can be rendered subservient to his comfort, but as a system cVsposed with order and design. He :Approves, and feels the highest, admiration for the :harmony of its parts,' the skill and efficiency of its :contrivances. Some of these which he can best trace and understand, he attempts to imitate, and :finds that, to a certain extent, though, rudely and itnperfectly, he can .succeed ; in others, that although he can, .comprehend the nature of the , contrivance, he is totally destitute of all means of imitation; while in others, again, and those evi- xlently the most important, though he sees the effect produced, yet the means by which it is done are :dike beyond his knowledge and his control. Thus he is led to the conception of a power and an in- telligence superror to-le:,,s own, and adequate to the ,production and maintenance of. all that he sees in nature ;--a powea and intelligence to which he may well apply the term infinite, since he not only sees- no actual limit to the instances in which they are enanifested, but' finds, on the contrary, that the farther he iia-luires, and the wider his sphere of observation extends, they continually open upon him in increasing abundance ; and that, as the study of one prepares him to understand' and appreciate :another, refinement follows ,on refinement, wonder on wonder, till his faculties become bewildered in mitniration, and his intellect falls back on itself, in . utter hopelessness of arriving at an end. When from external objects he turns his vievi- upon himself—on his own vital and intellectual faculties, he fink-3s that he possesses a power of examining aud analysing his own nature to a certain extent, but no farther. • In his own corporal frame he is sensible o a power to communicate a certain moderate amount of motion to himself and other objects; that this power depends on his will, and that its exertion can,be suspended or increased .at pleasure within certain limits; hut how his will acts on his limbs, he has no consciousness; and whence he derives the power he thus exercises, there is nothing to assure him, however he may long to know. His senses, too, inform him of a Multitude of particulars respecting the external world, and he perceives an apparatus .by which impressions from without may be transmitted, as a sort of signals, to the interior of his person, and ultimately to his . brain, wherein he is obscurely sensible that the thinking, feeling, reasoning being he calls himself, , more especially resides, but by what means he becomes conscious of these impressions, and what is the nature of the immediate communication between that inward sentient being, and that machinery, his outward man, he has not the slightest conception. HERSCHEL. -- Lardner's Cycloyedia.

THE following anecdote is extracted from a Belgian journal: -- "An individual at Antwerp lately gave a supper to forty poor hunchbacks! He awarded a premium of sixty florins to him whose hunch was the most prominent, and who was also proclaimed king of the feast. Oarriages were sent to bring the guests from their residences, and to take them back again when the festivities were concluded. They enjoyed the dance till a late hour in the night, and returned home highly gratified with the kindness and generosity of their landlord."

div.head: DARING- IMPOSTOR.
div.p: A DARING- IMPOSTOR.
THE STORY OF AN INNOCENT CONVICT
BY ALFRED E. CALHOUN.
CHAPTER XXLII. FAITHFUL IRENE.
After leaving the'Torabs, Irene told the hackman, who still waited at the curb for her, to drive her to her father's office.

The man recognised the name at once, and his manner, which before was sufficiently respectful, became at once obsequious. "The Leffertses, thorns big folks," said the driver to his companion, when he was again on the box and the horses in motion.

"Rich as turtle soup," said the driver's cOm- panion. "I can't, for the life of me, see what a fine, beauti- ful young lady like that wants to come down to them Tombs for," said the driver. " Soine times a rich young feller gets into a scrape; but just as soon as the officers and the courts find out who he is, then he's .mighty apt to get off, which don't seem quite fair, seem' how them's treated that aint got no money and no friends," said the driver's companion, who, being out of work at this time, and consequently out of money, was inclined to be morose.

"By Jinks:l" emelaimed the driver, who, being engrossed by the horses and hi S own thoughts, had not heard what the other 'said, "I think I sea through it now." "'Through what?" "Why, I know why she went to the Tombs." "You've got a long head." • _

" Yes,' th-a-t's why I recall that Mr.-Lefferts has a son; Flashy Frank they cah him; and between you and me and them horses, he's a tough one. Oh, I've often drove him when he was so drunk he didn't know where he wanted to go. I guessed then he'd get into a scrape sooner or later. Ah, if I only wanted to tell on these young bucks that has rich fathers I could make somebody's hair rise on end; but in our business it pays to keep mum," and to illustrate this opinion, the driver whipped up his horses and lapsed into silence. As soon as the hack stopped before Mr. Lefferts'a shipping office, a clerk came out, and while stand- ing, hat in hand, before Irene, he told her that her father had been made "ill by the discovery of the Lee forgeries," and had gone home. "Do you know Mr. Lee?" asked Irene. "Oh, very well, indeed," said the clerk, with animation' adding, with a blush, "and I liked him very well, too." ' "What evidence is there that Mr. Lee committed these forgeries 2" she asked. • "I don't think there's any exact proof yet, Miss," was the reply; "still, things look bad." • "What do you mean 9" "I mean, Miss, that the detectives have discovered that he was in prison for the same offence before, and the suspicion is strong against him, and I'm awful sorry for it. too." "Then you liked Mr. Lee 2" said Irene, with a kindlier feeling for the man. "Yes, indeed, Miss; he was one of the best ousiness men I ever saw, and he was so gentle- manly that no one would ever take him for a criminal."

Irene waited to hear no more, but re-entering the carriage, she asked to be driven home. A servant met her, as she was about to go to her own room, and told her her father was lying down, and that there was a gentleman in the parlour who had come in not a minute before.

Without removing her bat or wrap, Irene entered the, parlour, and found Dr. Putnam awaiting her. '"lt seems to be the fate of our friend, Lee, to get into trouble," said the doctor, as he shook hands with Irene.

"And do you think him to blame?" asked Irene, with a look in her eyes and a ring in her voice that told she was ready to resent. "I do not know what to think," said the per- plexed doctor. ' "It would seem," continued Irene, "that some conspirators make it their business to keep Mr. Lee in trouble."
lor some seconds the doctor sat with his head bowed, as if in deep thought; then looking quickly up, he said: "I am dazed. I am unable to make up my mind."
"To make up your mind as to what?" she asked.
"As to Lee."
"But surely, Dr. Putnam, you do not think Mr. Lee guilty ?" said Irene, the colour rising to her cheeks.

"For his sister's sake as well as his own, I cer- tainly do not want to think so." "Have you any proof_ that has not been pub- rli4pfl 7" "No ; and Ido not care to believe that." Then, with more earnestness, the doctor added: "I would gladly surrender all earthly possessions and all my professional acquirements, and begin life at the bottom of the ladder, *if Allen Lee could only con- vince the world that he is innocent of the crime for which he suffered, and of the heinous offences with which he is now charged." "But, Dr. Putnam,' she hastened to say, "you believe that Allen is innocent of the crime for which he suffered. You—you told me so. You told Flor- ence so; for she iepeated it to me with delight. Why have you changed 7" The doctor did not reply at once, but sat looking at her, and stroking his curly brown beard in a per- plexed sort of way. It was a case of woman's sublime faith contesting against man's reason. It was the tropic heat of , loving trust melting down the ice barriers of logical doubt.

"Where are his foes? Why should any man con- spire against Allen Lee?. These are the questions that have been racking my brain all day," said the doctor, sadly shaking his head. "Can you not imagine, Dr. Putnam 7" "I certainly cannot," he said; "for to conjure up a reason would seem to me to imply an evil mind."
"I think I know," she said, firmly. "Then, for Heaven's sake, tell me, and dispel the doubts that are perplexing and paining me," said the doctor.
"First let me ask you a question." "A thousand if you will, Miss Lefferts.' "You remember the affair at Long Branch last summer 7"

"I shall never forget it. It was not only a very thrilling incident in itself, but it was the very beginning of all these communications." "Dr. Putnam, did you not attend Allen Lee when he was taken unconscious from the water, after having saved me ? " • "I did, Miss Lefferts; and I esteemed it a pri- vilege to be able to assist so gallant a man. It was that act that made me his admirer and the friend of his family," said the doctor, earnestly. "I am sure of that; but here is another ques- tion: Do you remember that my father sent a sum of money to my rescuer, through Mr. Rey- bold ? "

"I do distinctly, for Mr. Reybold, gave me the money himself, outside the Life Saving Station." "You have no doubt as to that 7" "Not the slightest," Miss Lefferts." "Can you recall the amount 2" "I can." "How much waa it ? " "Exactly fifty dollars." "You are sure it was not a thousand? "A thousand 1" exclaimed the doctor. "Yes, a thousand." "As to that, Miss Lefferts, am as sure as that hive that fifty was the sum. But why do you ask me about this?" "I may not explain my reasons fully now, but I will say, my father sent by that same messenger one thousand dollars to Mr. Lee, and now Mr. Reybold insists that he gave all the money handed him by my father to you, whether it was fifty or a thousand dollars. So you see, Dr. Putnam, either you or Mott Reybold kept back nine hundred and fifty dollars, that were intended to show the impulsive gratitude of a loving father to the brave stranger who saved his daughter's life." The doctor was pale and flushed by turns as Irene went on. At length he managed to say: " Miss Lefferts, surely, surely you do not think that I have lied—that I have taken this money?" He was about to continue, but Irene came to his side, and laying her hand on his arm, she said, in a voice full of strength and sweetness, as if she were sure of her ground: "I certainly think nothing of the kind. I am just as sure as I am of my own existence that you gave to Mr. Lee the exact sum handed you by Mott Reybold; and my father is just as sure that the sum was for one thousand dollars. He had not that amount with him, but he sent a cheque by Mr. Rey- hold to one of the hotels, near by, and got the money. This can be proven. You need no further pro° to convince each other for years. "Mott Reybold 1" exclaimed the doctor, a strange glow coming into hs upturned face. "Can it be that he is at bottom of this r,
Irene cum vrebsea npr lips, anti, tor reply, roctoon her head slowly.

"I shall seuhim at once and have an exnlanation about the money. Oh, this is infamous,'" said the doctor, as he turned to leave. "Pr. Putnam, you have.a pre, heart and a clear brain, .1 do not say this to colipliment you, but because I can see how Loth can btmiiied:eo help me." • " I stand ready to-help you with my he if need be," said the doctor; gallantly. "But will you help me to prove Allen Lee's inno- cence to the world, for his •own sake, for his sister's sake, and'ior the sake of jostled 2" As she asked the question, she reached out her hand, and the doctor took it. „
"For the sake of ru,and for the peace of my o'wn tortured heart, I cl-.-fite life nnd fortithe to aiding you in tithi," said the do'cto-:, with all the solemnity of a vow.

With this understanding, and saying he would. call again in the rnornin:.,:., the doctor left. From the directory he learned where TlTott Rey- - bold lived, and as it was on the way to his own 'office, he called in there as he went past. The janitor of the bacnelor apartment house in which Mott Reybold and his partner had their quarters,- told the doctor that the man he was in search. of had gene out. "But," ,he said, :with a knowing smile, which the doctor did not at all comprehend, "if you waa to, call round here after nine or so,to-night, you'd be apt to find them both in, and they're the lcind of • young gents that has lots of visitors and. are always glad to see more." .'hat night, At half-past nine, Dr. Putnam called. at Reybold's quarters again, and the servant, who. must have taken him for an old- habitne, at once led Mm into the room, where a dozen or more men were playing cards, ani the money and " chips " onobthe tables showed that they were not there for racre: amusement.

Reybokl, in his capacity of host, was pa:7sing from table to table, talking in high spirits, when he caught sight .of the doctor, and, his face showed that he was frightened and angered ;. still he tried to assume a courteous manner, for he advanced and. said:
• "Glad to see you, Dr. Putnam. My friende :Arca are having a little social game. Won't you stay ancl, take a hand ?"
"Thanks; I snever play. Can I see you for a, few minutes on a private matter I"- said the dectgr, as cool as if he were about to begin a familiar oper- ation.

lleybold coughed and nodded; then he led his visitor into an adjoining room, and Said, after point- ing to a chair : "Well, Doctor Putnam, what is this private busi- ness you want to see me about 2" "You remember the rescue OF Miss Lefferts at Long Branch last summer ?" asked the doctor, with the chair in front of him and his hand on the back. "By Jove, I would not be permitted to 'forget if I wanted to," laughed Reybold. "It ,is the °no- thing I hear about early and late—all the tima, in fact.' _

"You remember handing me some money for Lee at the Life Saving Station 2" "I :recall something of the kind." "Bat you have no doubt as to that?" "Well, I will sayl have not," coughed Reybold° "It was fifty dollars, was it not ?" " Possibly ; but why do you ask?" "Because Mr. Lefferts, as I am informed, insists that he gave you a thousand dollars;. and I learn_ that you say 3 ougave me all the money you got." "And so I did,, ' said Reybold, growing flushed.

"But was it a thousand dollar". " I:don't'know • I did not examine the envelope., You see, Doctor, I have no curiosity about other people's money. "Did you not tell me it was fifty dollars;? and did I not count the money in the presence of yourself and DavisOn, captain of the statian 7" "Really, Dr. Putnam, I did not burden my mind with the details. lam not a newspaper reporter," sneered Reybold. "Then the details have escaped your memory ?" said the doctor, trying as he" spoke to catch the other's wandering gaze. , "I say nothing of the kind; but I am ready to. swear that if there was any money lost in the trans: .fer, I had nothing to do with it; I am not respon- sible for it," said Reybold, trying to .work himself , into a passion. "I am making no charges," said the doctor. "Why, then, are you here ? " "I am here to ask an explanation," said the doctor, with a ring of resolution in his "My memory as to the facts does not need re, vising—" "Well, what of it?" "Only that this money matter is one of the many curious things in connection with Lee and yourself that I must know more about." "Must!" • "Yes, must!" echoed the doctor. "See here, Putnam," hissed Reybold, "if you; could be induced to mind your own business and let mine alone, it might save you no end of trouble." "This is my business." "Then go with it from here. Reybold flung open the dcor, and the doctor, without even a nod, put on his hat and left the. room.
(To le continued.)

div.head: HOW TO AVOID PREMATURE OLD AGE.
div.p: HOW TO AVOID PREMATURE OLD AGE.

The following advice is given by Dr. Benjamin Ward Richardson :—To subsist on light, but nutritious diet, with milk as the standard food but varied, according to the season. To take food in moderate quantity four times in the day, including a light meal before going to. bed. To clothe warmly but lightly, So that the body may in all seasons maintain its equal temperature. To keep the body in fair exercise, And the mind active and cheerful.. To maintain an interest in what is going on in the world, and to take part in reasonable labours and pleasures, as though old age were not present. To take, plenty of sleep during sleeping hours. To spend nine hours in bed at the least,,and to take care during cold Weather that the temperature of the bedroom is main- tained at 60 deg. Fahrenheit. To avoid passion excite- ment, luxury.

div.head: HOW SAVAGES ARE "CIVILISED."
div.p: HOW SAVAGES ARE "CIVILISED."

The Queen of Atani accepted our hospitality, but she was much more interested in European liquors than in European cookery. She determined ort tasting all the varieties of liquor we had before rashly deciding what drink she would prefer. A claret glassful out of every bottle produced she swallowed with equal gusto. A bottle of Glasgow raw grained whisky finally met her approval. She filled out half a tumblerful, and rolling up the white of her eyes poured the fiery stuff 'down her throat.. In apparent ecstacy she renewed the dose, and alarmed us by reaching out her hand for the hi:Azle: -Her Majesty was rapidly • getting drunk, ;lila what to do with her when she got helpless was a serious matter. We made a signal for the most. important attendant on shore to take her away, Her Prime Minister, or some equivalent personage, ventured to remonstrate, whereupon she lifted the- empty bottle; and swinging it about she let him have it at his head with the strength of a bullet. Something desperate had to be done to get her on shore. Casting about for some invention Cameron bethought himself of his: bagpipes. Going forward he got everything ready, and with a tremendous blast started a wild Highland pibroch. With a look of terror and dis- may her Majesty wrestled out of her tight herth„ and trying to get hurriedly on shore was saved' from falling headlong into the river by the timely assistance of her attendants. It was a great struggle to land her, and, something breaking, a bustle of enormous proportions which she wore upon her stoniach fell off into the river. Shorn of the im- menSe robustness which is supposed to (rive dignity in that part of the world, her Majesty hurried from the scene of her discomforture a greatly altered woman. With the afternoon- the women were crowding back-to their canoes with their purchases. Trade gin had done its work; mothers with and without infants were staggering and howling like demons. Fighting had been freely indulged in, These Poor savages were behaving as ferociously as civilised drunkards, with this difference, that many 3ra.eotintri gaenaitnnodftohtlehdemwi r iocdmlsotetnhoi fni t. htelii3edu rtltrineh/keeeeinli iit(ti(f!reeleonnszct;e, viwenartyos which even girls and boys had fallen. To our en- accustomed eyes the spectacle presented wonderful resemblance to paintings of the infernal regions, but in these the ,artists had fallen far short of the the incident si before us. We sickened for some savage region civilisation had not touched-. From the French and English factories the crowd still gathered, and with no feeling of regret we steamed away from Atani.—From Up the Niger."

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS
div.p: THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS
AT WARRINGTON.

The municipal contest which took place in War- rington on Monday was a notable one in some respects. In the first place, it was an all-round Contest in the fullest sense of the word, for two candidates fought for one seat in each of the nine wards of the town. In the second place it was a fight for supremacy in the Town Council, for, al- though the Conservatives have for many years had a majority in the Council, that majority is now so narrow that the winning of a couple of seats by the Liberals would reverse the relative positions of the parties. Another circumstance that gave additional interest to the" fight "was the fact that it is pro- bably the last municipal struggle that will take place before the general parliamentary election, and it therefore gave an excellent preliminary opportunity for the two parties to gauge, to a cer- tain extent, their strength in view of the impend- ing parliamentary contest. The electioneering campaign was, taken as a whole, a brief but spirited one. The Liberals were, up till within the last three or four weeks, too Much engaged in the organizing and carrying out of their great bazaar to give a great deal of at- tention to electioneering matters, and, owing mainly to this cause, they were so late in bringing out can- didates for some of the wards as, no doubt, to con- siderably damage their chances of success. During last week, however, much hard work was put in by the candidates on both sides and their supporters, and several meetings were held. During the contest many references were of course made to such muni- cipal "questions" as the depots, the baths, the aboli- tion of gas meter rents,and the paving of the streets, but, essentially, the struggle was a trial of strength between the two great political parties. During the polling on Monday, the Tory voters were well supplied with beer, the liquor being free in some quarters, whilst in others it was sold at one penny per quart. TOWN HALL WARD.

div.head: O. or VOTERS, 1,044.
div.p: O. or VOTERS, 1,044.

• The retiring Councillor of this ward was Mr. W. Pier- point, and he was opposed, on behalf of the Conserva- tives, by Mr. James Smethnrst. The polling place was the Drill Hall, the presiding officers being Messrs. J. L. Tunstall and E. Aubury 'White, and the poll clerks Messrs. J. S. Francomb and C. H. Brook. The person- ation agents were Messrs. Barlow, C. B. Beaumont, F. G. Lloyd, and J. Chalmers. There was, probably, more interest centred in the contest in this ward than in any of the others. It was known from the election which took place in the ward last November that the parties were pretty evenly divided, and the Tories made no secret of tlieir intention to do their utmost to wrest the seat from Mr. Pierpoint. In Mr. Smethurst they had a candidate, who at all events proved himself to be a most arduous canvasser, and amongst some of the electorate he seemed to be popular through his connection with local " soup kitchens" and the aged peoples' dinner. In fact some of the less knowing electors appeared to be under the misapprehension that it was Mr. Smethurst who provided these good things out of his own pocket, a misapprehension which was perhaps to some extent due to the arts of the electioneering agent. There is a con- siderable proportion of female voters in this ward,and as far as these were concerned Mr. Smethurst polled rather heavily. WHITECROSS WARD.
NO. OF VOTERS, 891.

Mr. G. Plumpton was the retiring Liberal Councillor for this ward, and the Conservative who challenged his return was Mr. W. Bellion. also a resident in the ward. The polling place was St. Barnabas school, the presiding officers being Messrs. Thomas Lythgoe and Joseph .Williams, and the poll clerks Messrs. George Norman and A. Brimelow. The personation agents were Messrs. G. Plumpton, jun., and F. Shaw. There have been three elections in Whitecross Ward previous to the present one, and in each case a Liberal was returned, Councillor F. W. Monks being unopposed. The Conservatives, however, seemed to be particularly desirous of defeating Mr. Plumpton, and they throw all the energy they were possessed of into:the contest. On the other hand Mr. Plumpton and a capital band of workers were not behindhand in their efforts, and consequently the work of bringing up voters went on briskly from the opening of the poll to the close. The Conservatives kept " the tap" open, and there was at least one case of persona- tion. BEVVSEY WARD.

div.head: NO. OF VOTERS, 772.
div.p: NO. OF VOTERS, 772.

In Bewsey Ward Mr. T. Flood, the retiring Liberal Counciller was opposed by Mr. W. J. Shaw, of Dallam- lane. The polling place was 623., Tanner's-lane, the presiding officers being Messrs. J. W. Whittle, and John Fairhurst, and the poll clerks Messrs. P. L. Speakman and Robert Henry. Messrs. H. Tyler and E. Turley acted as personation agents. It was not expected that Mr. Flood's position in this ward would be seriously en- dangered by his Tory opponent, but nevertheless the Liberals did not allow themselves to be caught "nap- ping." This being essentially a working-class ward, the polling officers were kept particularly busy at the dinner •hour and in the evening when the ironworkers ad other workmen were disengaged. It was pretty generally con- cluded by observant bystanders that Mr. Flood would be returned by a substantial majority.

div.head: ORFORD WARD.
div.p: ORFORD WARD.

NO. Or VOTERS, 686. Mr. W. 11. J. Jenkins,. solicitor, was the retiring con- didate, and he was opposed, on behalf of the Liberals,by Mr. J. Bonnell. The polling place was Silver-st. school, the presiding officers being Messrs. Arthur Bennett and E. J. Hall, and the poll clerks, Messrs. J. M. Bate and G. F. Freeman. The personation agents were Messrs. Upson and H. Barlow. For the greater part of the day quiet- mos prevailed in the neighbourhood of Silver- at. schools. and none of the excitement which is usually associated with a contested election seemed to pervade the neigh- bourhood. At the same time a good deal of quiet un- ostentatious work was done by the supporters of Mr. Bonnell and Mr. Jenkins, and a large proportion of the voters was polled on one side or the other. ST. JOHN'S WARD.

NO. OF VOTERS, 1,292. Mr. Garner, the retiring Liberal candidate,was in this ward opposed by Mr. J. Dobson,who is a member of the Boardof Guardians and lives at Lumb Brook. The poll- ing place was the club-room,John-st.,the presiding officers being Messrs. W. H. Woodcock, G. T. Moore, and F. W. Walker, and the poll clerks Messrs. W. Smith, G. Riley, andE. Whittle. The personation agents were Messrs. T. Ravenscroft, J. P. Welsby, T. Harding, T. Jackson, T. Breiey, and J. Maguire. So far as the number of voters gc this is by far the largest ward in the town, and as its aitecedents were doubtful—having on one occasion re-

div.head: 11116 L
div.p: turned a Liberal and on another a Conservative—neither side could feel any assurance of victory. Both candidates have devoted a lot of time to canvassing the electors, and on the election, day no effort was spared on either side to bring up the voters, and the result was a heavy poll. Mr, Dobson, although not a resident in the ward, nor in Warrington either for that matter, put in a claim to be the " ratepayers' candidate," while Mr. Garner On his side asked the burgesses to vote for their" old and tried representative the workingman's candidate."

div.head: FAIRFIELD WARD.
div.p: FAIRFIELD WARD.

NO. OF VOTERS, 792. ' Mr. T. Hutchinson, the Conservative member who retired from the Council, found an opponent in Fairfield Ward in Mr. W. Walker, architect. The polling place for the ward was Brick-st. School, the presiding officers being Messrs. C. H. Unsworth and G. Gibbon; and the poll clerks, Messrs. Sydney Wallhead, and F. Howard. The personation agents were Messrs. P. Goulden, C. Willcocks, J. Brown and H. W. J9nes. There was a quiet election in this Ward, and although the Canserva- Lives pretended to be " cocksure," as the saying is, of re- turning their man they did not relax any efforts to get the voters up to the palling booths, and for this purpose made constant use 'of the considerable number of vehicles they had at their command. Mr. Walker, on his part, though handicapped by being brought rather late into the field, made a plucky fight on behalf of his party.
HOWLEY WARD.
NO OF VOTERS, 993

Mr. W. Bolton, brewer, who was the Conservative mernber for the Council who retired for Howley Ward, was opposed by ,Mr. J. Mounfield, jun., builder, who resides in the ward, as the representative of the Liberals; while Mr. William Diggle came out as an Independent. The polling place was the National School, Church-street, the presiding officers being Messrs. J. Longland and W. S. Howard, and the polling clerks Messrs. E. J. Smith, and J. Smith. The persona- tion agents were Messrs. '3lNg, Muskett, A. Mounfield, jun., and r. Taylor. Although there were three candid- ates in the field for the ward, the contest practically lay between Mr. Mounfield and Mr. Bolton. Mr. Digglewas a " quantity " that Could be, and was very much, neglected. Mr. Mounfield was late in getting into the field, and consequently Mr. Bolton had a good start, of which he made good use. On the election day there was a good deal of stir about the polling place in Church- street, and the candidates were often "in evidence." Mr. Diggle made a boast of not having asked for a single vote, though, it is said he admitted having "visited eligible widows, and had told them that if he was elected a member of the Council he was sure to be appointed Mayor, and would of course, want a Mayoress to assist him in the discharge of his important duties." It is not known whether these "eligible widows" formed the bulk of the 14 votes which he received during the day. Mr. Bolton, in the course of the day, paid a visit to the Liberal Committee-room and objected to a bill that was posted outside, instructing candidates " how to vote" and having a large cross opposite the name of Mounfield. He declared that this was an illegal device, but it was rightly concluded that if there was nothing more illegal than this done during the election there would not be much to ccrnplain of. It was generally observed that Councillor Bolton would have been better employed in trying to stop the mysterious but free flow of beer. There was one case of Tory personation in this ward.

div.head: ST. AUSTIN'S WARD.
div.p: ST. AUSTIN'S WARD.

NO. OF VOTERS, 657. Mr. James Fairclough, who was one of the Conserva- tive members retiring from the Council, was opposed in this ward by Mr. C. J. Helmes,son of Alderman Holmes. The polling place for the ward,was Holy Trinity Schools, the presiding officers being Messrs. W. J. Forshaw and John Harrison, and the poll clerks, Messrs. G. Vernon and A. Boyle. Messrs. H. Heacock, H. Rankin, T. G Litton, and T. Ashley acted as personation agents. In this ward there was a -fine object lesson in "Tory intolerance!' Part ot Trinity schoolroom was taken up with the polling booths, and the other part the Tories had obtained as their committee rooms. As is known there are no other buildings adjacent to , these schools, the surrounding land being vacant. This land belongs to Lord Winmarleigh. and the Tories were not content with appropriating the only available n3rtion of the schools, but they also forbade the Liberals to erect for the purposes of a committee room any temporary struc- ture on the vacant land. The Liberals met the difficulty by hiring one of Messrs. Maginn's large buses, and this they placed in the dead end of Winmarleigh-street, and utilised it as a committee roam. They were ordered to remove the bus by Alderman Wright, but they declined, and .during the morning Mr. Julian Winser, the chairman of the Liberal committee of the ward, received a letter from Mr. John White, agent to Lord Winmarleigh, informing him "that the land which the electioneering omnibus was standing on was private poperty, and if he continued his act of trespass, he would hold him and Mr. Holmes legally responsible."
LATCHFORD WARD.
NO. OF VOTERS, 890.

_ Mr. S. B. Stringer again 'the field in Latchford Ward on behalf of the Liberal cause, his opponent on this occasion being Mr. W. 'lnsley. The polling place was St. James School, the presiding officers being Messrs. J. Bolton and P. Davies, and the poll clerks were Mr. F. Timperley, and the Rev. F. Lake Good. The persona- tion agents were Messrs. H. Hankey, A. Percival, W. Gleave, and R. Dowd. Latchford has always been a Tory stronghold, and on this occasion Mr. Stringer had a strong candidate against him in Mr. Tinsley. The contest in this ward did not therefore, cause much ex- citement. • Both sides, however; worked hard to bring up their voters, and with regard to this the Conserva- tives in this, as in other wards, were much better sup- plied with vehicles than their opponents.

div.head: BALLOT PAPERS
div.p: THE BALLOT PAPERS

The following shows the number of ballot papers re- iected in each ward :—Whitecross Ward, 2; Orford Ward, 5 ' • Bewsey Ward, 2; Fairfield Ward, 6: S. Aus- tin's Ward, 4; Town Hall Ward, 6; Howley Ward, 8 ; St. John's Ward, 1, and Latchford Ward, 6.

div.head: ANNOUNCING THE POLL
div.p: ANNOUNCING THE POLL

The polling booths were closed promptly at eight o'clock, and the ballot boxes were at once despatched to the Town Hall where arrangements of a very com- plete character had been made for the counting by the Town Clerk. Owing to the large number of wards con- testen. three sets of counters were engaged. The votes recorded in Town Hall and Whitecross wards were counted in the Mayor's parlour by Messrs. G. F. F. White, T. Cooper, A. N. Howard, and E. Reddish. In the Council Chamber the votes given in Bewsey, St. John's, Fairfield, Howley, and Latchford wards were counted by Messrs. E. J. Hall, Ainsworth, J. Layland, J. Bolton, Woodcock, Williams, W. S. Howard and Forshaw. The votes for St. Austins and Orford wards were counted in the Committee room by Messrs. S. Sutton, J. Fairhurst, F. H, Wilson, and J. W. Whittle. Several of the candidates were present while the count- ing was taking place. Soon after eight o'clock a crowd I began to gather before the Town Hall to await the announcement of results. In the course of a little over half-an-hour or so the crowd had grown so numerous.as to fill the whole of the roadway in front of the Hall and to spread far away to both the right and left. It was, in fact, a much larger gathering than is usually seen on the occasion of a municipal contest. The first announcement to be made was the result of the contest in Fairfield Ward, and other results were an- nounced at short intervals in the order given below. As usual, a good deal of cheering took place when the figures were read out, but by far the noisiest demonstra- tion of mingled amusement and derision was made when it was declared that Mr. Diggle had polled only the small number of 14 votes in Howley Ward. Soon after this Mr. Diggle was himself seen coming up the steps in front of the Town Hall, and he was given a good- humoured ovation by the crowd. He had evidently not heard the announcement, for he eagerly inquired what the result of Howley election was. and he was so persist- ently told on all sides that he had been returned by a majority of 14 that he seemed at last inclined to believe there was something in it. It was not till some time after that he was acquainted with the sad reality, but he took it in good part. Mr. Diggle appears to be proof against all kinds of disappointments. The following are the results in the order they were announced : FAIRFIELD WARD. Hutchinson (C) Walker (L)
