div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 7, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 7, 1891.
BEWSE y WARD. Flood (L) Siaw(C) 233
.Majority WHITECROSS WARD. Plumptan (L) Bellian (C)
Majority

:These results leave the two parties in the Town Coun- cil in the same numbers as before. Five Conservatives and four Liberals retired and the same number of each party' were returned. The only changes are that while Mr. Bonnet! displaced a Conservative, Mr. Jenkins' in Orford Ward, Mr. Smethurst, a Conservative, has de- feated Mr. Pierpoint, a Liberal, in Town Hall Ward. The following is a complete list of the members of the Town Council :—Aldermen J. Burgess, S. Chandley, J. Harrison, C. J Holmes, R. W. Francomb, J. Platt, T. H. Sutton, J. E. Wright, E. Greenall. Councillors J. Ashton, S. J. Beaman, J. Bonnet!, G. Blackurst, W. Bolton, A. Browne, J. Gannett, F. Dixon, R. T. Fairclough, J. Fair- dough, T. Flood, J. H. Fleming, J. Garner, J. S. Green, L. Greening, R. Heaton, J. Hepherd, J. Hill, T. Hutch- inson, F. W. Monks, J. Muir, G. Plumpton, F. A. Roberts, H. Roberts, J. Smethurst, W. Tinsley, and J. Walker.
• ..... There are 36 members of the Council—including the nine aldermen, of whom 19 are Conservatives and 17 Liberals.

MEETING AT THE LIBERAL CLUB. Soon after the poll had been declared there was a very numerous gathering at the Liberal Club, the large billiard room being crowded to excess. Amongst those present Were Alderman Platt, Councillors 11. Roberts, G. Plumpton, A. Browne, J. Bonnell, T. Flood, and Garner; Messrs. W Pierpoint,J. Walker, C. J. Holmes,W. Walker, W. Roberts: T. B.Biernan, T. Morris, &c. Hearty cheers were given both for the successful and unsuccessful can- didates. Mr. W. Pierpoint was elected to preside.

The CHAIRMAN said he had been engaged in fighting all his life; he was fond of fighting, and he hoped he should never loose the faculty of fighting. The fact that he had been beaten that day would have very little effeet upon him,except that it would give him the opportunity of fighting again. (Loud applause.) He had not been fighting against men who had been fighting fairly all round. (Hear, hear' and "Soup.") One man who had been canvassing for the other side said- that an Orange lady said that he was a Roman Catholic. (Laughter.) He should have been worse if he had been a Roman Catho- lic. (Hear, hear.) By another person he was described as an Orantteinan—(laughter)—and this, he believed, was all done in the extent of one street. Not only that: They had had the brewers fighting hard against them, and using every illegitimate means which they were cap- able of using, and which they always did use and always would use in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) He was not go- ing to cry over that matter, and he only mentioned that because he perhaps ought to do so. They were not a dispirited party in Warrington. (Applause.) At the list municipal elections their Tory friends vontared to pro- phesy, but they had learned this year not to prophesy, and all the better for them. (Hear. hear, and laughter.) But there were some people in Warrington connected with the press who ought to be ashamed of themselves. They were men who went to church,to the same church he went to, and they prayed and said" Save us from all uncharitableness," but he would ask these gentlemen whether they were satisfied with their Tory organ in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion he thanked the workers in the ward for the services they hid rendered him; and expressed a hope that if the occasion arose they would again give their assistance as freely as they had done that day. (Loud applause.) Councillor ROBERTS said they all knew perfectly well that the Tory party in Warrington had moved heaven and earth—(hear, hear)—and perhaps something that did not altogether belong to one or theother—(laughterl —to secure a victory at that election. Their own organ had been preaching of the immense importance of that contest, and he believed that the future Conservative candidate, whoever he might be, had been quietly wait- ing the result of the elections. From headquarters the summons had gone forth to every Conservative in Warrington, that all petty personal differences must be sunk—no matter who or what the candidate was, he was to be supported at all hazards. He believed that the Conservatives had polled their full strength that day in every ward in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) As far as the Town Council was concerned they stood in numbers as they were. Seeing that they were a discredited party and disorganised, without leaders and a good many other things besides that that the otherside have—(hear, hear) —they had come out of the election wonderfully well. They wanted to see how that election had turned out in the aggregate and there was some small grain of com- fort for them in the result of the day. The total Tory poll was 3,397, and the total Liberal poll 3,270, showing that the gross Tory majority in an election, un- precedented on their part for the efforts they had made, was only 127. He said that spoke volumes for the possibility, and the probability, • of carrying a Liberal candidate at the next Parliamentary election. (Loud applause.) With the figures they had before them there was not a man amongst them who would hesitate, with the best man they could get, to tight the Parliamentary battle whenever it came. (Applause.) He was not going to attach any blame to anybody, be- cause he believed the party had worked wonderfully well, but he could see places in regard to the different wards where, at a general election, they could do considerably better than that day. If they would put their shoulders to the wheel before this and the Parliamentary election, he bad not the slightest doubt they could win the borough. (Applause.) They had that day for the first time seen leagued together, publicly and without any attempt at concealment the Tory party and the beer party. (Hear, hear.) He wanted them to recognise the fact that a candidate who ba,d come out pronouncedly in the interest of the beer traffic had been championed by the chairman of the Conservative party at the ward meetings. The Tories had done things that day that they dare not repeat at a Parliamentary election. (Hear, hear.) In the case of his own ward, if they could only have closed three public-houses their majority instead of being 49 would have been nearer 249. The same thing applied to Gther wards. (Hear, hear and "Rowley.") They would have those places watched at the next Par- liamentary election; and they would take good care to prevent a repetition of what had occurred that day. (Hear, hear.) In Warrington they had a very strong women's vote, and that vote, unfortunately, was very largely Conservative. If they could have eliminated from the poll that day the women's vote of both sides, he had no doubt the majority would have been the other way about, and that vote in a Parliamentary election would not count. (Hear, hear.) They were not dis- couraged. They had fought a good fight. They had had the best men and the best cause, andit was now a duty incumbent upon each of them, as a united party, to leave no effort unattempted to secure at the Parliamentary election the political redemption of the town. (Loud applause)

-6uncilior T. FLOOD said he had beef,' bitterly taunted with being the ally of a party that was disreputable that was the Irish party, but he gloried in the fact that: a large part of the support he had received that day had come from the Irish party with which he had been so long identified. They knew in Warrington that the Irish vote had gone solid for the Liberal party. (Hear, hear, and applause.) In his own ward he had every' hing to be proud of. It was said that he was returned three years ago as an experiment, and he was told that his actions would be very closely watched,and that it would behove him to steer a very straight course. He had had three years' experience, and that day he had been re-

turned to have, another three years' experience. (Ap- plause.) . Mr. C. J. TloLum said as one of the poor unfortu- nate beaten candidates he could Only express his hearty thanks to those who hlcl laboured so hard on behalf of the Liberal party to return:him. St. Austin's ward was the only ward, apart from Latchford, which last year returned a Conservative, and he had had against him an exceedingly strong candidate, and therefore it was not much of a surprise to him to find that he was the lowest on the poll. The fight had been a good-natured one all round, and he did not regret having fought on their behalf. He. was not discouraged, and possibly on some future occasion he might be induced to repeat the dose. (Hear hear, and applause.) Mr. W. ROBERTS said they had had a hard and severe struggle in Orford Ward, but, thanks to a splendid band of workers, they had utterly routed the Tory party there (Applause.) His only regret that night was that their friend Mr. Pierpoint was no lOnger a member of the Town Council—(hear, hear)—but if he would fight Or- ford Ward, they would return him by as good a major- ity as that of Mr. Bonnell that day. (Loud applause.) Councillor RONNELL also thanked his workers in Orford Ward, and said that his opponent, Mr. Jenkins, was a genial fellow for whom he had the highest respect. He knew Mr. Jenkins would not strike below the belt,. and he (Mr. Bonnell) was determined that he should not strike below the belt either. (Applause.) Mr. S. B.STRINGEn said he was a defeated candidate for the second time, but he was not discouraged. (Hear, hear.) He was prepared to fight Latchford ward again when he could act with his chin up and canvass for a good cause. (Hear hear.) In that case he had had a good opponent, and he did not think they could have found a stronger man in Latchford than Mr. Tinsley, a man who employed labour, and had been for many years in the war, while he (Mr. Stringer) was a comparative stranger. He had not a word of disrespect to say of the opposite party. He thanked heartily all those who had worked so hard for him, and he hoped they might again be called upon to do battle and that the next time he should have to thank them for electing him to the Town Council. (Applause.) Councillor G. PLumProN said he felt quite sure that Whitedross would remain a Liberal ward, and would continue to be repreiented in the Town Council by three Liberals. They had had a tough.battle on that occasion, and he felt sure that if the Conservatives had fought a fair battle the Liberal majority would have been con- siderably larger than it was. (Hear, hear.) They had had to fight the beer barrel. (Hear, hear.) The beer had not, only been fighting them that day,but it had been fighting them during the last three weeks. Tbeir men had been got -together night after night at two or three public-houses, and that day some of them were got into those public-houses to prevent them from voting, and some who were fetched out of public-housas to vote he was sorry to say could scarcely walk in the polling baoths. (Hear, hear.) It was not Liberal meney which did that; it was Tory money. -(Hear, hear.) If the Tories would fight fair in Whitecross Ward he felt sure the Liberal majority would never be less than 100. (Hear, hear.) He felt sorry that their esteemed friend, Mr. Pierpoint, had not been returned; it would be a great loss to the Council. (Hear, hear.) It WIR a great loss to the town, and he should not feel satisfied until Mr. Pierpoint was again in the Council. (Applause.) He should like to see Mr. Pierpaint Mayor Of Warrington, and he was sure if he were Mayor of Warrington and they voted him first-class fare to go to the Lord Mayor's banquet he would not go third-class. (Hear, hear and laughter.) He was a gentleman that would uphold the dignity of the town. He hoped also to see the day when Mr. Pierpoint would be the member of Parliament for Warrington. (Applause.) The Tories did not like him ; they were afraid of him ; he was too independent and outspoken for them. (Hear, hear and anTnange./ Mr. Plumpton also thanked his workers for thehalp they had given him during the election.

Mr. Joseph MonNrrEt.p. jun.. who was greeted with cries of "Lost through th-? beer," said he would rather a thousand times be beaten than have his hands fouled with mud. (Hear, hear and applause.) A. Tory coun- cillor had said to him that morning that it was no use for a teetotaller to go to fight against the beer, as the beer would win. They were, however, not ashamed of having fought, and he thanked his workers for the help they had given him. (Applause.) Mr. W. WALKER said that, although he had had some of the foulest things said about him in Fairfield ward, he believed that his opponent, Mr. Mitchinson, had done everything that was satisfactory. He thought they had been put to a great disadvantage in Fairfield ward by the lateness with which they took the field. (Hear, hear.) _ _

Mr. JOHN WALKER moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman, and said the one weak or dark snot in that election was that they had lost their best friend, Mr. Pierpoint, as a member of the Town Cnuncil,but against that he might say that he knew Mr. Pierpoint had no desire himself to he in the Council. Mr.Pierpoint would now be mere at liberty to do other work. They were on the eve of a Parliamentary election, and if they lost some of Mr. Pierpoint's services in the Town Connell, they should gain more from him as leader of the party. (Applause.) He would say, however, that they had been a little disorganisel; they had been attempting a little too much. They had had a big bazaar on their hands, and Mr. Pierpoint was especially full of that. Sneak- ing,ton, as one who had worked with him in the Town Hall Ward, he might say that Mr. Piernoint had been so anxious that every _ward should be well worked, that he had neglected his own. That would not happen when they had a Parliamentary contest. (Hear, hear.) In that election they -had been trying to make Warrington better than it had been, and he would call their attention to the fact that Councillor Hutchinson went hack to the Town Council pledged to vote against Councillor Bolton ho.yinO, o cout th, Watch Committee. (Hear, hear.) He would also point out that in Rewsey Ward their opponents had found that beer was not all powerful, for in that instance they had promised a full-licensed house, hut the electors had said" Get thee behind me. Satan." (Applause.) As Councillor Roberts had pointed out, they had had the women voters against them to a certain extent in that election, while they should not have them in a Parlia- mentary election, (Hear, hear.) At the General Elec- tion in Warrington the !majority against them was 501, but that day the majority was only 127, and he thought, with that great gain in those few years, they might all conclude that they had at least a fair chance next year oF returning a Liberal for Warrington. (Applause.) Conneillor FLEIKING seconded the vote of thanks, and said he hoped they should soon -find Mr. Pierpoint a safe seat somewhere. (Hear, hear.) Councillor littowNit, in supporting the vote of thanks, said Howley Ward had been won by beer and nothing at all else. Mr. Mounfield had come out at a great dis- advantage to himself, and he deserved the best thanks of every one of them. (Hear,hear and applause.) The vote of thanks to the Chairman was then passed with acclamation.

Mr. PIERPOINT, in responding, said that during the nine years he had been in the Town Council he had never given a single vote to which any Liberal elector or honest Tory eloctor could take exception. (Hear hear.) There was no honest Tory who could believe it was a fit and proper thing that Councillor Bolton should sit upon the Watch Committee., Managers of police forces in other towns had told him thht it was a most improper position for any member of the beer interest to occupy. (Hear hear.) It was for the protection of that branch of the trade which respectable licensed victuallers did not believe in that Councillor Bolton went on the Watch Committee. (Hear hear.) During the time he (Mr. Pierpoint) had been in the Town Council he had had no interest to serve except that of the ratepayers. He had no insanitary prope.ty that wanted protecting, no little jobs that wanted doing. He was independent of jobs both in and out of the Council. (Applause.) He had the satisfaction of knowing that during the nine

years he had done his work honestly, and therefore he hail nothing to e proa h hinAelf with. He was deeply indebted to the Irish voters of Warrington that day (Applause.) The Irish voters had polled solidly for him in his ward, and he believed they had done the same in other wards. If the English Liberals had only been as true to their convictions as the Irish Liberals had been they would have occupied a different position. (Applause.) Hehad no hesitation in saying that if the Liberal party of Warrington would only keep their shoulders to the wheel they would eventually make Warrington a Liberal borough. (Loud applause.) The proceedings then terminated. MEETING AT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB.

A meeting was held, in the Conservative Club, after the declaration of the result. A large number of members of the club had congregated in the billiard room long be- fore the meeting commenced,which it did at a late hour, and a scene of considerable excitement prevailed there. On Mr. Smethurst making his appearance in the room he was clamorously cheered, and more than once elevated on the shoulders of his admirers, amidst the most exuberant applause. Soon after half-past nine the room became so crowded that it was announced that the meeting which it had been proposed to hold Caere would be held in the large hall of the club, and thither the numerous company tumultuously repaired. Mr. R. Pierpoint, president of the Conservative Association, took the chair, and he was supported en the platferm by Aldermen Sutton and Wright, Councillors Smethurst, Tinsley, Hutchinson, Bolton, James Fairclough, Heaton, C,annell, and Hepherd, and Messrs. W. Bellian, John Roberts, Alfred Woods, and V. Gill.—The CHAIR- mor. who rose amidst much cheering, and a cry of " Our future member," said he congratulated those present exceedingly, not only upon the results of that day, but upon the hard work that had brought it about. (Applause.) They had been defeated in the White Cross Ward, but only by a small majority, and the former Liberal majority of 193 had been reduced to 47. (Applause.) In St. John's Ward there was a small majority against them,but so small that the result might easily have been turned into a majority the other way. In tho Orford and Bewsey Wards the majorities had been unfortunately rather large against the Conservatives, but the successful man for Orford was a very good can- didate, and an old member of the Guardians, whom it would had been very hard to beat. As to St. Austin's Ward they should have been content if the Conservative majority had been 6, or at most 11, but they found that where it used to be such a close thing, their majority was no less than 66. (Enthusiastic applause.) Then they had in Howley Mr. Bolton returned by 76 majority. He (the chairman) was a little afraid at one time, when he heard of Mr. Diggle attacking the seat—(loud laughter) —but he was given to understand that that gentleman ' only took 14 votes in all. (Renewed laughter.) Ia Latch- ford Mr. Tinsley was returned by 140. (Loud applause.) They always looked upon Latchford as a place where they might', expect to win,but did not expect to get such a majority as that. But he was keeping the best to the last—he need hardly say that he referred to the victory of their friend Mr. Smethurst. (Loud Applause.) He had not only got in, but got in by a majority of 41. and he had taken the seat from the other side, which they calculated on holding, and which was occupied hitherto by one of the most important of their party. (Applause.) He congratulated him and the Conservatives on what had been done in the Town Hall Ward. They had shown that day that the Conservative party, if now and then they took a nap, yet knew when the opportunity really arose and the call was made, how to wake up and to work hard. In all probability before the municipal elections came on again they would have an opportunity of exerting themselves in a Parliamentary election. The chairman concluded by calling, amidst ringing cheers, upon Mr. Smethurst. Mr. SMETHURST, who was received with great enthu- Siam. responded to the call. He thanked those present for their reception of him, and both the Conser- vatives and the Liberals who had supported him. He had been told that the Town Hall Ward was one which it would be a miracle for his party to carry. But he stood there as one who had been persecuted on behalf of some people, because he would not subscribe to what he did not believe in, and as one who had had the whole Liberal body against him, who had worked night and day and up to the last moment, and vet he stood there returned as the Conservative candidate. (Apolause.) Mr. Smethurst referring to the questions of the trades unionists—(a voice : They are it for owt ")—said he had refused to answer the question as to fair wages in the way desired by them, because supply and demand must always regulate wages. As to the question whether he would vote for the labouring men under the Corporation having a fortnight's holiday and being paid for it he had replied that if the trades unionists found the money for the men to go to Southport he would vote for their having holiday. (Applause.)—Dr. CANNRLL next made a few remarks. He claimed that the Conser- vatives had beaten both teetotalism,trades unionism, and radicalism ; and observed that the Church of England clergy and the Nonconformists had also been against them.—Mr. TIELLIAN. the defeated candidate for White- cross Ward, said he felt proud of the position he stood in, though disappointed at. his (Meat. He was sorry to say that his defeat proved that Englishmen did not stick to their promises. (Much interruption. Cries of "You are wrong," "You are no Englishman," and "You are a Staffordshire man.") They had known him as a journey- man and as an employer of labour, and knew that as the latter he paid the wages he demanded as the for- mer. They had had a fair chance. f:indqing what he was by rnis time. Mr.Bellian explained that he had been indisposed to answer in the affirmative certain questions of the temperance party, but that he had an- swered affrmatively with explanatory notes, the three put by the Trades Unionists.—Mr. JAMES Fernmorron briefly thanked his constituents for their support.—Mr. Councillor HEATON also, on behalf of the de- feated candidate for St. John's -Ward, who, he said, had worked so hard, that he was not present, thanked his supporters. Although they were defeated, he remarked they were not disgraced.—Councillor Tinsley thanked his Latchford constituents for his return, and Mr. Shaw the defeated candidate for Bewsey Ward also spoke, In the ward he said Radicalism was stronger than Toryism, and if aTory won there he would have to he a better man than him self. (Cries of" No.") He would give them the hope that next year he would stand again. (Loud applause.)— Councillor Bolton next addressed the meeting. He thanked the Conservatives and Liberals who had voted for him. but not those Conservatives who would not vote at all. His majority ought to have been 176 instead of 73. Referring to the Trades Unionists he hoped that they would sink their political opinions when it came to trade questions in the Council,and look to Conservatives as well as Liberals for support. He complained of the manner in which a few Radical fellows, calling themselves trades unionists, had placarded him, and complained that they had not taken him and other Conservatives into ,their confidence as to what they wanted. The trades union delegates he described as a few men who met in a back room to elevate their noble selves. The sooner they meaded their ways towards the Conservatives the better because they were as ready to help them as the Radicals were.—Mr. John Roberts, Mr. Councillor Hutchinson, and klderman Sutton afterwards spoke, and a vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the proceedings.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

.The_fortnightly meeting of .this Board was held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday morning. Mr. Balharry presided, and there were also present— Messrs. Ratcliffe, Heaton, Davies, Jolley, Diggle, Hood-Wright, Clarke, Humphreys,furton, ton, Mather, W. Houghton, Smith,Dignum, Aukland; and Hibbert : J. C. Sutton (clerk), and other offi- cers. Mi. Henley, Local Government Board In- spector, was also present.

div.head: HOUSE COMMITTEE.
div.p: HOUSE COMMITTEE.

This Committee recommended that a lunatic attend- ant, &c., be appointed at the Workhouse at a salary of £25 per annum with uniform, rations, lodgings, &c.— The minutes were confirmed, and several applications, which had been received for the post, were handed over to the House Committee.
THE PORTRESS'S SALARY.
On the proposal of Mr. RATCLIFFE the salary of the por- tress was raised from £23 to £25.
A GRATUITY.

On the motion of the CHAIRMAN, a gratuity was awarded to Mr. B. Shearer, relieving officer, for the ex- tra service he has recently rendered in connection with the vacancy in the relieving officership of the Newton District.

THE WORKHOUSE AND SCHOOLS —SUGGESTIONS EY THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD INSPECTOR. Mr. HENLEY, the Local Government Board Inspector, said there were two or three small matters he should like to call the attention of the Guardians to, and which had been reported upon by Mr. Morrison, inspector' to the Local Government Board. One matter was with re- gard to the event of a Are, the water supply being turned off at night, and there being no telephone to the fire station, which was half-a-mile away. He attached the greatest possible importance to the saving of life, and he hoped the gnardians were satisfied that in case of fire persons who could not get out of bed themselves could be conveyed to a place of safety. When a fire occurred on a ground floor there was always a great danger of the smoke filling the corridors and people being stifled before they got out. There ought to have been means of getting .these people out, and the offis!ers should satisfy themselves that they could remove helpless people in the event of fire occurring. (Elear, hear.) It was no use locking the stable door after the hmse was stolen. Their male hospital was crowded during last winter, and he observed from the visitors' book that this matter had had the attention of the guardians. It was said that there was ample accom- modation in the house for the number of inmates, but he need hardly tell them as guardians of experience that this was an absolute fallacy and a most deceptive estimate. A Workhouse might appear to have a consider- able margin in certain parts and yet be terribly over- crowded in particular parts, as they had 13 different classes which they could not mix with each other. He was the last person to ask them to add a single brick to that Workhouse unless it was necessary, but he pointed out that there had been an increase of 14,700 in the pop- ulation of the Union during the last ten years, and what was adequate before would not be adequate for the increased number. It was certainly economy to be in advance in the question of buildings in any Union, and though at present there was no great pres- sure in any Workhouse in the country, they did not know when the pendulum might swing the other way and then the guardians might have to adopt the demoralising plan of an extended system of out-relief. He also advised the guardians to en- gage a night nurse for the hospital. Referring to the school at Padgate,he mentioned certain details which had been reported upon by Mr. Moorson. He suggested that apparatus for athletic exercise should be provided in the boys' play-ground, and also that about an acre of the land connected with the schools should be set apart for games.—Mr. ACKLAND Mid this latter subject had been before the Schools Committee several times, and they considered that there was already sufficient play- ground in the present yard.—Mr. HENLEY said it would be much pleasanter for the children to have an open field for games, as there was always more or less of a barrack-like aspect in a yard with walls around it.—Mr. ACKLAND said the children were allowed out in the fields after the crops had been taken off.—Mr. DIGGLE thought there ought also to be swimming baths.—Mr. HEATON said the yards at Pad. gate schools were the best in the country.—Mr. HENLEY next called attention to the case of a boy who had lost his toes in consequence of frost bites during last win- ter. The boy, it was reported, had been in a low and , scrofulous condition.—ln answer to a question, Mr. ' MINES, superintendent of Padgate Schools, said he saw the boy on the morning of December 24th sitting by the fire crying., and on being asked why he was crying he said his feet were sore. On his shoes and stockings being taken off Mr. Mines noticed the peculiar appearance of his toes, and, thinking they were frost-bitten, the boy was put to bed and certain remedies applied. The doctor was also at once sent for. On the doctor coming he ordered a certain treatment. On another visit soon after the doctor also brought Dr. Smith, of the Infirmary, with him, and the latter gentle- man recognised the lad and knew his parents, and said he would be subject to frostbite. The boy was kept in bed for many weeks and had constant medical attention, but his toes "sloughed " off. He was, however,now out, and walking about.—Mr. HENLEY asked how long the boy had suffered from the frost bite before it was dis- covered.—Mr. MINES said it had only attacked him on the morning on which it was discovered, there being a very .severe frost.—Mr. HENLEY thought everything had been done in the case which medical science could suggest. He also intimated that that would be his last visit to that Board, as lie was about to retire from his position of inspector.—The CHAIRMAN referred in complimentary terms to Mr. Henley, and moved a vote of thanks to him.—Mr. RATCLIFFE seconded, and Mr. HEATON supported the proposal, which was agreed to with acclamation.—Mr. HENLEY suitably responded.

div.head: VISITORS TO THE ASYLUMS.
div.p: VISITORS TO THE ASYLUMS.
Mr. RATCLIFFE moved that Messrs. Turton,Diggle and Mather be appointed a Committee to visit the asylums, and this was agreed to.
MR. DIOGLE AND THE BOARD.

Mr. DIGGLE said that, owing to the length of the meet- ing, he would leave the resolution of which he had given notice as to certain matters at the Workhouse over till the next meeting.—Mr. HEATON hoped that Mr. Diggle would say what he had to say at the meeting of the House Committee, of which he was a member.
This was all the business.
A NEWTON ELECTOR QUESTIONS MR. CHAMBERLAIN ON FREE EDUCATION.
The following correspondence has taken place between an elector in the Newton Division and Mr. Cnamberlain:—
Newton-le-Willows, October 31, 1891.

Dear Sir,—Will you kindly permit me to address myself to you respecting the question of free edu- cation—a working-man's boon, to confer which I know of none who has done more than yourself? In the year 1885 I had the pleasure of hearing you deliver a speech at Warrington, which had, I be- lieve, much to do with bringing this important sub- ject within the range of practical politics. If memory serves me right you used words on that occasion to the effect that rather than deny work- ing-men the benefits of free education you would cut off a right hand. That speech was delivered just about the eve of the general election, and it was freely quoted during the campaign in the adjoining division of Newton, where Sir Richard Cross was opposed by Colonel M'Corquodale. The Con- servative can lidate (Sir Richard, now Lord Cross) used it largely as an argument sx by a Liberal Government should not be returned to Parliament. He urged through- out the division that the free education doctrine which you were propounding was dangerous; that it wciuld do away with religious training in our schools, and 'would thus deprive Churchmen and Christian people generally of one of their fundamental principles ; and he warned the electors to beware, and to hold fast their religion, which, as Englishmen, was so dear to them. The argu- ment was repeated by other Conservative speakers largely throughout the country, and in the Newton Divi- sion it was soon afterwards freely admitted that the free education scare, as it was then called, lost the Liberals the election. The same thing was said of War- rington and other constituencies. Since then many things have happened, and amongst them the pas Sing of a Free Education pill by the pre- sent Government (which includes Lord Cross) largely assisted by yourself. From all I can gather, the many dreadful things which were going to happen if free education became law have not occurred. On the contrary, day schools seem to be prospering more than formerly, and the children's morals, which we, as par- ents, are always anxious to protect, seem to be quite as safe as before. This leads me to ask the question—and r know of no one better qualified to answer it than your- self—in what respect does the Act recently passed by the Conservative and Unionist Government differ from the scheme propounded by you in 1885, and which was then so vigorously attacked? Were the predictions 11 respecting the sacrifice of religious principles groundless or have the Government inserted some special protect- ing clause which was not originally intended by your- , self ? As a parent, this is an important point which has never yet been clear to me, and as there are doubt- less many others equally without inf ormation, I beg to think that a reply from you would serve a wide and I useful purpose.—Apologiziag for troubling you, and thanking you in anticipation, I remain, &c. Highbury, Moor Green, Birmingham, Nov. 2nd, 1891. Sir,—l am directed by Mr. Chamberlain to acknow- ledge the receipt of your letter on the 31st ult., and, in reply, to say that he is not aware of any difference in principle between the lines on which he proposed to deal with free elementary education and those on which is based the legislation actually passed by the Govern- ment.

The opposition to the agitation in 1885 no doubt pro- ceeded from fear on the part of many members of the Conservative party that free education was intended only as a step towards the destruction of voluntary schools.— I am, Sir, yours faitilfully, (Signed) J. WILSON..

div.head: WRECK OF THE MOSELLE.
div.p: THE WRECK OF THE MOSELLE.
Advices received at Southampton state that Captain Rowsell, commander of the Moiell s, wrecked at Colon, was washed overboard 'and drowned. He leaves a widow and family.
DEITH OF THE OLDEST CLETtGYMA.ii.

The Rev. Joseph Eludon, vicar of Chillingham, Northumberland, the oldest clergyman of the Church of England, died on Saturday. He was ordained in 1817, and would have reached his 100th year next January.
TRAGEDY IN COUNTY DURHAM.
SHOT DEAD ON HER WEDDLYG-DAY.

A farm labourer, named Johnson; on Saturday morn- ing, shot his landlady, Mrs. Addison, with whom he had lodged for the past eighteen years, at fietton-le-Hole, Durham. The tragedy took place in the street. John- son directly after the crime surrendered to the police. Mrs. Addison had recently become acquainted with a man named Andrew Simpson, and they were to have been married on Saturday. Mrs. Addison was on her way to church to he married when Johnson fired his gun twice, and the unfortunate woman died almost immedi- ately. Jealousy was the cause of the cri:ne. The prisoner is about 53 years of age. He had been loitering about Addison's house during the past few days. Mrs. Addison leaves two sons and a daughter, all grown up. The affair has caused a great sensation in the Hetton dis- trict, where the parties were well-known.

div.head: TILE EARTHQUAKE IN JAPAN,
div.p: TILE EARTHQUAKE IN JAPAN,
4,000 LIVES LOST.

Until Monday it was impossible to telezraph an ac- curate statement of the loss of life and property occa- sioned by the recent earthquake in Japan. Even now the figures can only be given in round numbers,and they are subject to correction at a later date. Every effort has, however, been made by the Japanese authorities to obtain information regarding the extent of the calamity and the following figures represent the ofrical estimates: —Killed, 4,000; persons injured, fully 5,000; houses destroyed, 50,000. The area covered by the earthquake was wider than at first supposed. It extended inland to the region of the lakes. Several large towns are re- ported to have been laid in ruins. The disaster has caused dreadful suffering. No Europeans have lost their lives.

div.head: TVE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: TVE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
RESULT THROUGHOUT THE COUNTRY.

In those boroughs where changes have taken place the Liberals have gQined sixty-nine seats, the Conservatives fifty-one, the Liberal Unionists six, while one change is noted as an Independent. The Liberals gains were three in Crewe, Salford, Ipswich, Wakefield, Bury, Liverpool, and Northampton; two in Ilkeston. Hereford, Bath, Preston, Leeds, Hull, Pontefract, Huddersfield, West Hartlepool, Hastings, St. Helens, Nottingham, Croydon, Plymouth, Gloucester, Macclesfield ,Bristol, and Birming- ham. The Liberal Unionist gains were one at Chelten- ham, Salisbury, Stoke-on-Trent, York, Kidderminster, and Dewsbury. The Independent who gained a seat got it in York. A trade unionist was returned at Swansea, and a Labour candidate was successful in Nottingham, and also in Gateshead. In Bradford the Liberals attri- bute their serious loss to Labour candidates being inter- posed between the two parties.

div.head: POPE AND 111 S CARDINALS.
div.p: THE POPE AND 111 S CARDINALS.

-- Signor Be Ceasare writes from Rome that the Pope has lately not been well, and is obliged to keep to his bed more than usual. He is much embarrassed about the choice of a successor to Parocchi. In the course of thirteen years Leo XIII. has changed his Secretary of State four times, while Pin Nono had only one during the whole of his Pontificate, from 1849 to 1876. During the present Pontificate no less than 73 cardinals, most of them created by Leo XIII., have died, and many of his intimate friends. At the death of Pio Nono there were 64 cardinals; there are now only 15, and if the Pope lives some years longer the future conclave will consist of cardinals all of his making a thing that never happened, with one exception—under the reign of Urban lll.—on which fact Barberini coined a medal with the sarcastic motto, " Non vos me elegistis, sed- ego elegi vos." It is stated that the Pope made his will late month, and that in it he distinctly disclaims all personal inclina- tion as regards the choice of his successor. It is added that another will relating to temporal matters, the purport of which is of course secret, is in the hands of four cardinals.

cannot be difficult to imagine what is the feeling of the Tory candidates who did not deign to send an answer of any kind. There are some Tory work- men who are members of Trades Councils, and if they cannot now see how the wind blows they are "blind as never bat was blind."

The struggle in Warrington on Tuesday was, so far as the Tories are concerned,of the most desper- ate and unscrupulous kind. The Corrupt Practices Act was set at defiance ; " open houses "were kept - in some of the wards; and plenty of carriages , were provided for electors who had in the first instance been made too intoxicated to find their way to the polling booth. Smarting under the defeat of last year, and afraid they might not be able to win by fair means, they let it be seen that they were willing to win by foul means. They proclaimed that they were caught napping at the last election, and talked confidently of "sweeping the board" at the present election. But they have not done so; their great scheme has failed. Five Tories and four Liberals came out of the Council, and five Tories and four Liberals have been returned to the Council. It is a case of "As you were," with this difference—that the Tories have won a seat in Town Hall Ward, and lost a seat in Orford Ward. It is a matter of great regret to the Liberals of Warrington that Mr. William Pierpoint was not re-elected for Town Hall Ward. He was late in the field, and, more than that, he was occupied too long in assist- ing other Liberal candidates instead of watching his own interests as a candidate. As an able and experienced business man, and a straightforward advocate of the best interests of the borough, his retirement will be a distinct loss to the Town Council ; but it will be a gain, we believe, to Liber- alism in Warrington, seeing that it will leave himl more of liberty to devote his energies to the organisation of the party, which is far from being in a perfect condition. Indeed, taking all things into account—the fact that consequent upon the work attending the recent bazzar the annual ward meetings had not been held—it is satisfactory to find that the Liberals held their own. Notwith- standing all the direct and indirect bribery and corruption which were practised by the Tories, the total majority of the votes which they polled over the total polled by the Liberals was 127 only. This includes, of course, the votes of the female electors, who are more ready to go to the poll on . the Tory side than on the Liberal, and the major- ity of whom are, to begin with, on the Tory side. The Tory majority at the last General Election was 501; and if it can be reduced to 127 at a hard- fought municipal election, notwithstanding the
_ female franchise, and notwithstanding too, the

"free tap "—which dare not be used at the General Election—there is, to say the least of it, a fair chance of winning in the Parliamentary contest which will take place next year. What the Liberals have got to do is to set to work immedi- ately,hold public meetings in each ward for the ap- pointment of Ward Committees,and follow up with the educational work vilaich is still needed amongst a portion of the electors. The Tory majority in Warrington is melting away, and it will resolve it- self into a minority, if the Liberals make a right and a full use of the period which will ensue before Parliament is dissolved.

MR. T. W. LEGH, the member for The Church the Newton Division, made a speech Question. on Church matters at the opening of a sale of work, at Earlestown, on Saturday, and took occasion to refer to disestablishment pros- pects. He seems to think the question is not ripening, because he hears less of it than he did some years ago; but if he imagines that the move- ment will die out he is labouring under a gross delusion. It is true that the subject is not im- mediately to the front in England, but let him attend political meetings in Scotland, or in Wales, and he will soon be made aware that the Church question is in both countries a burning question. So strong is the desire for disestablishment amongst the majority of the electors of Wales, that no Liberal Government could exist for long (Home Rule once disposed of) which did not take steps to ensure its becoming an accomplished fact. And it is pretty much the same in Scotland. It is perceived that England will be the last link of the State chain; and practical politicians are,therefore, directing their forces, in the first instance, to Wales and Scotland—just as, twenty years ago, they were directed to the disestablishment of the church in Ireland. We are quite aware that the view taken by church authorities is that the Established Church in Wales is really a part of the Church of England ; but that does not get rid of the grievance so far as the people of Wales are concerned, nor will it prevent disestablishment being applied to Wales before it is applied to Eng- land. An Act of Parliament is all powerful in these matters, though if Church people insist upon England and Wales being treated as one body they can hardly complain if, in the end, a single Act of Parliament should disestablish the Church in both England and Wales. For ourselves, as we are believers in Home Rule, we think it desirable to let each country apply the Home Rule principle in determining whether it will have a State church in its midst or not.

In the course of his speech, Mr. LEGH referred to what he described as "a religious competition in addition to competition in other things;" and he added that" they as Churchmen should have an opportunity of showing that they were able to do as well as other people." But we would ask—how can Churchmen have this opportunity unless they stand on a footing of equality with other sects— that is to say unless they start even in the race If one church is to be endowed by the State to the extent of several millions annually, and another is to have nothing at all, it is absurd to speak of the members of the endowed church as having " an opportunity of showing that they are able to do as well as other people." Then as to competition : that is a healthy thing under certain conditions; but so long as one church has a monopoly of endow- ments,how can it be said that it is in legitimate and healthy competition with other churches? There was a time when monopolies were granted by the State, but they have been abolished as injurious to trade. How is it that such men as Mr. LEGH do not perceive that there are just as sound reasons for putting an end to the Church monopoly ? Touching the poor attendance at church which has bee* disclosed by the religious census in Liverpool, Mr. LEGH had a word of comment on the view taken by the Bishop of Liverpool, who declares that the Church is under-manned, and that there ought to be more church buildings available. Mr. LEAH regards this as an inversion of the argu- ments of temperance reformers who say—" In- crease the facilities for drinking and you increase drunkenness." But it seems to us, on the contrary, that the line of argument is parallel. In both cases it is assumed that the increase of facilities for attendance will lead to increased attendance; whether the result be good or bad is beside the issue as a poiut iu reasoning. Mrl lacal doesn't

say whether he believes that the best way of gett- ing churches filled is to build more churches; but, as a representative of the party of privilege and monopoly, he is consistent, if not reasonable, in joining in the cry of " Church aui State and no surrender."

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 7. 1891.
TAKING the country through, the "The Moral Liberals have made a substantial of it."

gain, as a result of the Municipal Elections. It was not to be expected that they would gain much, seeing that they had been so successful in previous years, told their further ad- vance is exceedingly satisfactory as an evidence of the still "flowing tide." Several seats have un- doubtedly been lost to the Liberal party through the intervention of labour candidates. The work- ing-classes have a perfect right to take measures to ensure that they shall be better represented in the future than in the past ; but what some of them have yet to learn is that they can best achieve the end they have in view by acting in conjunction with the Liberals as a party. In St. Helens, both the labour candidates were defeated, for they fought, so to speak, single-handed. In Warrington a labour candidate was returned as a Liberal three years ago, and he was again returned to the Coun- cil, on Tuesday last, by a very large majority. If there were any doubt as to which of the two great political parties is most favourable to the claims of labour, that doubt may be said to have been removed in Warrington by the answers to the questions which were subnaitted by the Trades Council. The reply from the Liberal candidates was in every case an unqualified "Yes," while the Tory candidates, for the most part, eith9r sent no answer or sent an an- swer which was unsatisfactory. One of them, Councillor BOLTON, let the cat out of the bag, as soon as he had been returned, by describing the members of the Trades Council as "a nuis- ance" and as men who had "sold their cause." Seeing that a Tory Councillor could say these bitter things, after sending a favorable reply, it,

div.head: "ToUCII AND Oro."
div.p: "ToUCII AND Oro."
Sir Gilbert Greenall declines to again contest Warrington. He has been considering the result of the Municipal Elections.

Mr. Timothy Healy's tongue is in an unruly member. Some time ago its use resulted in his getting a severe thrashing; and this week he has been horsewhipped for saying most offensive things about Mrs. Parnell. It is about time Timothy kept his tongue between his teeth.

The protest is rising against a knowledge of two dead languages being compulsory at Cam- bridge. Let those learn Greek who require it; but why insist upon it in the case of a student to whom it will be so much intellectual lumber? Regard for the dead ought not to interfere with the progress of the living.

There was a scene at Lyrnm Local Board meet- ing on Thursday night. The Chairman said Mr. Brazendale had failed to comply with the Company's requirements as to the water supply; Mr. Brazendale said the statement was " a lie," whereupon the Chairman, after a little more cavil,, abruptly adjourned the meeting.

Mr. Arthur Lee has commenced a series of lantern lectures illustrative of" The progress of the world." They are being given in Cockhedge Mission-room, Warrington, and they deserve to be well patronised. The views are of a most superior kind; and there can be no pleasanter or more instructive way of spending Saturday evening.

The earthquake in Japan seems to have killed people by the thousands—as if they were so many flies. Man boasts, and not without reason, of his power over the forces of nature; bat such a catas- trophe comes as it were to mock him in his pride, giving a new reading to Tennyson's lines : Our little systems have their day ; They have their day and cease to be.

St. Helens is setting an admirable example to towns of a similar size by providing branch libraries. A branch was opened at Sutton some time ago, and it has proved so successful as to justify the Corporation in opening a branch, on Tuesday evening, at Thatto Heath Park. There have been volumes of smoke in St. Helens for a long time; these other volumes will be more welcome.

It is stated tl4at the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children is about to extend its opera- tions, and proceed against the sellers of " lucky packets" and other questionable " chances" for children. It is held that the practice is An infringe. ment of the Lottery Acts. How is it that there is no branch of the Society in Warrington ? There are plenty of children who in various ways are being cruelly treated.

It was very good of the late Mr. R. J. Pierpoint to leave £lO to the poor of Runcorn, to be dis- tributed,along with relief, by the relieving officer; but by way of a hint to others who may be like- minded, we would venture to suggest that sums of this kind would be better spent if they were ap- plied in relieving the deserving poor who are just, and only just, above the pauper line. People of this class say least, and sometimes stiffer most.

" Tommy " Burns has made another dive from Walton Railway Bridge, and he has not yet broken his neck; but he ran great risk, for he. leaped off the bridge, on Saturday afternoon, with but six feet of water below him. If he will only oblige his admirers by diving in, say, four feet of water, they will cheer louder than ever; and they will attend in larger numbers, well knowing that their chances are increasing of being "in at the death."

We would direct attention to the letter of a Newton elector to Mr. Chamberlain on the educa- tion question, and to Mr. Chamberlain's reply.. It will be seen that the elector is perfectly familiar with the opposition of the Tories to Free Educa- tion when it was advocated at Warrington by the member for West Birmingham. He runs Mr. Chamberlain into a tight place, haying regard to his present alliance with the Tories, and he does it very neatly.

The Prince of Wales will be 50 years of age on Monday, as he was born on the 9th November, 1841. The " Graphic" for to-day is devoted to a celebration of the event. It contains a life of His Royal Efighess, along with a large number of portraits of the Prince, beginning with one of him as a child of five months old. The illustrations are numerous, and cover all the principal events in the life of her Royal Highness. The number is likely under the circumstances to have a large sale.

Are Primrose Leaguers really "daft," or are they only supposed to be? Here is an extract from a speech made at Frodsham, on Monday even- ing, by Mr. James Reynolds in his capacity as Ruling Councillor:—" Their friend Mr. Labouchere had said the Queen had a great deal too much money. Mr. Labonchere would like to confiscate and take it all to himself, but he would not give it. to them he (the Chairman.) was perfectly certain.',' We have seen many green things this wet autumn, but nothing so green as this choice bit of rhetoric.

At St. Helens, the Tories in some wards, resorted to a discreditable trick in order to pre vent a number of working-men recording their votes during the dinner hour. It is in the power of personating agents to require an elector to be sworn, if he has doubts as to his identity; and this power was used, about noon, to a ridiculous excess. The result was a block in the polling booths; and a number of workmen had to go away unable, in the dinner hour, to record their votes. The Tories always opposed working-men having a franchise, and they would now prevent them using it.

Everybody should read the report of the case heard, at the Warrington Police Court, before the Mayor and other magistrates on Monday. Jolift Allen, the landlord of the Pelican Inn, was sum- moned for allowing gaming on his premises on the morning of Oct. 28th. It came out in evidence that a number of members of "the trade," in- cluding the Secretary of the Licensed Victuallers Association, were caught playing "Nap," between three and four o'clock in the morning. The defence was that they were innocent of any intention to break the law! And the Mayorand other magis- trates were quite sympathic, for they dismissed the case on payment of costs. Wonderful tcrwns Warrington, to have reared so much sweet inno- cence; and" yet again wonderful "to have a Bench that can protect it, and take it as it were to its bosom.

SUDDEN DEATH ON RUNCORN FAIR GROUND. Mrs. Dodd, aged 28 years, wife of William Dodd, of Lunt's Row, Weston, dled suddenly ou the fair ground at Runcorn, on Monday afternoon. The deceased and her two children had a ride in a coach attached to the hobby horses, and while the machinery was in motion she was seen to fall forward on the seat. She was at once lifted out, a nd immediately expired. The cause of death was stated to be heart disease. A CREWE DIVORCE e...A.sE. In the Divorce Division on Thursday, before Mr Justice Jeune, William Lall, a fireman. in the em- ployment of the London and North-Western Rail- way, at Crewe, sued for a divorce by reason of his wife's adultery with a co-respondent named Harry Forster,who was said to keep a papershop at Crewe. ani The petitioner and his wife were married on tile Ist statedAugust,h t 1880, and tlde 2Sth June, 1890, he saw his wife separated in 1889. The petition in company with the co-respondent, who put his arm round her waist and the two went off toget'ler. Evidence was given as to respondent having hal a child, of which she said Forster was the father. The case was undefended. A decree nisi was granted for the dissolution of marriage, with costs again% the co-respondent.

div.head: VICTORIA-ROAD CHAPEL, WIDNES.
div.p: VICTORIA-ROAD CHAPEL, WIDNES.

On Wednesday evening a special service was held in the above place of worship, when the Rev. Thomas Cook, eonnexional evangelist, preached a powerful and eloquent sermon, basing his remarks on the text, "What a man soweth, that shall he also reap.' There was a crowded congregation. A collection was taken in aid of Mr. W. Sampson's ten days' mission, which is shartly to be commenced at the same chapel.

RMIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York. Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the" Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Onion, American. Aus- tralian, Oriental, and other lines.—John Walker, agent. "Examiner ' Office. Bewsev-et.. Warrington.—Advt. THEFT OF A COAT AT RUNCORN.

At the Runcorn Police Court. on Thursday, before Mr. J. Handley, a labourer, named George Walker, was charged with stealing a coat valued at 12s. Gd., the pro- perty of William Craddock, pawnbroker, Ch urch-st. ,Run- corn, on Wednesday, the 4th inst. The prisoner was apprehended by P.C. Crowder with the coat in his pos- session. In answer to the charge he said he gave a man 3d. for it.—Prisoner was remanded a week for inquiries to be made respacting him. MILTON LITERARY AND FRATBRNAL SOCIETY, WIDNES. The weekly meeting of this society was held on Wednesday evening, in Milton Congregational Church, when Mr. W. Harrison, 8.A., presided. A debate took place on the question "Should capital punishment be abolished? "—Dr. A. R. Hunson opened the debate in the affirmative—Mr. E. T. Winne followed with a very able paper in the negative. A lively discussion followed. On a vote being taken, nine declared themselves in favour of the abolition, and six against.

div.head: RUNCORN VOLLINTRER BAND.
div.p: THE RUNCORN VOLLINTRER BAND.

In aid of the fund for purchasing new instruments for this band a football match was played on the Runcorn grouud on Wednesday between W. Faulkner's Runcorn and Widnes team and H. Ashton's Warrington team ,and about athousand spectators assembled. The game was of an interesting description. Davies first scored for Runcorn and then Berry equalised for Warrington. Barnes dropped a goal, and Ashton placed a goal from a penalty kick, and "A. Barnes concluded the score with a try, which Ashton converted. Final result,Warrington : 3 goals, 1 trr, Runcorn and Widnes one try. The teams afterwards had tea together at Wilson's Hotel. PROPOSED TESTIMONIAL TO DR. O'KEEFFB OF WIDNES. After the ordinary business had been transact& at the weekly meeting of the Irish Nrtional League, Mr. P. Whelan presiding, a discussion took place as to the advisability of presenting Dr. O'Keeffe with a testimon- ial, on his retirement from the Widnes Local Board. Several members spoke in high tones of praise of the work accomplished by the worthy doctor for the rate- payers, and the hope was expressed that the public would show their appreciation of his many years' labour for the common west, by subscribing to a testimonial. No definite decision was arrived at, and the subject will be further dealt with at a future meeting, AN INHUMAN HUSBAND AT WIDNIIS.

On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Thomas Cun- ningham, 18, Derby-road, Farnworth, was summoned by his wife for assaulting her on the 2nd instant. Clm- plainant also applied for a judicial separation.—Mr. Knowles, who appeared for the complainant, stated that in 1888 she was married to the defendant, who was her second husband. Soon after they were married,he became a habitual drunkard, and abused her evory night. About TM on Sunday morning last, she was in bed, when the prisoner came upstairs with a knife in his hand, and got hold of her by the hair and pulled her out of bed, saying that he had only one life to live, and it would be a case of a life for a life.—Defendant pleaded guilty, and as the wife was unwilling to have him sent to gaol, only a nominal fine of is. and costs was imposed for the assault. The judicial separation was granted, and an order was made for the defendant to contribute 3s. 6d. per week towards his wife's maintenance.

div.head: ALLEGED SMUGGLING AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ALLEGED SMUGGLING AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Major 'Hazlehurst and Mr. A. Thomas, Solomon Mason, tobac- ,conist, 3, Church-st., Runcorn, was summoned for hav- ing in his possession 27 ounces of cavendish tobacco, exposed for sale and not being enclosed in a wrapper as provided by the Manufactured Tobacco Act, 1863. Mr. speechley prosecuted on behalf of the Inland Revenue, and quoted the 6th section of the Act, which says that if any tobacco of either of the descriptions called respec- tively cavendish and negro head, whether of foreign or British manufacture, containing or having mixed there- with any material or ingredient prohibited by any Act in force to be used in the manufacture in the United Kingdom of like description, and not being enclosed in a wrapper securely fastened by such label as aforesaid, or of which such wrapper or label shall have been cut, torn, obliterated or cancelled, or bearing any other mark •4,r appearance of having been opened or tampered with, stall be sold or exposed for sale, or being in the posses- Ilion of any importer, manufacturer, dealer, or retailer of tobacco, he shall forfeit either treble the value thereof or the penalty of £2O, and all such tobacco shall be for- , feited.--The defendant, who pleaded guilty, said he had the tobacco given him, and put it in the window for sale. He did not know anything about the stamps or wrap- pers.—Mr. speechley said the case was a clear one of smuggling tobacco, and although the magistrates could impose a penalty of £2O, they could mitigate it as they thought would meet the case. He, however, asked that in this case they would exercise their power of mitiga- tion sparingly. The treble value of the tobacco, includ- ing duty, was £1 2s. 9d.—The Benth imposed a fine of £1 and £4 12s. 6d. Coats. SPECIAL REDUCED TERMS FOR OCTOBER AIM NOVEMBER ONLY.—Re-opening. Tuesday, November 10th. Intending pupils will oblige by writing at once, stating what subjects they wish to learn, to our head Academy. 2, Brown-st., Market-st., Man- ateater, and full particulars will be forwarded.— Advt.

ACCIDENT ON THE SHIP CANAL, NEAR RUNCORN. On Tuesday a man named William Stewart, residing in Lock-st., Runcorn, met with a serious accident whilst working on the Ship Canal at Bigfleld, near Runcorn. He was engaged in stopping a train of wagons by means of a sprag, when the sprag flew out and struck him in the face, fracturinc, his jaw in two places. Be was im- mediately conveyed to the hospital at Latchford.

CLAIM BYi BUILDIR AT I{I7NCORN. At the Runcorn County Court, on Tuesday, William Farrell and eon, builders, South-Bank, Runcorn, sued Edward Doyle, of Ann-st. Widnes, for £1 175., value of certain flooring boards belonging to them, and wrong- fully taken by defendant.—Mr. F. A. Lake defended. —The plaintiff alleged that Doyle tooks the boards form a sale by auction of the property of William Hall, and that the boards belonged to them, but as they failed to Identify the boards, or produce the auctioneer who sold them, the Judge nonsuited them, without hearing any witnesses.

CLAIM FOR WAGES AT RUNCORN. At the Runcorn County Court, on Tuesday, Frederick Coogan, Trenthana-st., grocer's assistant, sued Messrs. Johnson and Co., grocers, Church-St., for £3, being one week's wages due, and one week's wages in lieu of notice. Mr. E. W. Humphreys appeared for the plain- tiff, and Mr. F. A. Lake defended. Plaintiff stated that he had been employed by the defendant as assistant, at 30s. per week. During the month of July last Mr. John- son told him he could have a week's holiday, and it was arranged that he should go in September, and leave his wife to attend to the shop. Whilst he was in Ireland his wife wrote him saying that Mr. Johnson had called at the shop, and not finding him there, ordered him to leave at once. He therefore sued him for his wages of that week, and a week's wages in lieu of notice. For the defence, Mr. Johnson admitted that he was spoken to about July by plaintiff about having a holiday, but said that later plaintiff took upon himself to go without speaking to him, and left his wife in the shop, which he objected to. His Honor said it was very difficult to decide, as it was one oath against another. He believed the story told by Mr, Johuson, and gave judgment for the defendant.

div.head: "TOMMY" BURNS AGAIN.
div.p: "TOMMY" BURNS AGAIN.

" Tommy " Burns, the noted diver and swimmer, has announced his intention of jumping from the railway arches, which cross the canal at Earlestown, on Saturday afternoon at three o'clock. The height from the parapet of the arches to the canal is some- where about 80 feet, and there is no doubt a great crowd will assemble to witness the feat. COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT SUTTON HEATH.

On Wednesday afternoon, as Charles Lucas, of St. Helens-road, Prescot, was leaving his work at the above colliery, and was coming up the brow, when one of the waggons became uncoupled and came into contact with Lucas, crushing his legs very severely. He was attended to by Dr. Barlow, and is progressing favourably.

div.head: HUNTING ACCIDENT AT TARPORLEY.
div.p: THE HUNTING ACCIDENT AT TARPORLEY.

Dr. M'Culloch, of Tarporley,the local medical man in charge of Captain Mesham, of the Ist Royal Dragoons, stationed at York, who met with an accident in the Cheshire hunting field on Tuesday, issued the following bulletin on Wednesday "Captain Mesham has sustained a compound frac- ture of the skull. The brain is uninjured. The patient is doing well, and his recovery is very hopeful." RENT AUDIT DINNER AT NEWTON.

The half yearly rent audit dinner to the tenants of Mr. W. J. Lep in Newton. Earlestown, and Gol- borne, was held at the Pied Bull Hotel, Newton,:on Monday evening. The dinner which was of a sub- stantial character, was nicely served by Mrs. Bond, and was much enjoyed by the farmers present. After dinner Mr. Pardey presided over the subse- quent proceedings which were of a suitable char- acter. Several toasts wore proposed and honoured, swigs being given at intervals,_ _ _
(-7 KITCHEN RANGERS.—laarland Builders Ironmonger, War- rington.— Advt. SUNDAY SCHOOL AT PRESTON BROOK.

On Sunday afternoon the Rev. Herbert W. L. Smith, A.K.C.L., assistant curate of Daresbury,com- menced a Sunday School at the mission room, Pres- ton Brook. At 2 p.m., the time appointed for be- ginning. about 25 scholars put in an appearance, Misses Earp and Taylor assisting as teachers. On Monday evening, at 7.30, a Bible class for men and youths was started, and there was a fair attendance for a beginning.
UMBREii,AB RE-COVERED.—J. and W.PUTTON, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. A DEER CAUGHT IN ST. HELENS STREETS.

A somewhat remarkable capture was made at St. Helens on Tuesday night. Just before dusk a fine full-grown female deer was seen bounding along the lanes in the neighbourhood of Parr, and the unusual incident attracted a crowd of pursuers. who ulti- mately secured the animal by a rope. The deer was subsequently removed to the police station at the Town Hall, where it was securely fastened, await- ing a claim for its ownership. On Wednesday the animal was claimed on behalf of Lord Gerard, and it was stated to have escaped from Garswood Park. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.--J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-et., Warrington.—.Advt.
ANOTHER BRANCH LIBRARY OPENED AT ST.
lIBLBNE3.

On Tuesday night, the Mayor of St. Helens (Coun- cillor E. Johnson) opened a new branch library for the rapidly-extending district of Thatto Heath, on the Liverpool side of the borough. This makes the second branch library under the management of the Corporation, in addition to the Central Free Library at the Town Hall, and is an evidence of the popularity of the free library movement among the working-class population of the town. The premises, which include a residence for the care- taker of the Thatto heath Park,has been erected at a cost of £6OO, exclusive of the fittings. The library and reading room were opened with a stock of 1,146 volumes, and the daily and evening newspapers, as well as weekly periodicals, will be provided. In connection there with it may be stated that the central library contains 17. 346 volumes, the Sut- ton branch 1,710, and the 1,146 at Thatto Heath make a total of 20,202 books provided for the benefit of the residents of the borough. TERRIBLE ACCIDENT AT ST. HELEND.—A FOREMAN

CUT IN Two. A shocking fotalit3 occurred on a railway siding, near the copper works of Alderman D. ..NPliechnie, Ravenhead, St. Helens, on Monday night. Some shunting operations were being carried out when, by some means, a man named William Hill, residing in Garnett-st., Sutton, and who was employed as a foreman discharger in one of the departments of Mliechnie's works,was knocked down. He fell across the lines, and the wheels of several waggons pas.ed over his body. The poor man was terribly mutilated his body being literally cut in two. Death was instantaneous. On Wednesday forenoon, Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Griffin Hotel, Peasley Cross, on the body of the de- ceased. Evidence was given that Hill crossed some railway lines belonging to the Railway Company to speak to a pointsman about taking some empty waggons from the siding. He was returning while shunting operations were going on, and was , heard to scream. It was then found that he had been knocked down by some waggons ot coal, sev- eral of which passed over him. It was stated that the deceased man had no necessity to cross the lines, and at the point in question the lines and sidings were well lighted. If deceased had kept a proper look-out he must have seen the approaching waggons. A verdict o! .` Accidental death "was returned. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. andj W. Durrox, Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Ar'vt.

FUNERAL OF THE REY. W. WILSON, BURTONWOOD. The interment of the remains of the late Rev. W. Wilson, vicar of St. Michael's Church, Burtonwood, took place on Saturday afternoon, in the burial ground attached to the church. The body, which was enclosed in a polished oak coffin, with brass mountings, had been removed from Hoylake on Friday, to the deceased's late residence. On Satur- day afternoon, a very large number of the parish- ioners and others gathered near the vicarage and about the church, and shortly before three o clock, the coffin was borne from the house by Messrs. J. Warburton, Dallam ; J. Warburton, Dial Post; W. Fairclough, Brookhead ; and T. Norcott, members of the School Board, of which deceased was for many years clerk. The relief bearers were Messrs. T. Howard and J. Fairclough (churchwardens), W. Gough and W. Sephton. Following the coffin were Mrs. Wilson (widow of the deceased), Miss Ather- ton, Messrs. R. and J. Forshaw, J. Forster, W. Houghton, W. Webster' J. Grundy, W. Fairclough, T. Hewitt, H. Gawthorpe, A. Hewitt, and Dr. Mouncey. A great many people were also present in the church to show a last mark of respect for the deceased clergyman. The body was met at the en- trance to the churchyard by the Rev. F. Willis, recto: of Warrington, Rev. E. Edmundson, vicar of Parr, and Rev. J. Johnson, curate in charge,Burton- wood. The burial service at the grave side was read by the Rector of Warrington. The coffin bore a plate, on which was inscribed, "Rev. William Wilson, vicar of Burtonwood, died 28th October, 1891, aged 57 years." It was covered with beauti- ful wreaths which were sent by Messrs. J. Warbur- ton (Dallam), T. Norcott, W. Fairclough, J. Warbur- ton (Dial Post). W. Webster, W. Fairclough (Cause- way Bridge), Rev. T. R. Matthews (vicar of Earles- town), and the members of St. Michael's Church choir.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 7, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 7, 1891.
HISTORICAL NONCONFORMITY.

The Rev. John Yonge, of Warrington, delivered the second of his course of lectures on " Historical Nonconformity" in Bethesda Lecture Hall, Run- corn, on Monday evening. There was a good audience, and the Rev. James Martin precided. The lecture was illustrated by lime light views, shown by Mr. H. W. Handley. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON. Sankey-4., Warrington.—.Advt. CRUSHED TO DEATH IN A ST. HELENS COLLIERY. Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Victoria Hotel, Thatto Heath, St. Helens, on Monday, on the body of William Gee, 19 years of age, son:of Edward Gee, of 10, Cairo-square, Thatto Beath, who was killed on the previous Thursday evening in the Sutton Heath Colliery by the tall of a large piece of rock from the roof weigh- ing over a ton. Gee was engaged with several other men when the stone fell, killing him on the spot.— Evidence was given by Thomas Jacques and Thomas Halpin, the fireman, the latter stating that OA ice that afternoon the stone had " knocked " solid.— Mr. Stokes, the deputy;inspector of mines, said he had visited the place, and in his opinion no one was to blame.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.
_ UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.
HANDSOME GIFTS 1W MR. BRUNNER.

On Monday night,at Middlewich,it was announced at a meeting held to arrange to carry into effect the Technical Instruction Act, that Mr. Brunner, M.P., has decided to present the town with a house and grounds which he had purchased for .C 1,200. A few weeks ago Mr. Brunner urged Middlewich to adopt the Technical Education Act, and promised assis- tance, but great surprise and pleasure are evinced at the generosity of the member for Northwich Division. The house and grounds are to be arranged for u gymnasium, cookery and laundry rooms, and boys' workshops. On Monday the Town Clerk of Nelson received a letter from Mr. J.T.Brunner, M.P., enclosing a cheque for £5O for prizes or scholarships, to be spent as seemed best to the committee, either this year or a prize of .ClO a year for five years. Mr. Brunner,it will be remembered,gave a donation of .£2O not long ago to the Nelson Free Library.
GAs FITTINGS.—J. S. Garland. GaII Fitter, Bridge-at., Warrington.—Advt.
THI CLOSING OF A BEERHOUSE.

Christopher Kiernan applied to the magistrates of St. Helens, at the Police Court, on Saturday, for a temporary authority to sell intoxicating liquors at the Live and Let Live boerhouse, in Pocket Nook-st. It appeared that applicant's brother Patrick Kiernan, had been selling under a tempor- ary authority, but he failed to appear on the trans- fer day. Meanwhile the police had reported him for selling drink to a girl on Sunday morning, for which he was fined 40s. and costs. The house was closed on account of the temporary authority hav- ing lapsed, and his brother now sought to take pos- session.—Chief Constable Wood said he had made inquiries, and found that applicant was a man of good character. The Clerk (Mr. Davison) : But there is a conviction against the house ?—The Chief Constable: Yes.—The Chairman: We decline to grant this temporary authority, but you can renew your application at the transfer sessions on the 7th December. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-et., Warrington.—Adv. BILLIARD EXHIBLTION AT RLTNCORN LIBBRAL CLUB.

On Wednesday night Mr. J. E. Dawson, of Bolton gave an exhibition of billiards at Runcorn Liberal Club before a large audience of the members. The game was 1,000 up, and Mr. Dawson's opponents for the first five hundred were Messrs. J. Elliott and W. Bradbury, but they had not the slightest chance with him, and the game was called 506 368. Mr. Dawson's highest breaks were 63, (all spots) and 56, (17 spots). In the "second half" Messrs. W. White and Page opposed him, but playing with great confidence and very quickly Mr. Dawson ran up breaks of 144 (32 spots), 122 (27 spots), 37; 32 and 80 on, compiling the second 590 in less than an hour. The game was called Dawson 1,000; oppon- ents 534. During an interval Mr. Dawson Rave an exhibition of finger play, in which he displayed a wonderful control of the ball, and made some mar- vellous shots, and did some clever tricks. Re is a quick, clever, and tricky player, and he was fre- quently apolanded during his exhibition. PETROLEUM On6.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, Bridge-at., Warrington.—.Advt.

IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE MEETING AT GOLBORNB. On Saturday evening a meeting under the auspices of the Irish National League, Golborne branch, took place in the Assembly-room of the Golborne Liberal Club. Mr. G. W. Rawlin, C.C., of Rainhill, occupied the chair, and was supported on the platform by Mr. J. Pinkerton, M.P. for Galway, Mr. W. Burn, of Oldham, and several other influ- ential gentlemen. Mr. Rawlin said that when he was asked to preside he accepted the invitation with great pleasure, for one reason, and that was because it seemed to him a time, above all others, when English Liberals should not allow any doubt to exist in regard to the Irish question. (Hear, hear.) One of the lessons taught them by what had taken place during the last twelve months was that Ireland had been true to her tradition, although some had thought fit to follow Mr. Parnell in his action, and there were now two parties, one of which was weak and immoral, and the other just the opposite. (Applause.) Mr. Downs moved the following resolution: " That this meeting endorses the action of the Irish party, under the leadership of Mr. Justin McCarthy, and expresses its unabated confidence in Mr. Gladstone as the exponent of Liberal policy towards Ire- land." Mr. Burns, of Oldham, seconded.— Mr. John Pinkerton, i.P., who on rising to support. the resolution was well received, said it would be a grand thing if parsons took no part in politics. In the contest in Sligo not one single priest entered the polling booth except for the purpose of giving their votes. They were on the eve of a general election. He was glad that the Tories had succeeded in Man- chester and in Bute, for if they had received a knock-down blow at Manchester there would not have been the remotest chance of getting the Gov- ernment out of office until the full seven years had expired. (Hear, hear.)
