RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSLONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday. Mr. H.J.Grice presided,and there were present Messrs. W. Fisher, J. Pritchard, R. Abel, W. Timmins, F. Wiswall, H. Coward, J. Meadowerott, B. Bisbrown' S. Taylor, W. Hankinson, J. Dobson, H. White, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (secre- tary), M. Barker (surveyor).

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Mr. J. Mclntyre presided over the fortnightly meeting at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present Messrs. S. Taylor, J. W. Lightburn, P. Speakman, C.C., J. Baguley, H. E. Heywood, E. Aaron, J. W. Kirkham, T. Lea. J. Brandreth, J. Whitlow, Baxter, Pickering, and Colonel W. 0. Fox (ex-qfficio), and Mr. Ashton (clerk).

div.head: Vit. if. G. LINALER,
div.p: Vit. if. G. LINALER,

The Clerk read a letter from Mr. H. G. Linaker' of Frodshain, returning the cheque for £lO voted him for his services as acting clerk. Mr. Linaker said he could not accept that amount, and he would communicate with the Board further in due course.
A )3EQUEST TO THE POOR OF RUNCORN.

Under date Oct. 20th,111r. R. W. Pierpoint,tanner,Run- corn, wrote as follows to the Clerk :—I enclose you a copy of request of my late father and which we are de- sirous of now being carried out. Would you please be kind enough to bring the matter before the Board of Guardians in proper form and advise me of their deci- sion.—The request read as follows :—Runcorn. Oct. 27, 1885. I Robert Jackson Pierpoint request permission be sought from the Guardians of the poor to be permitted to give the sum of £lO to Mr. Ward or the relieving officer for the time being, the same to be distributed in sums of not more than two shillings and sixpence or as the total may afford to the poor of Rnncorn, at the same time they receive their pay allowed them for their relief until the whole be paid to them.Signed,Robert Jackson Pierpoint. —Mr. Speakman proposed that the desired permission ' be given and that the Clerk forward a letter of thanks to the widow and executors. The late Mr. Pierpoint, he I said, was a very kind mat of great piety, and with very great love for his fellows.—Mr.Lea seconded the motion, which was carried. It was also decided that the Run- corn Guardians superintend the distribution of the money.
THE VACCINATION OFFICER FOR RUNCORN.

With regard to this ra-atter the Clerk said the Local Government Board would sanction the appointment of Mr. Ward, if his relief district Were made co-terminous with the sub-registration district. This might be done by adding to the Ruacorn relief district the townships of Aston, Aston Grange, Sutton, and Stockham (taken from Mr. Riley) and Norton (taken from Mr De Prez). The relieving officers were quite willing so long as their salaries were not disturbed. There were not many cases of relief in these townships and the increase of work to Mr. Ward would be very little. In the first- named four townships there had only been 15 cases in three years and in Norton only two in the same period. It was resolved to ask the Local Government to sanction this alteration of boundary, and Mr. Brandreth gave notice of his intention to move the appointment of Mr. Ward at the next meeting.

div.head: FINANCE
div.p: FINANCE
On the recommendation of the Finance Committee

div.head: RUNCORN SEAMEN'S INSTITUTE. CHILDREIVB BEEHIVE.
div.p: RUNCORN SEAMEN'S INSTITUTE. CHILDREIVB BEEHIVE.

The Seamen's Institute, in connection with the Runcorn branch of the Mersey Missions to Seamen, is fast approaching completion, and the headquar- ters of Mr. W. Shaw, the missionary will be trans- terred from the Bottom Locks to that place. The Institution has cost about £1,500, and of this sum about .£6OO remains to be raised, and a number of young ladies of the Mission and their friends, on Wednesday, made on endeavour to raise a portion of the same by a "Beehive," which proved to be another name for a bazaar. There were no Queen bees; all were workers, and the following is the list of those who dispensed the products of the hive :—Misses Abel, F. Abel, E. Speakman, Price, C. Price, F. Hill, L. Houghton, Gregory, L. Sutton, Rhodes, Waterworth, Douglas, Allen, E. Shaw, R. Shaw, L. Coward, S. A. Osborne, E. Owen : treasurer, Miss B. Owen ; secretary, Miss Bowyer. There was a good attendance at the open- ing ceremony amongst those present being Mesdames Abel, Horsefield, Hill, Dykes, Ebbrell, Price, Roberts, Coward, and Miss Rigby.—Mr. Shaw, the missionary, in introducing Mrs. Abel to open the " Ibehive." referred to the active interest she had taken in the Mission and to the increased accommodation and the greater benefits that would be provided at the new institute.— Mrs, Abel in a brief speech expressed. her pleasure at seeing the young people take such an active interest in the Mission,and announced that she would give cushions for the choir stall and for about 16 other seats at the new Mission Room. (Applause.) She had much pleasure in declaring the " Beehive " open.—On the motion of Mr. Shaw, seconded by Captain E. Elliott, of the schooner Margaret Garton, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs. Abel, by aeclamcion, and the sales commenced. In the evening an entertainment was provided for visitors.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday night. Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were present Rev. Canon Wood, Rev Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. McDougall Mr. T. Handley and Mr. G. Moss (Clerk.)

div.head: WELCOME.
div.p: A WELCOME.

The members gave Mr. T. Handley a hearty welcome to the Board,and Mr. Handley in thanking them for their kindness, said if he could do anything for the education of Runcorn he should only be too glad.
SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.

The attendance officers had reported to the School Attendance Committee that the total number of children on the rolls was 3,586 an increase of 124 on the corres- ponding month last year. The average attendance was 3,012, an increase of 222 and the per centage was 839. —Dr. Gastaldi moved the adoption of the minutes, and, speaking of the defiant attitude of some parents who would not send their children to school,he said the Com- mittee would persevere in their present policy of bring- ing them before the magistrates.—Mr. Taylor seconded the motion. In answer to Dr. Mc Dougall the Clerk said during October 36 parents were brought before the magistrates, as compared with twelve during the same period last year.—The chairman said there was no ex- cuse now for not sending children to school,a,s the objec- tion against fees had been removed, and if the Board persevered in the line they had adopted it would instil into the minds of parents the necessity of the education of their children.—The minutes were carried.
INCREASES_OF SALARY.

The School Management Committee recommended that the salary of Mr. R. H. Jarvis be increased to £6O per annum, and the salary of Mr. Stubbing to £55 per annum both being assistant teachers at Greenway-road school. It was further recommended that an allowance of ls.per week be made to W. Berry, the caretaker at Greenway- road schools, for extra services, in connection with the evening classes. Also that a sum not exceeding £5 be expended in prizes for the successful students at Green- way-road schools.—Canon Wood moved and Dr. McDou- gall seconded the adoption of the minutes.—Dr. Gastaldi said they were continually having applications for in- creases of salary, and it was time some decision was come to by the board as to where they would stop. He was in favour of a scale of salaries being proposed at one e —The Chairman said it wasthe province of the School Management Committee to draw up a scale and submit it to the board.—Dr. Gastaldi said it had been broached many times, and nothing done.—The Chairman said the Clerk would place the subject on the agenda of the Corn- mittee.—The minutes were passed. COAL.
The tender of Messrs. Simpson and Davies to supply best house coal to the Board schools at 16s. per ton was accepted.
AN APPLICATION.

Mr. G. Howard, school attendance officer, applied for an increase of salary. He pointed out that during the six years he had been in the service of the Board he had only had two advances of £5 each. The letter was referred to the Attendance Committee.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SA.NITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SA.NITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. Mclntyre presiaed and there were present, Colonel W. V. Fox, J.P., (ex-officio), Messrs. Aaron, J. Bagnley, Brandreth, Heywood, Whitlow, Pickering. Kirkham, Baxter, J. Ashton, (clerk), G. Ashton (assistant clerk) and J. Farrington (nuisance inspector.)

THR LIGHTING OF WILDHRSPOOL-ROAD. Mr. R. W. Francomb, mayor of Warrington wrote as follows: The Warrington Rural Authority are lighting their districts of Penketh, Latchford, Padgate, &c., with gas lamps, and if you can possibly see your way tc light up Wilderspool and Stockton Heath we shall esteem it a great favour, and shall be truly grateful to you. At present we have plenty of lamps from Warrington to the Foundry on Wilderspool-road, which is the end of the borough boundary,but after that we are in perfect dark- ness. This road is more frequented than any other road in or about Warrington, and the vehicular traffic is very great. It is impossible to get along witout knocking against people er being compelled to go into the road, where there is great danger of being injured by the numerous conveyances. "—The Clerk said the Authority had no power to light the road ; it was for the ratepayers of the district interested to form a Lighting Committee. —Mr. Whitlow said the road badly needed lightin..—lt was decided that the Clerk should point out to Mr. Fran- comb howthe matter stood.
THE POLLUTION OF KECKWICK BROOK. MR. EARP'S CASE.

Mr. W. R. Earp, of Preston Brook Tannery, accom- panied by his solicitor. Mr. H. J. Longton, of Warring- ton, appeared before the authority to show cause why legal proceedings should not be taken under the Riveis Pollution Act against him for the alleged pollution of Keckwick Brook.—Mr. Earp said he was perfectly pre- pared to risk legal. proceedings, but, acting by the ad- advice of his solicitor, he appeared there to settle the matter if they possibly could.—The Chairman said the Authority had no desire to go to litigation, but, on the other hand, they had a duty to perform which was not of a very pleasant character.—Mr. Earn :,I fully under- stand.—Mr. Longton pointed out in the first place that the fourth section of the Rivers Pollution Act stated that where any poisonous, noxious, or polluted liquid falls in- to a stream along a channel used, constructed, or in course of construction at the passing of this Act shall not he deemed to have committed an offence against the Act if the party who caused the liquid to fall into the stream showed to the satisfaction of the court that he was using the best practicable avaihble means of ren- dering harmless the noxious and polluted liquid falling into the stream. There was abundant evidence that this stream was in existence prior to the passing of the Act in 1876 and that it had been used by the tannery for many years prior to that. Prior to Mr. Earp taking the works lime and also soap waste was used for removing the hair from the hides.— There was evidence that Mr. Earp had used the best available means.—ln answer to Mr. Kirkham, Mr. Long- ton said the water flowed from one pit into another by the top.—Mr.Earp said he had made these pits in the in- terest of himself and the landlord more than anyone else, and he should be able to prove that notone twentieth part of the refuse went from his tannery as compared with any other tannery in proportion to the skins tanned.—Mr. Longton pointed out that the samples of the water of the brook which were the foundation of this case were taken at a dry season when there was nat the customary amount of water coming down, an 1 he went on to show that the brook was a sewer for the locality, and that the Preston Brook which joined it was a sewer for Preston e'th Hill. He contended that the Keetwick Brook was not a stream within the limits of the Acts, and the tannery had been used for 20 years. Sir Richard Brooke wet:the complainant in this case, and if the Authority declined to prosecute le could do so ; but, of course, as any one with commor sense could see, he wanted the Authority to fight his hatle. Mr. Earp and Mr. Lonetnn were requested to rctire whilst the Board considered the matter, and when Nr. Longton was again called into the room he was told that the Authority desired him to furnish the Clerk with a cepy of his evid- ence, and the Authority would take the advice of the Clerk at a future meeting.—Mr. Longton said he did not like to answer for people he had not ender complete control, but as for as he was concerned tho whole of the case was at Mr. Ashton's disposal.
Influenza in an epidemic form prevail; in parts of Dumfriesshire.

An old woman named Mary Clohertw, living at Middleton, was seriously bitten by rats, wh;ch attacked her while she was in bed on Tuesday night. At Liverpool, on Thursday, William lioufh, charged with keeping the Chatsworth Social Club for betting purposes, was fined £25, or two months' imprisonment.

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The Medical Officer (Dr. McDougall) reported that the number of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 33, and of these 8 were due to mesenteric disease, 5 to convulsions, 3 to fever. 2 to diarrhcea, 2 to inflammation of bowels, 2 to heart disease, 2 to inflam- mation of the lungs, and one each to angina pectoris, pernicious anaemia, epilepsy, apoplexy, debility, malig- nant disease of gullet, acute pthisis and premature birth. The above 33 deaths showed an average death- rate for the 12 months of 197 per thousand of the esti- mated population.

div.head: HIGHWAYS AND BUILDINGS COMMITTBS
div.p: HIGHWAYS AND BUILDINGS COMMITTBS

This Committee recommended amongst other things that the footway in Greenway-rd. from Victoria-rd. to York-st., be made with composition pavement, and that Messrs. Dunbar, Kelly, and Co.'s tender to do the work be accepted; that notice be given by the Law Clerk to the United Alkali Co. that unless the fence encroaching on the footway in Greenway-road is removed within fourteen days, proceedings will be taken to enforce the notice ; that a strip of land in Church-st., as shown on plan submitted, be purchased from Dr. Watkins at the rate of per yard. for the purpose of widening the street at that part, and that the present wooden structures be removed within four months from November sth next.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

Mr. John Weston, until recently the agent for Runcorn and Weston Sections of the Ship Canal, is engaged upon his autobiography, and as he has had nearly forty years' experience of public works, in all parts of the country, his narrative should prove highly interesting when published. He is now going in for contracting on his own account,in con- junction with a Wrexham gentleman named Woolley, and the new firm last week tendered for the contract of bringing water from Cowlyd Lake down to Conway a distance of 12/ miles. There were no fewer than 13 tenders from the chief con- tractors of the day, and Mr. Weston occupied a middle place between the highest and the lowest. Eventually Mr. Thomas Bugbird, of Carnarvon, whose son is well-known in Runcorn, secured the contract. He was text to the lowest with £21,050 for 12 inch mains. Mr. Weston's tender was £26,986. I, along with many others, wish Mr. Weston prosperity in his new calling, and hope that at some future day, he will be able to add to his book a few chapters of " reminiscences of a successful contractor."

There is in course of formation in Widnes, a Soiliety which will be known under the title of the "Widnes Educational Association." The prospectus issued states the object of the Association to be the promotion of efficient and unsectarian educa- tion by means of Board Schools in the town and district of Widnes, and this end is to be secured : By holding public meetings and lectures, and pro- moting the diffusion of literature and information, bearing upon the question of education. By being interested in the educational business of Parlia- ment, and the proceedings of the Widnes School Board, with a view to prevent any action being taken unfavourably to the cause of education or inimical, to the interests of the ratepayers. By promoting the election of persons as members of School Boards who are in favour of such an admin- istration of the Education Act as will provide a national and unsectarian system of education. Con- sidering the attitude of Denominationalists towards the School Boards, some answer of this kind is needed, and the objects set forth are very laudable and practicable of attainment.

It it highly gratifying to find the Runcorn Board of Commissioners so eLthusiastic and earnest in the cause of technical education. -The meeting on Thursday would seem to show that they are all united in a desire to carry on the Act thoroughly and successfully, and it speaks well for the public spirit of those who were in a minority on the memorable occasion when Mr. Taylor gave his cast- ing vote that they are heartily co-operating in the promotion of a suitable scheme. Conversion to a good cause is better late than never. The Science and Art Committee have dealt with the subject with promptitude and tact, and their initial efforts have borne good fruit, and if their final endeavours are as successful we may with confidence look forward to having in the near future a Technical Institute worthy of the cause and the town.

In many years of attendance at meetings of public bodies, I have seldom heard applause dur- ing the discussion of business. but Mr. Once, the chairman of Runcorn Commissioners, induced spontaneous and hearty applause on Thursday by his advocacy of technical education. His descrip- tion of Runcorn's three masted barque will make that little ship famous.

Amongst our local Wesleyans the annual foreign missionary celebration is an event anticipated with feelings of pleasure, and the enthusiasm evoked is of a hearty description. Especial interest attaches to the forthcoming missionary services which will be held to-morrow (Sunday) and the meeting which takes place on Tuesday evening. The Rev. Thomas Wilkes who has just returned from America, where he has been taking part in the Ecumenical Conference as a representative frum England, will both preach, and deliver an address, and it is expected that he will have much informa- tion to impart of that interesting and unique as- sembly.

Mr, George Marshall, of Runcorn, formerly chemist in Devonshire Square, has purchased Beacon:4l.dd House, the residence of the late Mr. Thomas Ilezlehurgt. The price given is stated to be .£7oo,and those likely to know say that the mansion and grounds cost over £lO,OOO.

Mr. Brunner, M.P. is not to have a walk over in the North wich Division. There have been rumours for some weeks that the Conservatives had found a gentleman to champion their cause in the person of Mr. A. Hamby Lewis, of Marbury Hall, and on Wednesday a deputation from the Conservative Association was appointed to formally ask him to become their candidate. Mr. Lewis is a young man abotit CO years of age, and is credited with being a capital platform speaker.

The members of the Frodsham Lodge of Free Masons on Tuesday night celebrated the festival of St. John and the ceremony of installing Bro. E. Marston, of Widnes and Frodsham, as W.M. was performed. The Provincial treasurer, Bro. Annett, P.M., and the Provincial secretary, Bro. Woodhouse, P.M., honoured the occasion by their presence.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. TIIIISDAY:—Before Mr. T;..S..Tirmnis and Lieut.-Colonel
Gaskell.

DRUN3HNNESS.—John O'Brien, lklidwool-st. ; Riley, Nelson-st. ; G. McEvoy, no fixed abode; Peter Douglas no fixed abode ;T. itollinson, Ditton ; and James By- lands were charged with being drunk and fined ss. and costs each.

BREACHES OF THE PEACE.—Mary Ireland. Patrick Duggan, and Edward Duggan were bound over for caus- ing a breach of the peace at Widnes, or in default of finding sureties, go to goal for seven days. ASSAULTING THE POLlCE.—Edward Duggan was also charged with assaulting P. C. Moore whilst in the execu- tion of his duty, and was fined ss. ann costs. MUZZLING ORDER.—T. S. Saul, Victoria-road, was ordered to pay costa for allowing his dog to be at large an muzzled.

QllARaiLsomm NRIGHBOURS.—Margaret Tobin ,Welling- ton-street, wassummoned by Mary Walsh, also of Wel- lington-street, for assaulting her. A cross-summons was taken out by Margaret Tobin. The Bench fined each ss. and costs.
THE EDUCATION ACT.—Robert Wright, A. Moss, Mus- pratt-street, J. Houghton,Cronton-lane,and Adam Cook, Railway-street,were each fined ss. for neglecting to send, their children to school.

div.head: lIHALIH COMMITTEE.
div.p: lIHALIH COMMITTEE.

This Committee recommended that Mr. Hankinson be appointed a member of the Committee in the place of Mr. Wynne Humphreys, resigned. That notices be served on various persons to abate nuisances. That the account of £1 owing by Mary Clark, for maintenance in the hos- pital, be remitted.—Passed.

div.head: MORE LIGHT.
div.p: MORE LIGHT.

The General Purposes Committee recommended that three lamps be fixed in York-street, and one bracket lamp moved ; that one lamp be moved in Greenway-rd. ; that the lamp at the west end of Castle Rock-road be moved to the end of Collier-street; that one bracket lamp be fixed in Parker-street ; and that three new pillar lamps be prooured for Waterloo Bridge, in place of old ones.—Passed. • TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

The Parliamentary Committee made the following re- commendation :—That a sum not exceeding £l9O out of the general district rate be handed over to the Runcorn School Board for the purchase of apparatus for the teach- ing of science and art to scholars not receiving instruc- tion at an elementary school, on the understanding that the School Board, on the establishment of a Technical Institute transfer such apparatus to this Board or the Committee having the control or management of such in- stitute,whenever they may be called upon to do so. That the expenses of the deputation to the Department of Science and Art at South Kensington, amounting to £8 ss. 2d., be paid. In moving the adoption of the minutes, Mr. Pritchard said the reason this sum of £l9O was asked:for was in consequence of the Scienee and Art department ceasing to give any grant after the 31st December. Some officers of the department had been waited upon by a deputation from the Commissioners, and those officers informed the deputation of their willingness to assist the Board by giving them the full grant towards the purchaso of apparatus absolutely necessary for instruc- tion at the Science and Art classes. The Department grant would come to 50 per cent, of the cost of the appliances. With regard to the classes already estab- lished they were quite a success. There were seven classes connected with the Science and Art Department, lin which about 150 youths received instruction in the various subjects taught. In addition there were 70 I pupils attending the evening classes, so that altogether, I there were 220 students receiving instruction in the ;evening schools. (Hear hear.) In answer to Mr. Meadowcroft the chairman said after the £l9O was spent there would be £l2O of thc Technical Instruction Fund left.—Mr. Pritchard, replying to Mr. Hankinson, said to purchase the apparatus now would mean a saving to the ratepayers of at least £lOO.—A discussion then took place on a matter of account, and the minutes were passed.—At a later period of the meet- ing the Chairman stated that a deputation from the Science and Art Committee had waited upon the author- ities of Stockport, Stalevbridge, and Hyde and had in- spected the technical schools and institutions. He moved that a communication be sent to Mr. Ralph Bates acknowledging the courtesy with which he received the deputation and the very handsome and hospitable man- ner in which he devoted the whole of the day to their convenience, and facilitated their acquirements of much valuable information.—Mr. Pritchard seconded the Imotion,which was carried.—Mr. Meadowcroft suggested that the Commissioners should be supplied with a list of the apparatus it was intended to purchase and also periodical reports of the proceedings of the technical classes so that they might know what was going on. The Chairman suggested that the information might be in the form of a monthly report from the secretary.— Whatever they did must be done within the scope of that penny, with the addition of wnat they got from the County Council and might receive from private sub- scriptions. The cost of a technical school would be about £3,000. The crest of the Board was a ship with three masts, and this ship could carry a great deal more canvas than she did, and he hoped the time was not far distant when she would be rimy equippea. They had launched her upon the boundless ocean of education, and he hoped that, wafted by favourable breezes, she would gently float int, the haven of prosperity. ([fear, hear and applause.) He paid a high compliment to Mr. Taylor for having given his casting vote in favour of adopting the Act. It was a very honourable position and one lie should have been proud to fill to have the power of deciding a point which would affect Runcorn to all time. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Taylor, in thanking the Chairman, said he was much gratified the other even- ing when he paid a visit to the classes to find so large a number of people from 15 years up to middle age ' taking advantage of the opportunities offered to them. —Mr. Meadowcroft offered his congratulations to Mr. Taylor for his very thorough and sudden conversion on this question. He was quite pleased to find he was so thoroughly in earnest and at one with his colleagues on the question.—Mr. Taylor said Mr. Meadowcroft was labouring under a misunderstanding. Thete was a strong feeling all round that they must know something about the water before they iaunched into levying a penny rate and he agreed that they must have full information. At the time he gave his casting vote in favour of the Act he had made so thorough an investigation that he had made up his mind that it was a most essential thing for the public good of Runcorn and especially the young people. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: MAGAZINE MUTILATION.
div.p: MAGAZINE MUTILATION.

The Free Library Commissioner repo-rted that two no- tices had been posted in the reading-room--one calling attention to the mutilation of magazines by frequenters of the reading-room, and offering a reward of 20s. for information that would lead to the conviction of the offenders—the second called attention to the disorderly conduct of some of the readers, and asked the co-opela- firm of the adults and well-conducted, in preserving or- der, and carrying out the rules and regulations.

FINANCE. On the recommendation of the Finance Committee, accounts amounting to £BlO os.Bd. were passed for pay- ment, and it was decided to accept the tender of Messrs. Dagnall and Co., Cannon-st., London, for the loan of £BOO, for a term of 'seven years, at £3 108. per cent. per annum interest.

div.head: P RESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: P RESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held on Thurday afternoon, when there were present Mr. James Burchall (chairman), Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. Johnson, Tyrer, Marsh, Hallas, Wareing, Davies, Lowe, Goldsworth, Mercer, Ranson, Davies, Kenwright, and A. F. Mann (clerk). RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported that there were 540 inmates this week, 545 last week and 525 in the corresponding week last year. During the week 2,873 persons had been granted outdoor relief at a cost of £239 us. 2d., against 3,167 at a cost of £292 19s. Bd. last year. RESIGNATIONS.—Mr. H. C. Welch and Mr. Thomas Seddon, School Attendance Officers, sent in their resig- nations as school fees inquiry officers, in consequenc, of all the schools in their districts having 'oeen declared free by the adoption of the Free Education Act. VACCINATION LT WIDNES.—The Local Goverment 'Board wrote assenting to the proposed arrangements for public vaccination in the Farnworth and Widnes (Lower) districts. Dr. C. Hutcheson, of Widnes, wrote appointing Dr. A. R. R. Hudson as deputy medical and vaccination officer, and Dr. Had- spn, of the Farnworth district, nominated Dr. Hutchinson as his denutv.—On the motion of Dean Finegan, it was decided to point out to the Local Govern ment Board that tho gentlemen nominated to act as deputies resided outside the respective districts.
. . WOOLTON SCHOOL ATTBSDANCE OFFICSIL. Mr. R. G. Waterman was reappointed school attend- ance officer for the Woolton district at a salary of /70 per annum. This was the principal business.

div.head: CHURCTI ASSOCIATION.
div.p: THE CHURCTI ASSOCIATION.

The Autumnal Conference of the Church Association opened on Thursday at Birmingham. Mr. Boville, chairman, strongly urged the abolition of the Bishop's veto, saying that the laity had now to face a condition of things under which an incumbent might change the form of divine service at his own sweet will without fear of interference. .

_ During the Thursday morning's sitting the, bishops' right to veto in such proceedings as the St. Paul's reredos cas was strongly condemned. In the afternoon a paper was read by Mr. L. K. Rankin on "The rights of the hity and their wrongs,"

div.head: FRODSHA.M.
div.p: FRODSHA.M.

THE LIBERAL Cturt.—On Saturday evening, a lantern exhibition, illustrative of Ireland, its natural beauty, past history, and present misery, was given in the club- room by Mr. Rhodes, the illustrations being explained by Mr. T. A. Rigby, of Sutton Weaver. , MR. JAMES REYNOLDS, J.P., AND THE PRIMROSE LEAGUE. —A public meeting of the Frodsham Habitation of the Primrose League, was held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Monday evening, when there was a large attendance. Mr. James Reynolds, J.P.,ruling councillor, presided,and in opening the proceedings,paid a tribute to the memory of the late Mr. E. A. Wright. The Primrose League, he said, was now about 1,157,000 strong, and he did not think they could find anything in the world that had sprung up in modern times in such a way, and had such an enormous number of people associating themselves together with one common object. Religion was the first object of society, and the second thing was to up. hold the monarchy. Before long they would have an opportunity of displaying the zeal and interest they took in local affairs, in the election of a county councillor for the Frodsham Division. Their friend Dr. Wea.ver,whom he thought every one present knew, had consented to contest the division against the present representative. They wanted to send a man to the County Council in whom they had some reliance.—Mr. R. Wright, a dele- gate from the Grand Council, then delivered an address. During the evening a musical programme was gone through.

PAROCHIAL COMMITTEES.—At the meeting of the Frodsham Township and Lordship Parochial Committee held last evening week, Mr. A. Thomas J.P., presiding, the Town Clerk reported that he had written Messrs. Linnell and Linaker with reference to the land required fsr the water reservoirand pumping station respectively, but as yet nothing definite had been done. It was decided that the Frodsham Gas Company be written to inquiring upon what terms they would guarantee a supply of gas for the proposed gas engine required for pumping, ,the agreement for such supply not to be terminated by either side without six months' notice having been given.—Mr. Heywood inquired whether there was any alternative scheme should no water be found at the proposed site.—Dr. Robinson replied that there was a sufficiency of water in Mr. Linaker's field.— The Inspector also drew attention to the running supply atrive Crosses, near to Mr. Basnett's which he had , gaugen himself for 18 months, the average supply being 32,000 gallons in 24 hours, and suggested that Mr. Timmins be requested to give this as a counter scheme. —The Chairman thought it would not be wise to enter- tain thoughts of that. Allusion having been made to ' the finding of an abundant supply of water when get- ting out the foundations of Mr. Gaskell's house, at Overton, the Inspector,in reply to a question,stated that according to his recollection such supply was a very

large one, but not adequate for a public supply.—The Inspector reported as to certain nuisances in the neigh- bourhood, and called attention to certain cattage pro- , perty at Five Crosses, which had already been a source of annoyance, and it was decided that a Committee, consisting of Messrs. A. Thomas, J.P., Thomas Lewis, R. Bate, W. C. CoHinson, and the Inspector, with Mr. C. E. Linaker, look up the whole thing and report it to the Committee later.

div.head: PEN KETH
div.p: PEN KETH
WALKING THE BOUNDARY

On Thursday the old --custom of 'Walking the- Boundary " was revived here. The party, which numbered about 20, consisted of two of the over- seers, the assistant overseer, and a number of the ratepayers and youths of the village. A start was made about eleven o'clock from renketh Hall Bridge, and after a walk extending over several hours the party eventually reached the starting point about 5.15 p.m. MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.

The opening meeting ef the above association was held on Wednesday evening in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. There was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. T. Gaudy (the presi- dent). An excellent programme, consisting of songs, recitations, pianoforte duets, &c., contributed by the members and friends, was gone through in a most praiseworthy inhnner. During the evening refreshments were handed round and partaken of. A vote of thanks to the friends who had contribu- ted the programme concluded the meeting.

div.head: RE-OPENING OF THE WESLEYAN CHAPEL.
div.p: THE RE-OPENING OF THE WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

The re-opening services in connection with the Wesleyan Chapel, were continued on Sunday. The pulpit was occupied all the day by the Rev. R. Waddy Moss, mathematical and classical tutor,Dids- bury College. There was a good congregation at each service. A collection was taken after each ser- vice in aid of the enlargement fund. The total amount realised was £.lO 128. lid. The re-opening serv;ces were brought to a conclusion on Monday evening, when the Rev. Charles Garrett (of Liver- pool) occupied the pulpit. A large congregation assembled to hear this popular and much respected ministea, the chapel being crowded. Mr. Garrett took his text from St. John i. 3542. At the conclu- sion of the sermon a collection was taken, which realised £8 15s. The total amount realised at all the services is £6O ss.

div.head: LIMM.
div.p: LIMM.

BAND or Hors.—The monthly meeting of the Primi- tive Methodist Band of Hope was held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Eagle-brow. A programme of songs and recitations was gone through, after which the Rev. G. H. Southall gave an address on temperance. A col- lection was taken in aid of the Band of Hiope fund. Mr. G. L. We!ford was in the chair.

" RMIS AND Rumss."—The boys from the Boys' Home, Brideewattr House. Manchester, gave an entertainment in the Wesleva.n Schoolroom on Monday evening, in connection with the Band of Hope. Mr. Edwin Brown presided. A blind boy, Tom Taylor, gave several selec- tions on the English concertina, flute, and whistle. Another boy, Sammy Rhodiss, gave "The Street News- boy." Mr. C. J. Whitney contributed an address on the work of the home.

BURNT TO DRATR —An inquest was held at the Nag's Head, on Tuesday afternoon, touching the death of Elizabeth Pollard, wife of Stephen Pollard, Massey Brook- lane, who was burnt to death on Saturday evening. Mr. Worsley was the coroner.—Stephen Pollard said the deceased was his wife, and was 72 years of age. She was not subject to fainting fits. She had been in the habit of going out against his wish. She held her hands to the fire to warm them on the night in question, and set her clothes on fire. He met her at the kitchen door, and the flames were over her head. He threw the con- tents of a rain tub over her. Dr. Brahazon was sent for, and he prescribed for the injuries. Witness was not above 20 yards away from where the occurrence hap- pmed.—The jury returned a verdict of "Death from. burns."

div.head: CA.DISHEAD.
div.p: CA.DISHEAD.

FoornALL.—On Saturday, Irlam and Cadishead "A team obtained 2 minors against 4 tries and 3 minors by St. Andrew's Manchester. The Ist. team was badly- beaten by Rusholme at Irlam, 8 goals being scored against nil. - TEA MERTING.—On Saturday, a public tea was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. After tea, an "experience meeting" was held in the chapel.. A fair number attended, several of whom gave testimony. The evangelist (Mr. Harkness) and the Rev. B. Yates were also present. • ST. MARY'S Misstow Room.—On Monday the series of - twopenny concerts in connection with the above church mission commenced. 'I he room (tinder the mission room) was fairly filled. Considering that one or two of the- artistes had only short notice, owing to the inability of ' several to fulfil their engagements, the entertainment. passed off in a creditable manner.
ASSAULT ON AN EA.RLESTOWN STATION MASTER. THE RIGHTS OF RAILWAY COMPANIES.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions Ott Wednesday, Jonathan Scranton, son of a fustian cutter, and residing at 49, Elgin-st., Warrington Bridge, painter in the employ ot the London and North-Western Railway Company, was brought up on remand from Newton Petty Sessions, charged with being drunk and disorderly at Earlestown rail- way station, on Saturday night, and with assaulting James Rothwell, night station master, and P.C.. Cameron.—Mr. Browne appeared for the defence. From the evidence of Rothwell, Cameron, P.S. Long- worth, and Peter Fitzackerley, furnaceman, it ap- peared that the prisoner arrived at Earlestown from Wigan by the train reaching the former place at 11.10 on Saturday night. He was accompanied by another man, and they were both drunk. Rothwell asked the prisoner where he wanted to go, and without any further conversation, he struck Roth- well, and knocked him down, and the other man,. held Rothwell, while prisoner kicked him. On get- ting up, Rothwell give information to the police and Swanton was taken into custody.---P.S. Long- worth and P.C.'s Cameron and Middleton went to the man, who refused to give his name and address. P.S. Longworth took him on to the platform and: left him there in charge of Cameron, while he went to get his address. While the Sergeant and Middleton were away, the prisoner threw Cameron down, and when getting up, he kicked him in the chest. When Sergeant Longworth returned a few minutes afterwards, he found them both struggling in the street, and on the ground. As the prisoner continued to kick, the officers carried him to the police station. Upon cross-examination by Mr. Browne, the witnesses said they did not. know what had caused certain serious marks on the prisoner's eye and hand, and the con- stable denied causing them with his baton, or stick, but thought he might have trodden on the. prisoner's hand in the scuffle. —He denied • also causing marks as of a kick on the prisoner's leg, which he exhibited. Mr. Browne also cross- examined Rotnwell as to the prisoner being locked- up, and toointed out that he had no power to give him into custody for assault, as he had done, but only for refusing to pay his fare or something of that sort. The bye-laws of the company stated this. Rothwell admitted that he knew this.—Mr. Browne: There was a similar case only a few weeks ago in which we got heavy damages from the Cheshire Lines Committee for having a man locked up. Mr. Browne admitted that his client was drunk, but said he had received sufficient punishment from somebody for whatever offence he had committed, in the injuries he had met with. Mr. Browne also referred to his client's previous excellent character, and said he had determined to be a teetotaller in future.—The prisoner was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly; and the costs in eaeht of the assault cases.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. BOND, M. P..
div.p: DEATH OF MR. BOND, M. P..

The Press Association says Mr. G. H. -Bond, m.t)., for East Dorset, died at his residence, Cre;ech Grange' Ware- ". ham, on Thursday morning, at bll-past one. He had been ailing for the past 18 Inonths. The immediate cause of death, was congestion of the lungs. Deceased, who was 46 years old, was a Conservative, and at the. election in 1888 had a majority of 655. The Liberal candidate is Mr. W. Maude, who has been forbidden by his medical adviser, to take part in politica/ meetings for the present.

MORE UNSEEMLY CONDUCT TN BANK PARK

At the Warrington Borough Magistrates' Court, on Monday morning, Peter Patterson, a butcher's assistant, and a married man was charged with behaving himself in Bank Park on Sunday morning, in an unseemly man- ner towards Sarah Allen, aged 14, and Sarah Solway aged 12.—Mr. Browne appeared for the defence. Mr. Ashton, assistant park keeper, and Sarah Allen gave evidence. Mr. Browne said the defendant was one to help the police some three weeks ago in trying to catch a man who was doing the very same thing that the defen- dant himself was charged with now. Was it likely therefore, that he would be guilty of such conduct ? He bore an excellent character from his employers. The Mayor said these cases were so frequent in the park that he was beginning to think it would be a good thing if the park were shut up. It was a sickening thing that children of such tender years should be grossly insulted by grown up men, and he would sooner have the park shut up than put to such a use. There were some qualifying circumstances about the case, and the defen dant would be fined 40s. and costs, (£2 9s. Bd. in all) in default a month's imprisonment with hard labour. THEFT BY A FARM LABOURER.-011 Monday, at the Warrington Borough Police Court, Patrick Connelly, farm labourer, was charged with stealing, on the night of the Ist, or the morning of the 2nd lust, a cap and muffler, the property of Anthony Mullins, ship canal labourer, with whom he had been lodging, at No. 6, Percival's- fold. The complainant left the articles hanging behind the kitchen door, on Sunday night, and missed them next morning. The prisoner was apprehended by Detective-Sergeant Monaghan, n the Scotland-road Vaults, and he had then disposed of the articles. The Chief Constable said the case was one of stealing the things to raise the wind for drink. The prisoner was fined 10s. and costs, in default 14 days' hard labour.

THEFT OF CHEESE.—On Wednesday, at the Warrington Borough Police Court, Ann Halliwell, 29, wife of Samuel Halliwell, was charged with stealing,about seven o'clock on Tuesday night, 31bs. of cheese, the property of Sam'l Carter, 155, Mersey-st.—lnspector Bowen said the pri- soner deliberately walked into the shop while Mr. Carter, I the manager' was in the kitchen, went behind the coun- ter, and took the cheese. The mansger followed her into the street, and gave her into the custody of P.C. Wade, George Carter said he saw her steal the cheese.—She was fined ss. ; in default, seven! days. CHARGE OF POACHING.—At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, John William Bradbury, Ellen-street,Warrington, and Llewellyn Howell,of Nichol- son-st., Warrington, were charged that on the lth ult.' , at Burtonwood, they were found coming from land in the I occupation of James Warburton, farmer, being in possession of a gun each, supposed to have been used for killing game. Mr. P. Davies defended. P.S. Devlin deposed to being in company with P.C. Dugdale on the morning of the 18th ult., about a quarter past 8, hearing two shots fired, and seeing the defenda,nts and two other men on Mr. Warburton's land. The defendants and one , of the other men had a gun each. One of the guns was bred, and, Bradbury and one of- the defendants' companions picked something up. They all left the field and he and Dugdale pursued them, and they ran away. About 12 o'clock they met the defendants again on the highway and took their guns from them.—By Mr. Davies: They took the defendants to Warburton's land to see if it was his field they had been in. They did not ask him to go. He took the guns from them before going into the field. He never saw any game in the field but had heard of hares being shot there.—P.C. Dugdale gave corroborative evidence. He said he and Devlin between 8 o'clock and 12 had disguised themselves. Mr. Warburton said he had seen Bradbury in the field often, but witness could not say he complained of his being there. Mr. Warburton never said Bradbury could not do any harm where he was. Bradbury refused to give up his gun, until witness produced the handcuffs and said defendants would be locked up. The Sergeant was close to him at the eime.—A gamekeeper in the employ of the Hon. Leopold Pox Poms, deposed to there being hares, rabbits, and pheasants on the land.—Mr. Davies said his clients had licenses to carry guns, and had the permis- sion of Mr. Warburton to shoot small birds on the land. But it was a nine days' wonder he was going to say to see a sparrow there. Certainly it was to see a pheasant. As to hares he should have thought that the smell from the adjacent Longford depot would have kept them away. But the shots were fired at a quarter past 8, and the defendants were searched at 12, and to prove the case it must be shown that they were coming from the land at that time, but this was not proved. —The Bench fined the defendants 10s. and costs each, their guns to be restored.

div.head: TRANSFERS or LICENSES.
div.p: TRANSFERS or LICENSES.

At the magistr;;;CO-tirt, Warrington, on Monday,the following transfers of licenses were made :—That of the late Wm. Jones, Curriers' Arms, Buttermarket-street, to Frances Jones, his widow ; that of the late Jame Shaw, Shakespeare Inn, Pinner's Brow, to Alfred Shaw, his son. An off license in Leigh-street, lately held by Betsy Unsworth, now deceased, to her son, William tins- worth.

A DETERMINED &tor DOOR THEFT. Edward Crosby, a native of Warrington; 32nd ap- pearance, was charged at the Borough Magistrates' Court on Thursday, with stealing a pair of boots from within the shop door of Messrs. Stead, Simpson, and Nephews. Horsemarket-st., the previous night. A man named Wm. Collier, deposed to seeing him pull away with some difficulty and some noise the boots from a hock within the door,and to informing the shepman. Mr. Kent, the manager, said the prisoner pulled away the boots with such force as to break the hook, snatching at them three times. The prisoner had been apprehended by P.C. Turner with the boots under his coat. He was now sent to gaol for three months with hard labour. CHARGE AGAINST A MARINE STORE DEALER. William Phillips Chorley,marine store dealer,of Butter- market-st., was charged at the Borough Police Court, on Thursday,before Alderman Sutton (chairthan),Alderman Greenall, Councillor James Fairclou,gh, and Capt. Ridg- way, with purchasing 251bs. of brass,this being contrary to the Act, which provides that 561bs. of metal must be the smallest quantity purchased. He was also charged with purcbasing metal from two boys, Arthur Waring and P. Percival, of Warrington, under the age prescribed'by the Act. Mr. Wallhead appeared for the defence, and admitted the charge, but said the things were sent to his tllent's shop on behalf of tradesmen dealing with such things, not taken from a casual person coming into the shop. The metal was taken as part of a large amount, which it was understood was to be sent to him.—The Chief Constable Pointed out that Mr. Chorley, as soon as he had discovered he had infringed the Act, had come down to the Police Station and reported the fact.—Mr. Wallhead referred to the fact of the boys Waring and Percival havinc, been dealt with at the last Newton Petty Sessions, and bound over to come up for judgment, if necessary.—The defendant was fined 10s., including costs, in each case.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATunDAY.--BefoFe Alderman Burgess (i.n.the chair), Mr.
L. Noisey, and Mr. Jolin GE;ddes. CRUELTY' TO HOR4E9.—Richard Martindale was charged with working a horse while in an unfit condi- tion, and Thomas Rowley was charged with allowing it

to be worked on the 24th October.—P.C. Smith said at three o'clock on the date named he was in Horsemarket- street, and saw a large vehicle coming down Cheapside. There were two horses attached to it, and the near one seemed uneasy about the collar. He stopped it, and on examining it found a wound the size of a two-shilling piece. The animal was trembling very much.—lnspec- tor Dowty said that Rowley had lost two horses in three weeks. He had bought the horses without knowing anything about them.—Fined 203. and costs each. • DRUNKENNESS.—Patrick Connor, and Patrick. McLarkin were charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Winwick-street on Friday afternoon. Fined ss. and costs.—Brian Kelly, for the same offence in Old- road, on the 24th October, fined ss.—Ellen Broderick, in Rose-yard, on the 26th October fined ls.—John Casey in BUttermarket-street, on Friday evening, fined 53. and costs.—Peter McLarkin, in Sankey-street, on Friday evening, fined ss. NOT IN HER EIGHT SENSES.—M ary Ann Hanlon was charged with stealing from the dwelling-home of Mr. Wm. Craddock, in Dallam-lane, on the 27th ult., an apron and two handkerchiefs, value Is. Mr. Hunt said the prosecutor was a second-handyclothes dealer, and kept a shop at 13,Buttermarket-st. The prisoner was a domestic servant, and had lived for a fortnight with Mr. Craddock. She was dismissed on the • 22dd, and next day the apron was missed, and afterwards the handker- chiefs. D.S. Monaghan went to the house where pri- soner was lodging, and got some pawntickets from her. He then went to Tunstall's pawnshop and found the apron there. The handkerchiefs were found in pri- soner's possession. Mr. Craddock, in giving evidence, said it was sometimes thought "that tho prisoner was not in her right senses." D.S. Monaghan proved finding the articles. A conviction was recorded. DRUNK AND BEGGING.—Thomas David, for being drunk and begging in Buttermarket-street, was fined 53. and costs.

SCENES IN A LODGING HOUSE,—James Daley was:charged with receiving more lodgers than his house was regis- tered for, for allowing his kitchen to be used as a dwel- ling-house, and for allowing a married couple and another woman to sleep in one room with no partition.between the beds. The offence was committed on the 24th Octo- ber.—lnspector Cox 'said that he, in company with Ser- zeant Cheeney, wont on Sunday last to visit defendant's common lodging-house in Scotland-road. He saw twelve men sleeping in the kitchen downstairs. In a room up- stairs there were four lodgers in excess. In another room he found a man and his wife and another sleeping in the same room.—Sergeant Cheeney also gave evidence as to overcrowding. The house was registered for 52, and there were in it 67-1., the" half" being a child under tea years of age.—Mr. Browne. who Appeared for the defendant, said that the woman was placed in that room by defendant's deputy, who was under the influence of drink at the time. As to the men in the kitchen being allowed to sleep thare, the police had often brought mon to his client's house and asked for them to sleep there when the lodging houses were full, to prevent them from walking about the streets all night.—Mr. Hunt said the house was inhabited by a very low class of people, and Mr. Daley did his best to keep the house as it should be. —The magistrates fined him Ll Us., including costs,for the three offences. _

The defend- ant said it was because the fire was not made.—lle had been convicted before for assaulting her. INSANITARY PREMISES.—Moses Williams, forgeman, 116, Pierpoint-st., was charged by Mr. Norman, sanitary inspector, with keeping his house in an insanitary state. The place, Mr. Norman said, was just like a pigstye. The defendant had been convicted of keeping a lodging- house without a license. All his children were now suffer- ing from some infectious disease.—Mr. Hunt said Mr. Morris, manager of the forge where the defendant was employed, gave him'an excellent character, but his wife was a dirty, drunken woman.—An order was made for the abatement of the nuisance in three days, and a fine of is. a day thereforward till abatement. ABSENTEES FROw SCHOOL. —Mr. Geo. Riley prosecuted the following parents for non-attendance of their child- ren at school.—Francis Cleary, forgeman, Win wick-rd., ss. ; John Craddock, joiner,Orford-st.,Joseph Kirknarn, forgeman, Bewsey,23. 6d. William Monaghan,labourer, Buttermarket-st., is.; Jamas Moseley,forgeman, Lovely lane, ss. ;Joseph Youlter, forgeman, Bewsey-rd.,2. 6d. ; Mary Towey, labourer, eleventh appearance, James Ward, labourer, Friars Green, ss. each. WEDNF.SDAY. —Before Aldermen Holmes (chairman) and Chandley and Councillor James Fairelough. WIFE ASSAULT.—John Tickell, slater, 14, Hind-st., was charged under a warrant with assaulting Ann Tickell. his wife, on Sunday night,by striking her on the eye with his fist. The complainant deposed to the as- sault, and said both she and her father had to sleep from home on the night of the Ist inst., on account of his vio- lence. He made accusations against hereas to other mcn, and threatened her life.—Mrs. Walsh gave evidence, and said the defendant was intoxicated. She saw him abus- inc.,', his father-in-law.—The defendant said the complain- ant had provoked him by insults, and by getting drunk. —P.S. Chantler said the complainant was a very steady woman.—The defendant was bound over in two sureties of £5 each to keep the peace for six months, and mulcted in costs, 103. 6d. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—MichaeI Rabbit, in Irlam- st., on Tuesday afternoon, 2s. 6d. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman). and

Wright. - NON-MAINTENANCE OF A SON.—John Bennett, charged by Inspector Spinks with non-contribution for the main- tenance of his son on board the Clio training ship., was ordered to contribute is. a week. INSANITARY PREMISES.—John H. Potter; 123. Bewsey- road, was charged with not abating a nuisance caused through a defective drain on his premises at 23, Butter- market-st. Mr. Norman, inspector of nuisances, proved the case. He said he had written to Mr. J. Shaw-Green stating that he would withdraw the summons on condi- tion of his writing to him promising to comply with the conditions of the notice for abatement,and he had replied that there must be some misapprehension. An order was made for abatement of the nuisance within three days, and payment of costs. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—Richard Chadwick, sen., of Lythgoes-lane, proprietor of a shooting gallery, was charged by Inspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., with causing a horse to be travelled while in an unfit state in Wilders- pool-road, on the 28th ult.—Mr. Dowty said the horse was excessively lame on the near fore leg and suffering, from enlargettent of the pastern joints, and was being led by the defendant's son, who had been sent to bring it from Warrington to Runcorn, where the defendant was with his gallery. He was fined 10s., including costs. A WOMEN'S QUARREL.—Mary Lowe was charged , with , assaulting Ellen Barnes, a married woman, on Monday last. The complainant said she was coming home after 'taking her husband's breakfast when the defendant, who had been doing mangling at witness's house, and owed her 6d., came up and struck her in the face saying that would pay her.—The defendant said the complainant had been talking about her owing the 6d., and when she called about the matter shut the door in her face and laughed at her over the window curtain. On the day in question witness met her and spoke to her about the matter. The complainant dared her several times to strike her, and she did so. Witness then struck her in the face. The defendant was bound over in the suns of £5 to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay costs, Bs. MORE UNSEEMLY CONDUCT TO FEMALES .—Frederick Sharpies, of Lythgoes-lane was charged with unseemly conduct on the 2nd, 3rd,and 6th inst., in the yard of the old foundry, off Lythgoes-lane, towards Jane Brierly, married woman, of Margaret-st., who on the occasion was standing at her bedroom window. Mr. Brown e de- fended. The conduct of the defendant had been watched from the bedroom window by P.C. Turner,and a woman whom he as took a witness. Mr. Browne pleaded not guiltv.and made a strong defence,but the defendant was fined 20s. and costs, £1 15s. 6d. in all.

Clapin relieved, when Crompton fielded the ball splendidly and sent over to Riley, who failed to receive, and a capital chance was thus lost. A minor point followed, and almost immediately after- wards the" wearers of the green "were again attacking Clapin's charge, but Taylor Wood saved at the expense of a minor point. Passing across the field was mulled by Nicholson, when a good opening presented itself. Davies got in after a smart run by Crompton, but the ball was brought back for some informality, and scrimmaged at the quartet line. Houghton coolly dodged a trio of opponents, but failed to make much headway, and lsalf-time was called with the play in mid- field. The Runcornians got away after the restart, and scrimmaging took place near the home line. Davies essayed at goal without success, and, after a slight relief by Nicholson, Abrams made tracks for the line, but only a minor point was scored. A long kick by Houghton kept the front line well ahead, when Crompton missed an easy chance from a long throw in. Nicholson ran well down, and smart collaring by the Park forwards greatly improved their position, but a wild attempt at goal from the centre kid t the ground, and operations were resumed at the centre. Spence picked op smartly and parted to Nicholson who ran grandly through his opponents, but was brought down near the line. A rush to the centre was followed by a dangerous movement by Crompton, who kicked towards the line. but Anderson was in the way and cleared to the quarter line. Several strong attempts to break through were foiled by Hough- ton, who rid himself of the ball with capital judgment. Loose forward play to the other end gave Nicholson a chance, but the visitors' defence was faultless. A long spell of even play Look place at the centrerCrompton,the one side. and Claniia on the other,keeping their forwards well employed. At length Gayter led on a long rush, and,following a series of tough scOmmages near the line, Davies rushed over and planted the oval between the posts, Crompton adding the premier point. The Park rushed to the visitors' line after the restart, but the ball was quickly scrimmaged clear, and shortly afterwards time was called, with the score in favour of Runcorn by 2 goals (10 points) to nil.

Warrington took a weak team to Kende on Saturday, and they did not expect to win. But thEr unexpected happened on this occasion, for they managed to secure a verdict, though the Hornets did a lot c 4 pressing towards the close of the game.

J. T. Bate, the smart Warrington half back;„, again figured prominently in the County match on Saturday against Cambridee trniversity. At the very opezing of the game he sent a fine pass across to Hurst, and this speedy three6quarter quickly placed the ball over the line. Very soon after Bate picked up from behind a scrimmage and was himself over almost before the other side had preceived *hat he was about. In fact a,ll through the c,rarne he showed brilliant half back play, and proved himself thoroughly worthy of a place in the champion dounty team. Lancashire, it should be added, beat the University by 2 goals, 4;-tries, to 2 goals, or IS:', points to 10.

div.p: RUGBY.

RUNCORN "A " TEAM v. BIRKENHEAD PARK.—This match was played at Runcorn on Saturday. May started for the home team, Gaskell returning with a run to mid-field. May transferred to the Park quarters. Hollingworth getting over, May failing at goal. After the drop out, some very even play was witnessed in mid- field. Gaskell experienced some very hard lines. Hollingworth getting away, transferred to May, who got over in splendid style, from half way. The same player did the needful. Some splendid passing was shown on both sides. At half-time the score was Run- corn, 1 goal, 1. try; Birkenhead Park, nil. Final result —Runcorn, 2 goals, 5 tries, 6 minors; Birkenhead nil. WIDNES V. TYDISSLRY (A. Teams).—This match was played on Saturday, at Widnes. The visitors kicked off, and immediately looked dangerous, but Foster saved well and play was returned to midfield. Widnes next pressed. From a line out, the ball was rushed out to the visitors' goal line, and Morris got over, placing the ball between the posts. The same player failed at goal. Tyldesley next ran the ball into the home quarters, and seemed likely to score, but missed several good chances. Widnes began to press again, and repeatedly tried the visitors' d3fence very severely, but nothing further waS scored. Half-time score : Widnes, one try • Tyldesley, nil. Final result: Widnes, seven points ; Tyldesley, nil.

WARRINGTON Sr. MARY'S V. 13-ROUGIITON AMATEURS. —At Broughton. The Saints won the toss, and the Amateurs kicked off, with a slight wind behind them. The game started very fast,and after about ten minutes' play, one of the Amateurs' backs made off with the ball, but Hampson ran up and took the ball clean from him and scored near the posts, the kick at goal failing. Soon after the drqw-out. the homesters scored, but the kick at goal failed, and at half-time the score was a try each. On changing ends the Saints played up splendidly, the backs kicking and passing well, the forwards showing up in the loose, and the game soon settled in the Aim: ateurs' 25. where Bennett picked up and scored a neat try, Holsby kickinc, a goal. The Saints charged the kick off, and rushed' the ball down the field, Longmore scoring. the point again being improved. Directly after Carey outran his opponents and scored behind the posts, Helsby kicking the goal, the game ending in a decided win for the Saints by 3 goals, I try to Amateurs I try.

WARRINGTON RANGERS V. STOCKTON HEATH.---Thege local teams met on the ground of the former on Satur- day. The home team kicked off, and the opening stages found the Heathens defending. The game was confined to the forwards, the Rangers proving far too smart for their opponents in this department. Thompson and Clarke had repeatedly hard lines in not securing a tang- ible point, as it was only the effective tackling of the visitors that prevented certain scores. Not to be denied, however, the Rangers kept up the attack, and at last, taking advantage of a mull, Whitfield rushed up and secured the first point for the homesters in a favourable position, but Clarke failed at goal. Nothing more of importance occurred up to half time, when the score read—Rangers, 1 try, Z minors ; Stockton Heath, nil. Upon the restart, both teams played with great dash, Lawless for Stockton Heath shining conspicuously. On one occasion that player finely intercepted a pass in- tended for a Ranger, and punting well down the field, forced the home team custodian to kick dead. The game continued to be stubbornly contested,. Clarke and Savage, for the Rangers, Brodie and Cross for the visit- ors, being prominent by their good play. The latter portion of the game was all in favour of the homesters, Massey having hard lines in having the ball kicked from under him when just on the point' of grounding, and a minor only was recorded. Nothing further was scored, and the game finally ended in a win for the Rangers, by 1 try, 3 minors to Stockton Heath 1 minor. WARRINGTON "A" V. STrDON.-The " A" tearn..after an absence of several weeks, again made their appear- ance on the Wilderspool ground, but owing to the late arrival of the visitors, the game was considerably de- layed. The opening of the contest was sensational enough to satisfy anybody, a&some grand passing be- tween Lawless, Lally, Potts, and Webster enabled the latter to romp over in the first minute, Turner making a fine attempt at goal. Frorrathe drop-out Sutton were assuming the offensive, bur, following some kicking be- tween the rival backs, a bout of passing amongst the home forwards gave Daniels possession, who, after getting clear of his opponents, lost a try by passing. This was succeeded by a smart piece of wark by Foulds which was, however, more than, nullified by Daniels's kick, and some strong forward play, in which Knowles and Buckley were notable, carried the leather to the line,. Lawleas scoring. Warburton placed a goal. Immediately upon the resumption of hostilities, Bailey made a capital, run into the Sutton quarters, where La.wless threw to Webater, whose kick was mulled, Russell gaining a further try. The visitors were showing poor abilities, and were con- stantly pressed, until off-side by Warrington tookt play to the centre. The stay was ofshort duration,for, through the instrumentality of Daniels and Lally, the oval was forced to the goal, and from a kick across- Webster secured his second try. Directly after the kick-off, Daniels threw grandly across to Webster, the visitors' defence being taxed in consequence,and although Sutton subsequently transferred the scene of warfare to midfield, Hampson, Rowlands;and Warburton renewed the attack.. Potts hereabouts picked up and ran splendidly through his antagonists, obtaining a try, and half-time arrived with Warriogton 1-4-0 to nil. Re-starting, a run and kick by Warren made matters more even for the visiting team, but matters soon settled down as a counterpart of the former,half, Buckley, Thampson, Turner, and Russell showing up. Lawless then got away, and passed finely, but the chance was missed, a minor accruing. Following this, an incursion into the Warrington half by Wilson came as a welcome innovation, but Rowe, Buckley, Knowles, and Hampson soon had the leather fluttering about neutral territory. A mis-kick here let in Lally, who ran in splendidly from half-way, and a minor was afterwards conceded. A run by Potts counterbalanced the Sutton men's effort to get away, but finally Dale, Carrigan, and Foulds broke through to the home 25, Lawless, Knowles, Bailey, and Rowlands retaliated, another minor being conceded. The light was now get- ting bad, making it difficult to follow the game, although from a pass by Daniels, Webster got his third try. This was succeeded by Lally obtaining another grand try from midfield, the same player placing a goal, and the game ended—Warrington, --3;2 Sutton, nil. TYLDESLEY v. WIDNES.

Played at Tyldesley, on Saturday. Splendid play by Hanson and Berry kept the visitors defending. The In- ternational half got over, Shaw kicking a goal. Berry got roughly handled and retired, giving the visitors an opening. Shaw kicked well, putting his men on side. Shepherd got overt but the ball was ruled back. Berry here reappeared and made a good run, but lost his ball. Plumpton dropped at goal, the ball going dead. The same player scored, Brannan kicking the goal. Half- time score—Tyldesley, 1 goal; Widnes, 1 goal. Final result—Tyldesley, 1 goal, 5 minors; Widnes, 1 goal, 4 minors.

div.head: BIRKENHEAD PARK v. RUNCORN.
div.p: BIRKENHEAD PARK v. RUNCORN.

These clubs met on the Upper Park enclosure on Sat- urday before a capital attendance of spectators. The teams were as follows :---Runcorn—Houghton, back; Davies, Crompton, and Pendlebury, three-quarter backs; Abrams, and Evans, half backs; Faulkner, Riley. Hughes, Williams, Gayter, Hampson, Shaw, Massey,and Dolan, forwards. Birkenhead Park—A. C. Clapin, back; E. T. Nicholson, H. Hale, and J. D. Anderson, three- quarter backs ; A. H. Spence, and A. M. Ker, halfbacks; T. W. Lockwood, P. H. Lockwood, A. G. Wood, G. D. White, A. J. Chadwick, C. F. Anderson, C. Craig, and J Baxter, forwards. A start was not effected till half an hour after the advertised time, when T. Lockwood kicked off for the Park. Riley returned to half way, and following a sharp rush into the Runcorn half, the home van dribbled strongly down, and the ball was taken over the line, but only a minor point accrued. Following the drop-out Hole missed the ball, and heavy scrimmaging took place at the Park quarter line. Crompton checked a couple of rushes,and the visiting forwards kept the play closely confined to the home line, until Houghton had a shie at goal, which went wide to Nicholson, and passing to Hale, the Runcorn 25 was reached. With a big effort the Park forwards got within -a few yards of the line but a strong push, followed by a capital punt from Davies, quickly changed the venue. A rush to the Park end caught Clapin faulty, for failing to hold the ball,Faulkner kicked on and registered a;try near the post, which was easily converted by Crompton. Cen- tral play ensued, when a fine passing movement among the visitor's, forwards took place, but a penalty kick to the Park neutralised matters, and a moment later, when Riley failed to pick up, scoring seemed certain for the home side. Houghton came to the rescue, and Craig replied with a fair, catch ; but Nicholson's attempt went wide of the mark: Smart following up gave the

div.head: WARRINGTON VI KENDAL HORNETS
div.p: WARRINGTON VI KENDAL HORNETS

This annual favourite fixture was opened on Saturday at Kendal in charming weather. Fully 1,500 spectators assembled, almost a record gate for a club match in dais district. That Warrington have one of the best reserve teams in the country was fully borne out OA the present occasion, fer,although six of the usualfirst team failed‘to make the journey,a call was made on the "'champion 'A' team," and creditably were the places filled. "Smack "Bate, of course, was an absentee, no doubt i reserving his energies for Wednesday in, the' match Lan- cashire v. Cambridge University. The Hornets had all on, with the exception of Braith- waite, and at 3.15, Ashton kicked off with the sun in his eyes. A capital start was mode,.as the kick-off gravi- tated into touch about five yards from the line, Kendal never recovering the lost ground until disaster had be-- f allen them. Kendal got the oval working amongst their backs, but Heesom and Barnes tackled their men surely, and Antrobus was almost in from a pass, by Bate. As. kick from Hine travelled to Barnes.. who made tracks through the thick of his opponents, and passing to Hee- som, the latter transferred to EVans, but the chance was slowly taken, and the last-named was pulled up under the posts. Heesom again shone brilliantly,, and Ashton heading his forwards, who were playing. a brilliant game, took play in the mouth of the Hornets' goal. Berry on three occasions foiled Hine in his effort to clear, but eventually a cross dribbling movement was-snapped up near the line, and Berry, Thornley, and Teare passing. well, the last-named dashed over in a favourable posi- tion for Heesom to kick a goat. The drop out was well. returned by Barnes, and his brother tackled Winskey: well before he could reply. However, E.' Wilson dribbled fast, and for a while play was at the half-way, Hine and Boscow on one occasion exchanging kicksariver their for-- wards. Heesom got clear in intercepting a, pass to Allan; but unfortunately knocked on when but a few yards- from the line. The home forwards again. displayed won- derful art in the dribbling line, and ably led by Wilson and Parsons, Boscow had all his work cut out' to save his goal. His cool demeanour served him well, and taking the rushes without the least fear, drove the hemesters back with excellent screw kicks. TfieWarrington quar- ter fiag had been reached, and Randles. Teare, Moly- neaux, and Donohue each was prominent in several rushes. Railton, Hall, Wilson, and Allan passed well, ad play was on the line, but Ashton again showed his able judgment, for, collecting his forwards,they wheeled the scrimmage finely, and the movement realized relief to the half way. Sure tackling was the order., and then from another attack, the Hornets kicked death No soenerhad the drop out been effected than Antrobus got clear,• and running down the open, passed short to Heesom, with the result that Hall tank the oval, and handing over to Wilson and Railton, the latter punteal past Boscow, and a try was the result, Winskey beings credited with the point. The Kendal men were still having the better of it, and a couple of minors fell in quick succession from long kicks. On one occasion Thornley got away with a twenty-five yards run and then passed Heesom, who handed to Barnes, who punted to Hine,. ,only to find the" Kendal custodian punting with advantage. Beard got clear from a line-out, but the tackling had not deterior- ated, and another minor falling to Kendal, the latter point brought half-time—score, Warrington, a goal;: Kendal, a try and four minors. Oa resuming Barnes showed up with a run and kick into the7a7endal quarters, and another determined raid was made on the home 'Although Parsons, Hall, and Heap reliovod, the sound play of the Warrington forwards soon had the ball back 'again. Antrobus ran finely, but Winskey intercepted his pass. Barnes, Heesom, Evans, and Boscow kicked well, beingably seconded by a display of cross dribbling,Hine saving on the line. Boscow staved off many attempts to clear, and from a rush, the oval was taken over and Donohue scored, Boscow failing with the place. This success of Warrington infused some spirit-in the Kendal ranks, and direct from the drop out the oval was taken to the line, a minor accruing. Warrington defended ad- mirably, and Heesom and Evans werein turn applauded for fine tackling. Barnes and Bascom- with judicious kicking kept their opponents at bay,. and the monotony was relieved when Bate put in a tricky run, which affbrt was seconded by Donohue, Handles,. and Davies, half way being reached. Mulling on the part of the Hornets can be accounted for by the sharpness of the Warring- tonians. Boscow was in fine formi.and his kicks never missed finding touch. The last stagas of the game were chiefly noticeable for the fine defensive attitude set up by Warrington, and Kendal ,were frustrated in all their movements to equalize, a grandgarne ending in a victory for Warringtan by a goal and/ a try to a try and six minors.

Teams :—Warrington : Boscevr,.back ; Barnes, Heesom, and Evans. three-quarters;: Bate and Antrobus, half back; Ashton, Bandies, Davies,,Ber.y, Donohue, Thorn- lev,A. Barnes, Molyneux, and Teare, forwards. Kendal Hornets: Hine, back; Railton,. Allan. and Winskey, three quarters; Hall and Heap, half backs ;E. Wilson, W. Wilson, Parsons, Beard, Simm, Thompson, Mitchell, Whiteley, and Nicholson, forwards. ,

FOOTBALL. At a meeting of Lancashire County Committee, held in Manchester on Thursday night, the following team was chosen to represent the county against Cheshireat Whalley Range to-day (Saturday :—T. Coop (Leigh), back '• W. M'Cutcbeon na (Oldm), J. B, Stork (Liverpool), and F. Miles (Salford), three-quarter backs; S. J. Berry (Tyldesley), and W. Cross (St. Helens), half-backs ; S. J. Pyke (St. Helens Recreation), E. Bußough (Wigan), F. Kent (Salford), H. Flaslam, (Manchester Rangers;, It. P. Wilson (Liverpool, Old Boys), W. Holmes (Barrow), J. Jolley (Warrington), R. M. Masters (Leigh), and P.. Steel (Manchester), forwards.

The transfer of playersfrom one club., to another can-- not now be easily accomplished. Somehow or another these transactions have eome to be looked upon with suspicion, an from the action of the Lancashise autho-- rities during the past few days it is sometimes well grounded. inducements are not infrequently held out which do not conform co the laws of • amateurism, and they will not bear investigation in every case. The laws can scarcely be made too strict, but their enforcement seems to mean the expenditure of a. good deal of valuable time and, a vast amount of trouble..

There were six League games down for settlementon Saturday, and the usual surprise was furnished by the decisive overthrow of Everton at Deepdale. The interest in this return fixture was shown by the big attendance, 12,000)spectators being present. The North End once again demonstrated their superiority over their Liver- pool rivals, who have never yet beaten the Prestonians in a League engagement. This time theverdict was four to none in favour of the home team. The passing of the victors was splendid and the defenze superb. There were also 12,000 persons present at the match between the Wanderers ard the Blackburn Rovers at 80/ton. Two old stagers turned out for the. last-named, these being Arthur in goal and Douglas at half back. The Wanderers won bF four tetwo. but there was not that difference in the ex.--,zhanges, the Rovers playing , extremely well at times,

There seems to be a falling away in the play of Dar- wen, who for the last two or three weeks have done very badly. Thw were easily polished off by Aston Villa, although the clubs met at Barley Bank. Accring- ton were away at Sunderland, and, there too, the Lan- cashire club had to accept defeat. Derby county were triumphant cver Wolverharopton, and West Bromwich Albion were lust able to hold their own with Notts County.
