NEW WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOLS AT SANNEY BRIDGES.

For years past the Sunday school accommodation for the Wesleyan connexion at - ankey Bridges has been poor and insufficient.. The scholars have steadily increased, until now there are more than 200 on the books. The roora until recently in use was the old iron building formerly used as a preaching room. To carry out the new, scheme ad- ditional land has been secured both' at the side and back of the chapel. The new school and class rooms will be behind the chapel, ample spac& being left for a future chapel enlargement;: also. for a care- taker's house. The estimated outlay is about £1,350. The friends on the spot have given and are working nobly, and others are proffering generous help. I:600 in subscriptions has been already pro- mised. A bazaar will be held in the spring of next year from which large things are- expected, and it is confidently boped that the whole of the cost will be defrayed within a short time of the opening:. Owing to the necessity of cutting down the ex- pense, no architectural effect has been aimed at in these schools, but rather an increased acconamoda- tion,combined with a good and sound'constritction: _

' The new schools when completed will consist of a general meeting ha 11,49 feet lowg by3Ofeeb broad, a young men's class room 20 feel long by 15 feet broad, an infants': room 20 feet long by 15 feet broad, and a young- women's class-room about 14 feet square,toge,therwith three .smaller class rooms. At the end of the general meeting halltfacing the entrance a rostrum will be formed,. apprcatted by steps on each side, and fitted with a,reading. desk. The building will be faced on the outside with ,Padgate grey brick-z,- relieved withtruabon red • Dressed brick strinres and eaves courses and York _ stone dressings. The inside wails of the general meeting hall will be lined with white, Aston. halP bricks . above a red pressed brick dado. The joinerstWork will be executed in pitch 'pine throughout and stained• and Tarnished to an approved tint. Full and ampJe means have been adopted to ensure efficient ventilation by means of fresh air inlet shafts, Dobin tubes and: ap- proved extract ventilators placed in the ceiling. The building vvill be heated by means of pipes and coils welred on the high pressnreisystem,.. The work.is-being carried out from thedesigns and under the superinten- >dence of Mr. Percy Silcock, architect,. and 41r. John Longshaw, builder, Parker-it., Warringtoni

div.head: 31MORT&I,,STON'ES
div.p: 31MORT&I,,STON'ES

, The laying of the memorial stones of the new.Stinday 'school took place on Saturday-afternoon; A preliminary service was conducted by theßev:J. Gunnell,superinten- dent minister. There was a large congregation. The rev. fzentletnan delivered an address: The necessity, of the provision of the new sckeol . and class rooms-must, he said, be patent to every one • of. them who knew the ;facts of the case. From the erection of the chapel in,the year 1884, to the present time they had had very poor and inadequate accommodation for their , Sunday Sohool and Church purposes, and the inconvenience had been felt notably as to the former, because the- iy-epula- don of the neighbourhood had4grown steadily-frorn,the time the chapel was built; and during the past two years it had grown rapidly. If he might judge from the num- ber, of children they had to baptise the population ,renst be a very prolific•one, and it was only right that they should make provision for its growing needs: The first difficulty they had to contend within seeking-. to do this was the limited space they-had at command. They hadlound the land at their disposal not sufficient toeneet their requirements, and had acqqired an additionalpiece. Theland would be vested in the same trustees -as held the chapel, the tenure being 3dasehold. They could not obtain a freehold in that neighbourhoed , and, The term of lease- was for 999 years. He hoped somebody there would be living to , see that terminated. ..(Laughter.) Theybad the land at a yearly rental of £7.1.15.; that capitalised at 2A years' „purchase was about £l5l, which they took to be the I value-of the additional land.. At a meeting held in December in the chapel, the-scheme was launched, when there-was a most generous response on the part of the friends of the chapel, and in the course of an hour or less, there were promises o 2 'about £4.00. Considering that with one or two exceptions, the population con- sisted of the artisan class, this was remarkable, and he might say the like of it he had never seen in his expe-• rience. The rev. gentleman explained the nature of the -axiditionial accommodation: to be provided, which in— cluded, in iddition to a-large -room for Sunday school,: and church purposes, six class-rooms and two vestries.. The plans, he ssid, had been entrusted to Mr. P. Silcock,, and the work of building had been let to Mr. Longshaw4 for the sum of £1,011; :bat to allow for furnishing and extras,£l,3s3 would bethe least that would be required,, which was, he was-surprised to find, only 2310 different from.the estimate for building the chapel in 1884,:£1,3431 The subscriptions amounted to £6OO ; and he calculated that the bazaar, opening services, &c., would brink this up to £893, so thatthero. would still be a.,deficiency of £sBo': They must not rest upon their oars, but con, time to ply them very Vigorously until they got tothe end of the debt. The rev, gentleman apologised for the fact that there was no tea meeting that day by explain- ing that there was no oonvenient place foe the purpose. —ln the course of the service hymns wore sung by the children.—After the service the congregation proceeded to the site of the new sobool where four memorial stones were laid, one, after the other, by -the following persons :—Mrs. Garnett, who laid a cheque for :ZCI on the stone, Mrs. Freeman, who contributed 25 guineas, Mrs. Gunnell, who performed the duty on behalf of Mrs. Thoraas Starkey Smits, whose contri- bution was £25,-- and Mrs. Ross, who laid a stone on behalf of Mr. W. Barlow who though/present, dithnot as, was explained by-Mr. Gunnell, feel quite equal to the taskhimself, The contribution for this stone amounted to £25. Mr. Broug,h, on behalf of the teachers and officers of the school, thanked Mrs. Freeman and her husband for the kindly interest they had taken in the • work being carried on at Sankey Bridges. The &Imlay school children having laid their offerings on the Stone, amounting to £lolls. 9c1., a number of bricks ware. by invitation, laid by different persons, whose contribu- tions amounted to £lO 10s. Among those present at the service, and the subsequent ceremony were the following ladies. and gentlemen :,—The Revs. J Gunnell, T. Ross„, and. A.. Freeman, Mr. and Mrs. and the Misses Garnett, Mrs. R,Cook, Mr. and Mrs. C. E: Parker,,Mr. and Mrs. G. Silcock, Mr. and. Mrs. James Summersgill, Mrs. Snoddy, Mr. W. Brough, Mr. S. B. Stringer, Mr. W. Hickman, Mrs: Ross, Mrs. Free- man, and Mr. W. Barlow; Mr. and Mrs. Charita Doig, Miss B..Dutton, Mrs. Sncddy, jun., Mr. and Mrs. Join 'Waring, Mt. and Mrs. Bailey, Mr: Biddle,„, and Miss Clark.

A Reuter's New York telegram says Rio Janeiro, despatch to the "-Herald,'" dated Wednesday, says the fight betwebn Congress and Marshal Poodore da Fonseca has. reached a climax. The President, being a military man, many fea7ed he might proclaim, himself dictator. To prevent this Congress passed a. law determining the process by which the President of the Republic could be impeached. The President vetoed the, measure, but his veto was overruled by' Congress., The President there- upon dissolved Congress, and z decree was published yesterday. Martial law, was at the same time proc]aimed at Rio and other States of the Confederacy. The disso- lution of Congress may result in the choice of another President_ In case of an uprising, Marshal da Fonseca will probably have the Army and Navy solidly at his back.

Mr, WlSinley, Republican candidate for tha governor- ship of Ohio„ and author of the famous Tariff Bill, has been elected by a majority believed to be at least 14000 votes. Mr. Campbell, the defeated governor, is a Democrat..

Great excitement prevails irl Birmingham, Pennsyl- vania, owing to six brutal murders having been perpe- trated under mysterious circumstancee within the last few days. All the victims were brained with an axe, and the perpetrator is believed to be an insane negro. The date fixed for the opening of the Liverpool Assizes, according to present arrangements, is the 3rd of December, the judges being Mr. Justice Lawrence and Mr. Justice Collins. div.head: FASCINATING LION.
div.p: A FASCINATING LION.

About sixty years ago, according to Gerrard, the Lion Hunter, a young man named Seghir, belonging to the tribe of Amamera, established in the Aures mountains, fell in love with a young girt who had been refused to him by the father on account of his poverty, The young people, however, were much attached to each other, and one fine evening the girl ran away with her lover. The distance being considerable between the two douars,* and the road extremely perilous, Seghir had armed himself from head to -foot. Already the most dangerous part of the road had been cleared, and they were beginning to hear the dogs of the douar towards which they were rapidly advancing, when all at once a lion, who till that moment had lain concealed behind the bushes, rose and walked straight towards them. The young girl shrieked so fearfully that her cries were heard by the people in the tents, and several of the men immediately seized their arms and rushed out to the rescue. When they reached the spot to which they were directed by the screams of the young maiden, they saw the lion walking slowly a few paces in front of Seghir, with his eyes stead- fastly fixed upon him, and leading him thus towards the forest. The young girl did all she could to prevent he.r lover following the lion, or induce him to let go herself, but in vain , he kept dragging her on in spite of all her efforts, saying: "Come, my beloved, come; our master will have It so; we must go!" "But your weapons," she cried; "what are they good for if not to save me ? " "Weapons? I have none I" answered the fascin- ated wretch. Then addressing the lion, he said: " Great lord, believe her not: I am perfectly un- armed, and will follow you wherever you will." At this moment the Arabs, eight or ten in num- ber, who had come to the rescue of the unfor- tunate couple, preceiving that the lion would very soon have them in the forset, fired, every one of them, upon him; but on finding that he did not tall, they took to their heels. The lion sprang upon Seghir, and with one bound crushed him to the earth, smashing his head at a bite; after which he lay down by the side of the young girl, placing his buge paws upon her knees. • The Arabs now finding tbat the lion did not condescend to pursue them, took courage and returned and having reloaded their guns, prepared again to fire; but being afraid of killing the girl, they told her to try to get a little way from the lion, which he allowed her to do, without ever los- ing sight of her. The moment the guns of the Arabs were levelled at him, the lion sprang Into the midst of them, seized one with his teeth and two others with his claws, dragging them together, so as to make, as it were, one bundle; then, 'placing under him that mass of palpitating flesh he instantly smashed the three heads, as he

bad done that of Seghir. Those who escaped ran to the douar and told the story, but no one was bold enough to return for another attack. The lion then carried the woman into the forest. Next day the Arabs came to carry away the bodies of the four men; as to the young girl, nothing was found but her hair, her feet, and her clothes. Is it true that the lion has the power of fascina- tion over weak organisations? All I can say is, that the Arabs answer in the affirmative, and give _numerous examples. * A douar is an Arabian village.
MILITARY PEDANTRY-WELLINGTON'S STRATEGY.

. The issues of modern warfare do not depend solely, or even mainly, upon stereotyped strategical combinations. A live, wide-awake, energetic, active enemy cannot be mechanically fought down by rule and plan alone. The general who expects to make a name or save a nation in these days, should be fertile in expedient, prompt in action. His brain should be constantly on the alert for favourable opportunities to strike, and he should be able to turn them to account there and then. Dash, daring, enterprise, and quick intelligence are essential to success in almost all callings, and above all in military affairs. Often has the proverb, "he who deliberates is last," peen literally verified on the battle-field. Take an authentic anecdote in illus- tration of the fact.

On a certain occasion during Wellington's cam- paign on the Pyrennees, that "Great Captain" being displeased with the dispositions General Picton had made for receiving the assault of Marshal Soult, who menaced him in front, ordered the plan to be entirely changed. But the difficulty was to delay the attack of the French until the change could be effected. This the "iron Duke" accomplished in person, in the following manner. Doffing his cocked-hat and waving it in the air, he rode furiously to the head of a regiment, as if about to order a charge. Thereupon arose a tremendous cheer from the men, which was taken up by corps after corps until it reverberated along the whole extent of Picton's line. As the roar died away. Wellington was heard to remark, musingly, as if addressing himself—" Soult is a skilful but cautious commander, and will not attack in force until he has ascertained the meaning of these cheers. This will give time for the sixth division to come up and we shall beat him." It turned out as be anticipated. Soult, naturally enough supposed those tremendous shouts announced the arrival of large reinforcements, and did not attack until too late. Had he struck at the right moment he would have won an easy victory; as it was, he met with a bloody repulse.

div.head: "NEAR ENOUGH TO CHOLERA."
div.p: "NEAR ENOUGH TO CHOLERA."

Daring the camping of a regiment of regular troops at Santa Rosa, Cal., the picket found con- siderable difficulty in preventing the men from ab- senting themselves without leave, a circumstance for which the mintjuleps of the town bar-room and the large contingent of pretty Santa Rosa girls were chiefly accountaole. . _ _ . . . _

One particularly sultry evening while the sentinels were pacing their beats, with their tongues fairly banging out of their mouths with heat, and wonder- ing whether the pirates in the mess-tent would drink every last drop of beer before the " relief " came, one of the guards observed a private approach- ing who was staggering about in a state of great conviviality and with an enormous water-melon under each arm.

"Who goes there?" challenged the sentinel. 4, Er—hic--er frien'," responded the truant. "Ad- vance, friend, and give the countersige." " Hain't got no—hic—countersign," amiably replied the private; "but I 'll er—hic—give yer er—hic— water-melon."

Pretty soon the officer of the day came round, and said to the sentinel, who was absorbed in munching a huge piece of water-melon stuck on the end of his bayonet: "Did Perkins pass you just now?" "Yes, sir." "Did he give you the countersign?" inquired the lieutenant, taking a bite himself as the man presented arms. "Well, no, sir," said the sentinel, confidentially ; "the pass-word was 'Cholera,' but he said 'Water-melon;' so I passed him, and put the other half in your tent.'
"Did, eh ?" mused the officer. "Hum ! Water- melon—eh? Well, I guess that was near enough to cholera I"

div.head: STABLING THE "OLD HOSS.*
div.p: STABLING THE "OLD HOSS.*

An anecdote is told of the early days when court was first held in Pittsburg, Penn, in a log tavern. An adjoining log stable was used as a jail, the stalls answering as cells for the prisoners. Judge T. was on the bench, and in the exercise. of his judicial functions severely reprimanded two young lawyers who had got into a personal dispute. A herculean backswoodsman, attired in a red flannel shirt, stood among the auditors in the apartment. He was much pleased at the judge's lecture—having him- self been practising at "another bar "—and hal- looed out to his worship, who happened to squint: "Give it to 'em old gimlet-eyes!" "Who is that 7" demanded the judge. He of the flannel shirt proud of being thus noticed, stepped out from among the rest, and drawing himself up to his full height, vociferated: "It's this here old hoss 7"
The judge called out in a peculiarly dry, nasal tone: Sheriff, take that old hoss,' put him the stable,' and see that he is ' not stolen ' before morning.
TERRIBLE RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN
INDIA.
TEN EUROPEANS KILLED.

BOMBAY, THURSDA Y.—A terrible accident has occurred to the mail trimn to Naupur, through the engine wheel breakin, :.he train vt-:t s partially wrecked. Ten were killed, inc': five five British soldiers, and about forty injured, int:iuding 31 Ilritish soldiers. The accident has causecl a gre:ti sensation.

div.head: Ik 1 k
div.p: Ik 1 k
MR. PEERS AND HIS BANTLING.

Sir,—lt is very satisfactory to find that, while Mr. Peers frankly professes agnostic tendencies, he, at the same time,admits that an agnostic can know something, ven though it be but his own ignorance. Such an ad- mission is all I want, for in precise proportion as an agnostic admits that he can know anything, in the same proportion does he become gnostic ; and, in so far, does his position conflict with the principles of agnosticism. This is seen more particularly when Mr. Peers places the gnostic " at one end of the scale," and the agnostic at the other. Now, in his former letter he defines the gnostic as "one who knows" : and if he places the agnostic "at the other end of the scale," it must be as one who does not know, that is, an ignoramus. Amor- dim:ly, Mr. Peers in this instance, exposes himself to the charge of the very ignorance with which he cr edits me.

It is only zidiculous for Mr. Peers to say that a gnostic professes to know all things, human and divine. Such a knowledge would amount to omniscience,and this know- ledge no finite being can possess. Nor is his attempt to prove that the gnostic knows, not merely all things human and divine, but the " Unknowable " any more successful. Such a paradoxical statement falls far more heavily on Mr. Peers himself, for he admits that the ag- nostic knows that "there are many things that he does not know." Now, in so far as he does not know them, they are unknowable ; and, therefore, it is Mr. Peers who maintains that ha can know the "Unknowable." Beedes, it is impossible for Mr. Peers to prove the exist- ence of the " Unknowable " without having recourse to ineZaphysical arguments. Such a course might be par- donable in a metaphysician who lived in the darkness of the middle ages, but sits ill upon the man who professes agnostiesm in the 19th century, and who accordingly is supposed to fling metaphysics into the limbo of the unknowable.

Mr. Peers's criticism of the statement I made regard- ing the "logical position of the laws of nature" is far from satisfactory. He here quotes only the first half, and the least important part of the sentence. The point in discussion, I said, was not the " logical position of prayer ; but the logical position of the laws of nature; or what I prefer to term the scientific aspect of the laws of nature." Mr. Peers. pouires upon the first part of the sentence; and emphasizing it into italics, entirely ignores the second and most important part. My reason for preferring the second part was that the first was "unmeaning " if not absurd, as Mr. Peers maintained, and the same objection applies to Mr. Peers's statement, viz :—" The logical position of prayer." Again, what he says concerning my statement regarding the laws of chemistry modi tying the law of gravitation, is a misre- presentation. By this, I do not mean that the laws of chemistry were different on one of the planets to what they were on our earth, what I said had no application to distance. According to the law of gravitation each atom in the universe attracts every other directly as the mass, and inversely as the square of the distance. Now the laws of attraction which bind the chemical atoms are entirely different. They do not vary. inversely as the distance. They differ greatly in different chemical conbinations, as is seen from the fact that some chemical compounds break up at ordinary tempera- tures, whereas it requires the electric spark to decom- pose the more highly stable compounds. This was the fact which I meant when I said that chemical laws were more selective in their combinations, and the law of gravitation absolutely universal. Mr. Peers under- takes to give his experience of these laws in Canada and the States. Such an experience is entirely irrelevant to the discussion; and, if Mr. Peers does it for my instruc- tion,l can assure him it is entirely superfluous, as .I have had experience of these laws, not merely during ply sojourning in Canada and the States, but also in China and Japan. It is truly surprising to find Mr. Peers exhibit sostroag a repugnance to discuss the question on it scientific grounds. Considering that, as a professed agnostic, he diverges so readily into the mazes of metaphysics, it might be thought that he would exhibit a stronger ten- dency to discuss the question on scientific grounds. Now, the question which I joined issue with him at the com- mencement was the pompous statement that the "linked concatenation of nature's laws" could not be broken in answer to prayer. This phrase was coined by himself ;it is the offspring of his own brain which, like an unfortunate bantling, he leaves to look after itself. Now, if Mr. Peers could pluck up moral courage to de- fend his premature but unfortunate offspring, it would inevitably lead to the scientific discussion of the question. But to Mr. Peers the scientific aspect of the question is especially obnoxious, for he stigmatizes it as a " red herring trailed across the scent," a most unfortunate eesignation to apply to one's intellectual offspring— "the linked concatenation of nature's laws "—consider- ing the pomp with which this premature bantling was ushered ito the world a tea, weeks ago. Now, whether Mr. Peers stigmatizes it as a red herring or as a green herring may not prove of much consequence, but the discussion of the question is absolutely vital and cannot .be blinked in such a contemptuous manner. If the linked concatenation of nature's laws is absolutely necessary and cannot be broken, then it is quite true, as Mr. Peers says, that prayer is useless. But it is equally true that, on such premises, it is useless to reason with a man regarding the right and the wrong, or the true and the false. Accordingly it would be absurd for a man to follow the dictates of conscience instead of the promptings of his lower nature, as the laws of nature cannot be broken, and cannot therefore be resisted. Moreover whatever the laws of nature have given origin to in the past they may do so in the future. Accordingly, as the lav f nature have, through the protoplasm of man's brain, originated mythologies and witchcrafts, &c., so may they do so in the future. On , such premises it would be absurd to try and improve man's mental and moral condition, as the laws of nature cannot be btoken. FinaLy, it is simply ridiculous for Mr. Peers to quote

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
SERIOUS ACCIDENT' AT CADISHEAD.

As Samuel Jenkins, of Cadishead, was walking home along the Ship Canal line on Friday night, he wa& knocked down between Cadishead and Irram, by a train consisting of an engine and a number of waggons. The whole of the train passed over him, causing a fractured skull. He was taken to the Ship Canal Hospital at Latchford, where be still remains.

div.head: FIREMAN DROWNED:
div.p: A FIREMAN DROWNED:

Another has been added to the already long list of fatalities which have occurred in connection with the Ship Canal. A fireman, emplbyeci on a dredger in the Bollin, was taking the damper off the chimney con- n.cted with the boiler on Wednesday morning, when, he slipped, and fell into the river, and was drowned. The body was recovered about ten o'clock the same day.

div.head: SAD DEATH OF A WARRINGTON MA N.
div.p: SAD DEATH OF A WARRINGTON MA N.

A man, Henry Smith, rope-runner, Bank Quay, who worked on the Ship Canal, met his death in a shocking manner on Tuesday morning on the Acton Grange section of the Ship Canal. It appear& that ha was sitting on the end of a waggon, trying to couple another one in iront of him, when he slipped and fell on the line, was run over, and almost instantaneously killed. His body was conveyed to the Latchford Hospital to await an inquest. An inquest was held at Latchford Hospital ye3terday morning.—Edward Murray, engine driver, said that on the day in question some waggons attached to a train he and deceased were on ran away while going down an in- cline, the deceased having neglected to couple them. Deceased was trying to couple the runaway waggons. when he slipped and fell between the rails. One waggon ran over him, but he managed to throw himself out of the way of the others. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."
MR. BRUNNER, ALP • AND THE
RUNCORN PUBLICANS.

Mr. Waterworth, of Runcorn, has received the following letter from Mr. Brunner in answer to the memorial presented by the deputation of publicans a fortnight ago : "Druids' Cross, Wavertree,Liverpool, Oct. 28th, 1891. —Dear sir,-1 have considered your letter of Oct. 20th I carefully. / acknowledge fully your right to combine for the protection of your interests, as I do the right of all tradesmen and workmen. I quite agree with your definition of the Direct Veto, but I have not heard that even the abolition of the retail sale of intoxicants, much less the reduction of the number of licensed houses, whether by magistrates or landowners, has caused much inconvenience, and the effect has always been exceed- ingly good. I cannot pledge myself to any scheme of compensation. If appeal is made to the law, the law is against compensation. If your appeal is made to my sense of right, I think that compensa- tion is due to the public rather than to the liquor trade. The declarations by eminent politicians on the subject mentioned by you were all made years ago. when men did not know the law as we know it ' to-day. I shall support the change in the law required to bring the beer-houses into line with the fully-licensed house which is advocated by Lord Randolph Churchill and others. The law declares that the most permanent improvements effected by farmers are exhausted in , twenty years. The beer-houses of 1869 have had 22 years' enjoyment. It is an entire mistake to say that we are in , ignorance of the effect of Sunday Closing. It has obtained in Scotland for very many years and in Ireland and Wales for 15 years and 10 years respectively, and the Royal Commission of 1889 which took local evidence throughout Wales was unanimous in its opinion as tothe effect of Sunday Closing. I am entirely at issue with you when you say that "the relation between the owner and occupier of licensed houses might be left to regulate itself if the fine were attached to the premises instead of the occupier." The existing relation between the tenants and the owners of tied houses (described by the "Times " as " unscrupulous monopolists ") is fraught with the most mischievous consequences, and is a mere trick to frustrate the law. I do not believe for one moment that the people of Runcorn have any vindictive feeling towards the publicans of the town. All that they desire, and all that I desire, is that the law shall be faith- fully obeyed, and that the mischiefs now arising from the excessive number of licensed houses shall be abated. —Yours faithfully-, John T. Brunner. Messrs. J. J. Waterworth, George Turley, and Arthur Hough. The following reply has been sent : " Egerton Arms, Bridge-st., Runcorn. 2nd November. Dear Sir,—Your letter of the 28th ult. to hand having reference to the deputation of the Licensed Victuallers with you, on the 20th ult. We are much obliged for your letter,which will be considered at a meeting convened at an early date, after which you will hear from us respec- ting your arguments in particular, and our action in general.—l am, dear sir, .1. J. W&TERWORTII.—J. T. Brunner, Esq., M.P.

div.p: L&NCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL

The Lancashire County Council met on Thursday at Preston; under the presidency of the Eight Hon. J. T. Hitbert. The date of the County Council elec- tion wao-fiked for Saturday, March 5, 1892. On a question with rega7d, to the muzAing of dogs, the Rev. L. C:-VVood said the order was now in force :only in the West Derby and the Salford districts. The Councilthad asked that the order should be al- ;together withdrawn.. Mr. Snape described the ;operations a the Technical Instruction Committee. IComplaints, he said, had been made that the Com- mittee did not give proper suppoit to secondary zelvools. When these sithools applied, their claire% would be fairly considered, but he thought they would not be ale to give a thorough, and effective support to such.schools till an Intermediate Edu— calon Act was passed.

div.head: CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.
div.p: CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.

Atlts quarterly meeting in. Chester. Castle, on Thursday, the Cheshire County Council discussed the desirability of establishing, in conjunction with several other counties, a special asylum for the reception of imbeciks or idiots under the age of eighteen. The matter was ultimately. referred to the Asylums Committee. A copy of a 'Otter ad- dressed by Lord Egerton of Tatton, chairman of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, to the chairmen of the various local authorities of the watersheds of the Irweill and Mersey,impressing upon suelvautho- rides the necessity of•enforcing the law against people putting solid refuse or cinders into ale tribu- tary streams, was laid before the Council by Mr. Duncan Graham (the chairman). Lord Egerton, in supporting his written appeal, mentioned that in the course of three months in one of the sections near Manchester 61,144 cubic yards were dredged out, but thaquantity of silt deposited by floods dur- ing the same period was 31.369 cubic • yards:. Mr. T. W. Killock, as one of the members of the Joint Rivers Committee for the counties of Lancaster and Chester, said that body wits doing all it could tv•en- force the Rivers Pollution Act of 1876,i and • would probably apply very shortly for stronger powers than it now possessed.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY..
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY..

The monthly meeting of this authority was held at the Workhouse, yesterdays morning. Mr. W. Long presided, and there were also present, Messrs. J. White, Heaton, Dobson, Aukland, W. Houghton, J. Houghton, Smith, Kilshall, Homplireys, Mather, Swinton, Jolley ; S. Sutton +(clerk), Dr. Sephton, (medical officer), W. Owen (surveyor), and P. liar- foot (inspector.) THE DEATH RATE.—The Medical Officer reported that the death-rate for the past month was 14.08, as compared with 18•07 during the past three months, and 17.2 in the corresponding month of last year.,. _

THE- LONGFORD DEPOT.—the Medical Officer reported that since their last meeting he had not received any complaint of nuisance arising fromiongford depot, and their inspector informed him that he had frequently. gone round there and the nuisance complained of last month had been considerably abated. That might have • been caused by prevalence of a strong north-east wind which had been blowing most dtzring the month, as well as to greater care in the management of the works. LAMPS FOR THE DISTRICT.---The Surveyor reported that several of the members of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee had visited Padgate, Orford, and Penketh. At Padgate they decided to recommend the Authority to have eight gas lamps fixed. At Orford the Inspector pointed out to the Committee the houaes which were without good drinking water, there being 47 without supply, and 11 _others without supply, but there being a supply within a reasonable distance. At Penketh the Committee decided to recommend the Authority to have 10 gas lamps fixed... This report was adopted.—Mr. W. Houghton afterwards moved a resolu- tion of which he had given previous notice, that the eharge for lighting be made against the districts lighted, and not a general charge on the whole of the Authority's district.—Mr. John Houghton seconded.—Mr. J. White proposed as an amendment that all parts of the Author- ity's district in which the mains of, the Warrington Cbr- poration were should be lighted with gas when required by a majority of the ratepayers, and that the charge be a general one on the Authority's •district.—Mr. Heaton seconded the amendment, which was supported by the Chairman.—On a vote being taken the amendment was carried by seven votes to six.—Mr.rW. lioughton thought. the decision come to was an uuf.ir nn, and he com- mented on what he considered over-representation of the extra-municipal parts of Warrington on the Author- ity. Whenever the account for gas lighting came up he should move the same resolution.

PLANS.—The Surveyor reported that the following plans were submitted, and might be approved as being in accordance with the byelaws.:—Mr. G. T. Gould, house at Great Sankey; Mr. H. Thornton, addition to cottage at Padgate. Mr. W. Wright having agreed to their conditions, with respect to the wooden erection for shop proposed on Liverpool-road, the plan might be ap- proved. Plans were also submitted by Mrs. Mercer, for two houses at Collins Green, but inasmuch as the pro- posed water had already on analysis been showmto be unsatisfactory, they could not be approved.—The report was adopted. This was the principal business.

div.head: RELIGION AND SOCIETY.
div.p: RELIGION AND SOCIETY.

A course of addresses on "Religion and Lie" was commenced in Cairo-st. Chapel on Sunday evening last. The Rev. Frank K., Freeston said these were the two greatest subjects which could occupy the thought of man. They could be considered separa- tely, as quite apart fromone another, or conjointly as most intimately related :and the former method had been the one too commonly adopted. But he would begin by making,two assertions, as the basis of all the addresses and the foundation on whicli they intended to build. The first was that religion could not exist by itself; but only in re'ation to life. As Ruskin had said, "'lf religion is good for any- thing it is good for everything." The second asser- tion was that life could not truly exist alone, but only in relation to religion. As another writer had said, "The man who has a religion, and be only,has life." If, therefore, religion and life were so insepa- rably blended,there could not be any possible part of life outside the realinsof religion, nor yet any sines. interest with which religion had no concern. It was concerned with social life, political li, commercial lire, recreative life, and artistic life, and to each of these subjects in turn: he wished to direct their at- tention and ask "What had religion to do with it r, In so doing he claimed that every reagious belie-zer no matter what might be his special theological faith, was bound;.not only to ask this question.. but also to find some.anewer.

Mr.-Freeston then proceeded to .apply the above considerations to" Religion and society." lie would not then define religien,and in speaking of society,he would include its. domestic, industrial, national and international aspects. If we believed in the Fatherhood of, God and the Brotherhood of Man, we ought to practise this belief in our actions and embody it in, our institutions. Whatever duties were admitted in . private life should also be demanded in public life. Personal, soaial, and industrial relations should all be governed by the same idealsar d• principles. Baia was this. the case?, No: society, speaking generally, was not governed by religious principles, but it ought to be, it could be, and it would be in the days to come asour srnse• of duty increased. He did- not imagine that any- one would dispute the truth of that contentioni and if they accepted that contention they were bound to put it into action. But then came the difficult question—what could be done ? They could help to demand better laws ;:the fact that they felt the want of them was the proof they were fit to receive them. They could take part in. great moral movements,, such as those on behalf at: temperance, cocial puzity,. prevention of cruelty, peace and arbitration, sanitary reform, and so 0n... They could do each of them a different thing in a different way to make society more of a brother- hood and less of a scramble and struggle. He who simply looked after himself and did nothing for others was not a. true Christian. But if only all. men would set themselves to realize their religion in their dealings with other. people, who could measure the mighty result 142 It would be the cul- mination of Christianity, the City of God on earth.
THE FATAL ACCIDENT AT A R,PLEIN STATION.

An inc Test was held at the White Hart Hotel, Sankey-st., on Saturday afternoon, by Mr. Brig- house, on the body of a pedlar named Michael Garland, 47'years of age, who was killed at Arpley Railway Station on Thursday. —Mrs. Gar- land said.! she- lived' at 9. Litt% Weint, Butter- market-st.,.und her husband was a pedlar, aged 47 years. She last saw him alive at half-past eight on Thursday morning, when he left the house saying he was going into Cheshire: lie was well acquainted with the station. They had lived in the town about 12 years. Her.husband wasa saber man,and had not " touched 'drink "for the last three months.—Wm. Foster said he was a porter in the employ of the Loudon and ,North-Western Railway,at Bank Quay. He found the. deceased on the down' line, at live minutes past seven on Thursday evening. He heard groaning on the down line; and went to the porter's room and gotoirlighi. They found him lying face down, with his pedlar's- basket lying near him.— George Ashburn Anice, porter at Arpley station,said he was ou duty.when the Mg; came into the station. He did not notice anyone go in front of the train. When he wentto Garland: he was not unconscious. Blood stains were found on the engine the same night.—Ann MiGowen, Ihilirmary nurse, testified that deceased was admitted to the institution at half-past seven on Thursday night, and died ten minutes after admission. He was injured on the back and head.,--A. verdict of " Accidental death ' was returned..

div.head: MR..PEARSON/S-ANNUAL CONCERT.
div.p: MR..PEARSON/S-ANNUAL CONCERT.

The third annual concert provided by Mr. It. H. ' Pearson, was givendn-thetic Hall, on 11, ednes- day evening, under distinguished patronage, and, like its predecessors; it was in every respect a great success. The halt was crowded, every available seat being occupied. The programme was an especially attractive one, including an unusually large number of really good English songs, while the vocalists-were efitheiiigitest c'ass. The artistes were :—Miss-Mary Davies, Madame Alice Gomez. Madame Antoinette Sterling„ Mr. Henry Piercy, Mr. Charles Chilley, . Mt. Maybrick (Stephen Adams), Madame Nettie Carpenter, (solo violin), Madame Zoe Caryll, from the Brussels Conservatoire, (solo pianoforLe),, and Sianey Naylor (conductor.) It should be •mentioned that the ante-room had beensuitably furnished; carpeted, and decorated, While the front of the orchestra,was adorned with a variety of ornamental Dlan is and terns, the whole effect of which was heightened by a number of coloured lamp,. wh.ch had been most tastefully arranged: The coiner& opened with a duet, violin and pi no, " Romantiache Stiicke " (Dvorak) by Mesdames Nettie Carpenter and Zoe Carvil. Both artistes acquitte& themselves admir- ably. Madame Carpenter is a born violinist; and she was loudly recalled4or her brilliant execution. later on, of the " Fantasie on Otello ' " (Ernst). On being recalled she substituted the " Chopin-Sarasate Nocturne," her exeentionof which lett nothing to be desired. Her contribution in the second part was a. " Chanson d' Amour ". b. " Jota Aragonesa," and she again delighted an enthusiastic audience with her clever double stopping and choice phrasing. Madame Caryll's pianoforte solos were" Rhapsodie " by Liszt, and la Vle,byCbaminide. Both of them were b illiantly played.. Madame Alice Gomez was the first to appear of' the lady vocalists, and she made a more than favourable impression with Sulli- van'a"Sleep,'lny love; sleep." She has a powerful flexible, and beautifully clear voice, which is under perfect control, while. her enunciation is admirable. In the s, cowl part she sang a new song by Stephen Adams, "Sweet Kildare," and had the advantage of being accompanied by- the composer. She was le- called, and, as the audience was not in the humour to be denied, she gave an additional song "At the fountain," also by-Maras. Madame Sterling was, scarcely up to her average in Molloy's "Voices,' but When she sang;the old Scotch song" We're all noddin," she roused' the audience to a high pitch of onthusiasm., This was followed up by "My boy Tammy," and of-both songs it must be said that they were rendered with that fine feeling, nice dis- , crimination,, and true dramatic instinct which area , only to be found in artistes of the highest class. Weatherly;s new song," The bee and the song,';,' introduced Mrs. Mary Davies to the audience. It is bright and perfect in its way,and it was brightly .and perfectly rendered'. The second song was the cld favourite, , "On the banks of Allan Water," which enabled the audience to compare her rendering with that of many famous vocalists; and it is due to her to say that she did not suffer by the comparison. She has a finei,clear, and well-trained voice,and ste is eapable MUT& of expressing the tenderest feeling and the utmost gaiety. She was especially lively and piquant in "Kitty," which followed upon an enthusiastic-recall. Mr.Mayblick's songs were !The three ages of love," and "The, golden guineas,':' the later his own composition. As an encore after the the last-named, he gave Els famous production, "They all-love Jack." He sang well, on the whole, though he- has a greater reputation as a. com- poser than as a vocalist, Mr. Charles Miley ,charmed. everybody by his charming rendering of I` the ever-green" Mary of !argyle." lie is a tenor of exceptional power and sweetness, but his voice can scarcely be, said to have been put to the beat use, in 'the second part, in "Au Revoir," which, is but an indifferent song. "If I could but forW thee," (Moir), was Mr. Henry Piercy's first song. He is deservedly a favouritoin Warrington, and on Wed- needay night, he was, as is usual with him, in ex- cellent voice. He afterwards gave a- thoroughly- characteristic rendering of " Kathleen Afavourneen, - and on being recalled he sang " Tho Thorn," with much feeling and loin greet power. The trio "Turn ,on,, old time, (Madame Gomez. and Messrs. Chilley and Maybrick),and the quintet "Blow gentle gales," (Meedames Davies and Sterling, and Messrs. Piercy, Chilley,and Mayhrick),ware both sung in tine atyle, Madame Sterling's contralto voice being used, with capital effect in the latter contribution. The duet "Cove and War,"by Messrs.Pievey and Maybrickwith which the concert closed,, was marred in its effect, through the disturbance of a number of patrons of the reserved seats, who left the concert while it was being sung. Dlr. Sydney Naylor acquitted him self most:satisfactorily as conductor; and it may be stated that the piano in use was a Bechstein Grand for which class of instrument Mr. Pearson is the agent in Warrington. The concert was brought to a closo. about a quarter past ten--in time for the speeial train to Latchford and Lynam at half past tea.
At the London Sessions, on Wednesday, George Lennex, describing himself as a journalist, was sen- tenced to twelve months' hard labour for selling indecerA prints, blocks, and manuscripts.

LIVESVdOL PROVISWItS, Fninat. —The Beef market rulesi quiet, with a slow demand passing. Pork his a slow sale at the quotations. Prices of Bacon are steadily maintained, and there is a better general Inquiry all round. Stocks of fresh landed meats are gradually getting Into small eompas„, Hams meet a free sale. and for fresh parcels of the cheapef brands, yesterday's prices cannot be repeated. In Shoulders' there more doing. Cheese steady. Rater without change. Lard is per cwt. higher in sympathy with America. MA-NCH/ER TRADE, Prang" —Vo-day, however, la, quiry is very limited. Cotton le not greatly altered. but "futures 'Y look a little better at the moment. "Spot," how- ever, is unchanged, and the day's business is eovered by the first estimate of 7.000 bales. Yarns•are not in great request, but spinners willh.g to meet the market may get business. In cloth the market is certainly not improving: China de- mand has almost gone out, and Indian offers are neither good nor plentiful. Good printers and finishing goods are very quiet. _

MUNICIPAL ELECTION, 1891. TO THE BURGESSES OF WHITECROSS WARD. -- LADIES and GENTLEMEN,—I desire to return you my warmest thanks for the renewed expression of your confidence by returning me as your representative tc the Town Council, I must also thank the gallant band of workers who have again shown themselves so earnest in the cause. Our opponents have not been over scrupulous ; but this will have no effect on my determination to do the best I can for all classes of ratepayers in the Ward. I remain. Ladies and Gentlemen, Your Obedient Servant, GEORGE PLUMPTON. Lovely-lane, Warrington, Nov. 3rd, 1891.

THE WARRINGTON WATERWORKS COMPANY. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that an EXTRA- ORDINARY GENERAL MEETING of the Warring- ton Waterworks Company will be held in the SMALLER Room AT THE PUBLIC HALL, RYLANDS-ST.. WARRINGTON, ON WED- NESDAY, rur 25.rx DIY or NOVEMBER, 1891, at eleven o'clock in the forenoon, for the following purposes viz. To receive and if it shall be so resolved to approve and adopt a final Report of the Directors and Statement of Accounts prior to the dissolution of the Company. To determine the application of the balance of moneys remaining in the hands of the Company under and in pursu- ance of Section 35 of "The Warrington Extension Water Act, 1890." To authorise the Directors to wind up the affairs of the Company, and to do all acts and things that maybe necessary or proper for the dissolution of the Company in accordance with the provisions of the said Act. MOURNING ANNOUNCEMENT. "THE LAST ENEMY IS DEATH." The custom of wearing black for the dead dates back to the time of the Romans. since when it has always been popular amongst Western nations. The great mortality of this coun- try. considering its sanitary arrangements, has given birth to a number of shops exclusively for the SALE OF MOURN- ING. These shops, subsisting entirely on one department, are compelled to charge exorbitant prices, as many a be- reaved one is able to testify, having found to her cost when the funeral was over, that she had made a bad bargain. Whilst making these statements we wish to draw the attention of Ladies to two facts :-1. That we are Manufacturers of Mantles, Costumes and Millinery, doing a large WHOLE- SALE TRADE in these departments, and that we supply our customers at the WHOLESALE PRICES. 2. Ours being a GENERAL TRADE, with a number of departments, we are not dependent on our Mourning Trade for the profits, and can consequently afford to sell at Lower Prices than our competitors. Our designs are copied from the latest Paris and Berlin models, modified to suit the tastes of our various customers. Every garment is thoroughly examined before being sent out, and for fit, finish, and style, we cannot be surpassed, whilst our prices will be found nearly half of those charged elsewhere. During the sale SPECIAL PRICES will prevail in this department. Ladies requiring deep or complimentary mourning will receive every attention, and they will doubtless be astonished at the value whieh they receive. BLACK CASHMERES. BLACK SERGES. BLACK CORDS. The annual sermons will be preached in St. Paul's Chapel to-morrow, in the morning by the Rev. Thomas Wilkes. The annual missionary meeting takes place on Tuesday evening, when addresses will be delivered bf Rev. Thomas Wilkes and Rev. W. Ripley Winston, missionary from India. FIRE AT RUNCORN. Early on Saturday morning a fire broke out in an out- house behind Ellesmere-st., stored with 112 bags of soot belonging to Mr. Dillon, sweep, of Egerton-st. The fire brigade extinguished the fire with commendable despatch. The smoke created a dreadful stench in the neighbourhood. The damage is set down at £l5, and is not covered by insurance.
